en: May Śrī, the illustrious Veṅkaṭanāthārya, the lion among poets and logicians,
the preeminent teacher of Vedānta, ever abide within my heart.

May the introduction of this treatise bring well-being; bearing in mind the teaching of the Lord of Śrīraṅga, I shall constantly instruct the disciplined in the commentary spoken by the Lord of Yogins, which rests solely upon the Truth, for the sake of devotion to Him.
I shall make meaningful, for the sake of many learned men, the title "Vedāntācārya" bestowed upon me by that Lord who has fashioned names and forms throughout the universe.
This [work] was composed by Veṅkaṭeśa, whose intellect is sharpened upon the All-Sustainer (Viṣṇu) and who possesses right vision through the two illustrious Varadācārya and Rāmānuja;
it should be served with the faculty of hearing by those of peaceful mind or by those seeking the attainment of peace.
He is perfected in the meaning of the Śārīraka [Sūtras], possesses innate and manifold virtues, and is a mass of milk from the speech-mountain.

Like a rising row of sunbeams dispelling the confusion, agitation, and distress of those who are bewildered, this work rises up— addressing the minds of those versed in the Vedānta— by removing from the collection of topics the faults of redundancy, contradiction, insignificance, incoherence, lack of subject matter, fruitlessness, and sublation of valid authority.
May this garland of verses, which has reached my heart, delight those who are attentive.
Who is so skilled as to be able to enumerate every object of knowledge within the profound realm of the Veda?
Even while showing only a mere direction, I should be scrutinized here by the wise.
Let there be no complete accomplishment; nevertheless, one who knows virtues [should look] at this vast and boundless jewel.
Is this a great pearl found in the ocean that has been discarded, now to be placed in the midst of a necklace?

First, the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*), whose meaning and logic are profound as the Veda, was mastered through various means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*): by way of distinctions, auxiliary elements (*aṅga*), application (*prayukti*), arrangement of sequence (*krama-viracana*), qualification (*adhikāra*), and extension (*atideśa*).
Thereafter, it was followed through all its specific details, including modifications (*ūha*), applications (*prāpta*), and cancellations (*bādha*).
Then, by means of the tantra and through its application, there follows the four-lakṣaṇī concerning the meaning of the deity.

Since the earlier dharma-section dealt with goals that were inferior and unstable, and its objects of inquiry had been pacified, and since it was joined with such [inferior] means of worship, one must now, in this section on the embodied self (*śārīraka*), investigate the Veda (*brāhma*) which possesses manifold greatness.

Why should one not first abandon ritual action and engage in reflection on the Veda, based solely on the initial understanding arising from the study of the entire *svādhyāya* along with its auxiliary sciences? It is not so, because there is no contradiction between the statements being of equal status.
There is a natural inclination toward the three aims of life (trivarga) first, because the practice of making one's efforts fruitful is a constituent part of spiritual discipline;

furthermore, in this scripture, which takes the form of an exposition, there is a fixed sequence determined by the order of primary importance. Here, [the nature of] the means of knowledge and so forth will be investigated later, while the meaning of the words is to be understood from the sentences.
If the example and the object of comparison are identical, then what is the purpose of placing "madhu" at the beginning?

Some have explained [the purpose] as the destruction of the three-fold suffering, while others [have explained it as] the fourfold means; in this section, the Veda recounts what occurred previously, ending with the consideration of ritual action as its fruit.

For the study of the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs indeed gives rise to doubt; what occasion is there here for other systems? This sequence is established by propriety, and not, moreover, by the application of a direct injunction.

"For that which is eternally attained and indistinguishable from the golden necklace already around one's neck, its acquisition is a delusion; it must be removed by the perception of its source in a mere fragment of scripture, and its cessation follows from that.
Thus, where is action of any use? Even the mention of its being an adversary [to knowledge] has been stated here in my discourse.
This manner of response was spoken at length regarding this idle chatter.

Some have seized the headless trunk of Mīmāṃsā, while others have grasped its head, which resembles Rāhu; yet what is the use of these wandering arms, whose intellects are stolen by internal contradictions?
Let us set aside for now the impelling of one's own rules and the rules of others through the entirety of study and reflection.
If there is a cognition of the entire falling [of the rain], why would those of refined intellect not perform a consideration of the whole?

Since the status of a single field of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) is established by the uniform assistance resulting from the necessity of a uniform effort toward what has been studied, it follows that they must form a single composition due to the expectancy associated with a fixed sequence.
Just as in the case of chapters and so forth, the difference in intermediate subjects and results does not constitute a division here;
likewise, a difference in authorship—contradiction regarding the meaning imagined through the defilement of the power of the Kali age—is likewise [no division].

If it is argued that because of the various distinctions such as specific attributes (*vaiśiṣṭya*), the deities mentioned in the earlier section are different, then how could there be a destruction of the prescribed sacrifice merely due to a difference in nomenclature?
Here, there is indeed a difference in the form of the objects to be designated (*uddeśya*) when the application (*prayoga*) of the offerings is stated differently.
But there is weakness in terms of substance and deity because the cognition is limited by the smallness of the skin and its object.

If it is argued that the many-fold contradictions shown here between what was stated by Jaimini and what was taught by the authors of the Sūtras prove that their status as a single Śāstra is forced, we reply: no, because of the firmness of the agreement between the two Bādarāyaṇas. Therefore, through the distinction of intended meanings (tātparya-bheda), there should be an avoidance of contradiction between the two sections (kāṇḍas) just as within a single section;

for this is established by the pacification of the confusion arising from words whose hidden intentions (gūḍhāśaya) were misunderstood when they appeared as objections to the Bādarāyaṇa [of the Pūrva Mīmāṃsā].

Having set aside certain doctrines established here in the earlier section that are to be refuted, some are to be explained, and in certain places, an exception to the general rule is to be made known;
thus, observing this uniformity in the method of inquiry everywhere with an impartial view, [the treatise proceeds].
If the treatises were one, the avoidance of redundancies and other such faults must be carefully considered by those who are attentive.

However, since the *Vṛtti* text attributes the sixteen-chapter work (*Ṣoḍaśādhyāyī*) to Jaimini, while the *Saṅkarṣa* originated from Kāśakṛtsna, how can the statement in the *Tattvaratnākara* be justified? To this we reply: we are not at all inclined to gratuitously contradict what has been well stated by that [author].
However, in some cases here, the application [of a term] is possible through metaphorical usage, provided there is a connection with a single intended meaning.
The enumeration in the *Sūtra* is auspicious, consisting of the sections on *Āśīr*, *Adhikāra*, and *Gaṇanā*, which is composed of consciousness (*cinmayī*) within the *Brāhma-kāṇḍa*.
Even though they are in immediate succession for that purpose, a distinction of topics (*adhikaraṇabheda*) should not be imagined by those of little substance. [The sequence is:
*Akṣomyā*, *Āśāhikā*, *Aṣṭādaśa*, *Gajamuni*, *Vasu*, *Mṛgāṅka*, *Tattva*, and *Atiśakvarī*.
In this [work], the composition of the *Pādanīti* consists of six *prayājas*, each having six syllables, and six *rasas*.

This treatise, however, consisting primarily of chapters concerned with the investigation of harmony, non-contradiction, and attainment, is divided into sixteen parts by way of the system of the sixfold divisions and so forth.
Among these, the first [chapter] declares the established subject matter; the subsequent pair [of chapters] deals with its opposite;
and the final [chapter] concerns the means for its own attainment—this indeed is the supreme Brahman, which is to be contemplated therein as well.

In that [work], in the first chapter, there is the discussion of words for the soul (*jīva*) and so forth—ranging from those that are extremely obscure, indistinct, distinct, to very clear—and subsequently, the unimpaired cognition through memory and other means; then the status of being an effect regarding the sense organs and so forth;

the presence or absence of defects in the third [chapter]; devotion and its limbs for the soul and others; and finally, meditation on the ascent of worship, its power, the process of departure, and the fruits.
May He protect us—He who is the embodiment of bliss, established in His own nature, possessed of infinite majesty, free from all contradiction, the refuge and the goal;
who, through the self, the ether, and the senses, brings about appropriate creation during the process of emanation while acting as the underlying principle of the system;
who is delightful due to His faultlessness and other virtues, the object of manifold worship, and one who is propitiated by the actions performed for His sake.
In this context, that which is to be known is that which cuts through evil, effects the movement through the brahman-channel, flows intensely, and bestows equanimity.

Having studied the Vedas according to the injunctions, and having desisted from ritual action by the force of those very injunctions, those who investigate the entire Mīmāṃsā system in due order cross over to the contemplation of the Supreme Brahman. Yet, in this present fourth age (Kali Yuga), where strength, intellect, vitality, and the means for such practice are seen to be limited— [The verse continues: ...the path of the Veda is obstructed; the world is overcome by the Kali age, and the scriptures are hidden by the darkness of ignorance. Therefore, O King, you must protect the path of the Veda, which is difficult to traverse and obscured by the darkness of the Kali age. For the sake of the world, establish the true meaning of the Vedas, which has been lost through the confusion of various doctrines. You alone are capable of rescuing the world from the ocean of suffering caused by false views. Thus, O King, you must protect the Vedic path, which is the source of all dharma and the foundation of the three worlds. May your majesty, like a great mountain, remain firm against the waves of the Kali age and preserve the light of the Vedas. By your grace, may the world be freed from the darkness of ignorance and attain the highest goal. Thus ends the first chapter, concerning the protection of the Vedic path, in the *Rājatarangiṇī* composed by Kalhaṇa. [Note: The provided text fragment appears to be the opening of a commentary on the *Rājatarangiṇī*, specifically the first verse of the first chapter.]
Because they cannot endure the waste of time, some fortunate ones find delight in the end immediately.

If it is argued that one should investigate for oneself out of passion and thus what is the use of the teacher’s words here, we say no; for the rule of approaching a teacher exists for the sake of attaining knowledge of Brahman, since he provides instruction on reality (*tattva*).

Furthermore, this is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) ascertained by those skilled in logic, because it proclaims that just as there is a teacher for the *sadvidyā*, so too is the realization of the Supreme Brahman obtained from a teacher; thus it is studied [in the scriptures].

If [the self] is already established, there can be no initial linguistic proficiency regarding it, nor is the application of definition and so forth appropriate in this case; what then is the use of a scripture for that which is already established? Furthermore, there would be no fruit for the listener in a cognition of what is already established.
Thus, when the inquiry into that [self] is paralyzed by the argument that the Upaniṣads are not means of valid knowledge like the Vedic injunctions, [the opponent objects].
He composed the commencement of the treatise by means of four appropriate types of reasoning contained within the four aphorisms.

If it is argued that since there is no derivation [of meaning] for established entities (*siddha*), like the word *svaḥ* (heaven), and since the result is obtained through the breaking of the primary sense (*lakṣaṇā*) by means of an *arthavāda*, then even that which is known through inference may be partially known from scripture;

and furthermore, since there is no contradiction even if it serves as an injunction (*vidhi*), a statement concerning another object might be a means of knowledge regarding its own literal meaning—[we reply: the straightforward and eloquent author of the Sūtras does not tolerate such a wretchedness of argumentation (*anvāruhya-ukti-dainya*).
In the beginning, it was stated that the generation of comprehension regarding the supreme reality in its established form occurs through two [means];

subsequently, the doubt regarding their futility was refuted by means of the scripture and the cognition produced therefrom. This ancient path, which follows the natural inclination of the various commentaries based on propriety, should be followed.
Some say that one [of these] is for the purpose of commencing the treatise, while others say that all three together constitute the treatise.
That which was counted by the noble Seneśvara, composed in verse by the servants [of Śrīraṅgam],
and clearly explained twice by Vyāsārya and Viṣṇucitta—
I too have heard it from the learned Vādihaṃsāmbuvāha, as if from the Śeṣakalpa.
Therefore, it is certainly established that the *Caturadhikaraṇī* is useful for the investigation of the Brāhmaṇas.
Some [schools] state here that the first and fourth systems (nayās) transcend [the others], yet this is unattained;
for if awakening is not established, how could one consider its fruit here as if it were already accomplished, due to the dullness of such an assumption?
Furthermore, that which they know as the two middle [systems] having form and name as their objects of production is also weak.
When a matter has been stated and required, a futile division of it is not appropriate in a treatise on ethics.
Thus, the introduction of the scripture is for the sake of action;
since initial proficiency is necessarily directed toward that end, all its words are solely intent upon it.
There is no other principle even in the Veda; consequently, the Upaniṣads are as good as barren soil.

When it is thus objected that an investigation into that which is already known is therefore not appropriate, [the author], having established [the need for inquiry] by demonstrating through many avenues that there is an initial lack of proficiency [regarding Brahman], declares that Brahman is the object to be investigated.
Pointing with their fingers at this or that object while employing various expressive parts of speech,
adults instruct children, knowing that the capacity to convey meaning arises through a sequential process. These clusters of words produce a cognition regarding some established, qualified entity.
If [the word] "also" (ca) occurs in reference to something to be done, then in some cases here, a restriction based on the power of the word itself need not be postulated.

In this beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), as one repeatedly experiences [objects], latent impressions (*saṃskārāḥ*) are accumulated; and the factors that awaken those impressions fall upon [the mind] spontaneously from an unshakeable stream.
The mental modifications (*vṛttayaḥ*) suitable for grasping the specific differences of various corresponding classes have those [impressions] as their cause.
Likewise, in the linguistic dealings of teachers and others, a child’s comprehension of things such as "novelty" (*aidamathyam*) occurs in that same manner.
Various types of training, whose diverse applications for one's own efforts are inferred by skillful mahouts and others, are employed by those who cause elephants,
birds, and other creatures to learn them; therefore, such specific forms of training exist among humans and other beings as well.
If that which is declared in the scriptures is not a kalpa, then how can any other path be considered a kalpa?

When one who has attained a certain goal strives to communicate that very object to someone else through gesture, he speaks it to him; another learns that word because it falls within the range of his intellect. If one here elaborates upon a matter for the sake of instruction as commanded, it is indeed appropriate for that specific purpose.
If it is argued that one who knows the truth exerts effort based on those words, let that [knowledge] be independent of instruction.

From such statements as "this is your son, not a serpent," the restriction of the object [of meaning] may occur in some cases through signs such as joy or fear, preceded by an attachment to that which is appropriate for it. Furthermore,
the power [of words] (śakti) restricted to each individual word would also be established here through the distinction of insertion and deletion (āvāpa-udvāpa).
In this context, the assistance provided by repeated observation and so forth is no different from that which pertains to the side of the effect (the probandum).

Let it be granted that there is an initial acquisition of proficiency regarding the effect; nevertheless, do you maintain that proficiency regarding the action occurs prior to the establishment of the word’s power (*śakti*) and intention (*tātparya*), while in the case of human speech it is otherwise, whereas in the Veda it is different?
Therefore, the power must be established by means of correct usage (*satprayoga*) which is invariably concomitant with and not otherwise accounted for (*ananyathāsiddha*).
"Who is this Pāñcāla?"—such is a sentence that possesses appropriate pauses, even when it consists of only a few established words.
Since the fruit [of the injunction] is established within the injunctions themselves by way of a result such as a location not mixed with suffering,

let the fruit— even though it belongs to an explanatory passage (arthavāda)— be accepted because it is based on the Veda (śrauta), just as "establishment" is the fruit in the Rātrisatra sacrifice. We accept that non-beneficiality belongs to the object of prohibition in accordance with the prohibition itself.
Therefore, even through the explanatory passages (arthavādas) which possess their own meanings, the Vedic cognition shall have an unerring object.
Thus concludes the section on the inquiry [into Brahman].

If [the Cause] is qualified by "origination and so forth," there is prolixity; if you say it is merely indicated (upalakṣya), then difficulties regarding whether it is known or unknown become entangled, and no examination could take place regarding that which has not been indicated.
Therefore, in this context of investigating the meaning of the word "Brahman" as it was introduced, how can it be so? Here, the Cause is what is indicated.
The meaning of the word "Brahman" has been stated as the storehouse of virtues, the destroyer of sin, and the one celebrated in the Puruṣasūkta and other scriptures.
The various characteristics of the individual (cella), their inherent distinctness, and the genus (brāhmaṇya) would constitute the qualifiers;

while "khaṇḍa" and "muṇḍa" [along with] "cow" (gaur) would be the expressions for the qualified object. Here, there is a unity of the word denoting the property (dharma). If, among these, one were like the others when combined, it would be fruitless because of the loss of that which is to be excluded (vyavacchedya).
Because of the sequence beginning with fragmentation and so forth, and because of the non-contradiction of the unreal, there is a distinction such as fragmentation and the like.

That which distinguishes [an entity] is necessarily restricted to the exclusion of its own respective opposites; there is no contradiction with other [definitions], as there is no conflict due to differences in time regarding production, persistence, and destruction.
It is easy to state that each [of these] individually serves as a definition here; the abundance of examples is for the sake of the greatness of our intellect.
Some, even when acting together, say that the result is the exclusion of those suspected meanings.

If it were already known, it could not be indicated; if it were unknown, it certainly could not be, since there is no perception of its connection with a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, the distinction between the known and unknown portions is difficult to express here except through a defining characteristic itself.

If Brahminhood were perceived even through the application of the word "Brahmin" to one who is known [to be such], then there would be no doubt regarding others. But if it is not so, then there is doubt.
Do not say so; for [the truth] is found in the glorious words of Brahmā, which pacify the doubts arising from various scriptures.

"As long as there is no comprehension of the qualified object (*lakṣya*), that which is understood from the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) must be the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*); and even if that [qualifier] is not understood, if the qualified object is subsequently understood, how could this [object] not be the indicated (*upalakṣya*)?
Therefore, the objection raised by the ignorant person—on the grounds that the two-fold interpretation permitted in the *Bhāṣya* is inappropriate—is [unfounded]."
In the case of different objects of meditation for the sake of liberation, both [meditation and non-meditation] apply, because there is an optionality regarding knowledge.

O children, just as a branch appears on a tranquil, vast moon, so too does the characteristic of being the cause—its qualities having been effaced by such statements as "That from which [truth, knowledge, etc. arise"—shine forth when it has reached the shore [of the Self].

The elders learned in logic know that here, in this single referent, the meaning resides in the qualificand (the subject), while the words, restricted to each individual term, provide a covering through various specific causes, just like the reasoning regarding the dawn-colored [sun] and so forth.

This entire universe, characterized by causal efficiency and governed by a fixed sequence of manifest and unmanifest applications, leads one to infer that it was projected by an omniscient being; thus, through the force of inference based on parsimony, [the Creator] is postulated as endowed with sovereignty born of karma. In this regard, investigation by means of scriptures is fruitless. Thus is he inferred.
In accordance with the tradition of Viśvāmitra and others, he has here delineated the All-pervasive Lord, who is to be known through the scriptures.
It is argued that the earth and other elements, being effects characterized by such qualities as being produced, must have a creator— just like a bracelet or a crown—
and that this creator is established as one who perceives atoms, the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), and so forth, and is omnipotent; but this is not so,
because there is no such universal concomitance (*vyāpti*) as the desire to perceive fragrance and the like through the ears and other senses.
One may not see every cause here, as a potter [does not see all causes for his work], yet by that much he is not a non-agent.
"All this, being an object of dispute, must have an omniscient creator as its antecedent because it is an effect;

for that which is not so [is] not so, like a human being"—this argument fails because there is no absence of other possible explanations (*anyathāsiddhi*). When such a reason is employed, the difficulty of unestablished pervasion (*vyāptyasiddhi*) and the like is insurmountable for those who do not know; thus, in the *Tattvamuktākalāpa*, the various definitions [of God] are shown to be subject to refutation.
Although the inference of another's self and so forth occurs through various types of logical marks (liṅga),

the method of universal concomitance (vyāpti) established by perception is certainly not relaxed in any variation of the subject (pakṣa). Thus, according to the principle of the statements of such authoritative persons, the marvelous declarations in the sacred tradition (āmnāya) are not false.
Due to the equality regarding the absence of sublation and so forth, there may be figurative usage and the like in that which possesses contradiction, as in the case of common worldly experience.

[Objection: Surely, those for whom the sacred tradition (āmnāya) is paramount sometimes recount that the Supreme Creator is to be inferred from tasks impossible for beings such as ourselves; let that [scripture] be the intended meaning of the "origin and so forth" (janmādi) aphorism.
Therefore, it is improper for a follower of the Veda to abandon the inference of God. [Response: No.

Because [the word] "somewhere" (kvāpi) refers to the teaching of propriety (*aucitya*), and because [the word] "since" (*yataḥ*) is a restatement established by the reasoning concerning existence (*sad-ukti*).

When the meaning of the *hr̥daya* (the heart) is stated as something to be performed, there would be no fruit for the listener if it were already established; however, when its fulfillment is achieved through devotion, why would even a false statement not be seen as having that purpose?

If it were merely for the sake of knowledge, then—since it is observed by others to be like an object—it would not be true upon examination; thus, in response to this objection, he declares that the purport of the scripture lies in the unlimited bliss which is not subordinate to anything else.

Even if there were a unity of purport with the truth of Brahman through some non-prescribed method, or even if there were a difference [of purport], [the analogy] would not hold because it remains unproven; thus, there is no equality with the statement regarding the number of teeth of a meat-eater.

Since being for the sake of one's own pleasure is compatible with falsity, the thought "it is not false" is not possible; for even in cases such as coaxing children, joy arises precisely from the cognition that the object exists as it is [in reality].
The statement that "all speech uttered for the sake of pleasure is entirely false" is like the talk of children;
for one who perceives bliss in speaking the truth, there is no subversion here—either through direct perception or through scripture.
Therefore, by refuting the doubt that the subject matter of untruth consists only in speech whose purpose is not otherwise established, [the author proceeds].
The three Vedas are authoritative, as they are established in the Supreme Brahman, which is Truth, Eternal, and Wondrous.

Some maintain that the words of the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* regarding the "rendering free from phenomenal proliferation" (*niṣprapañcīkaraṇa*) are injunctions for meditation; others say they are intended as injunctions for meditation; and still others declare that they are figurative expressions of non-dualistic statements devoid of attributes (*nirdharmādvaitavākya*).
These [theorists] have many confused prattleings that contradict their own positions and their own words.
This eon is a secondary eon (bāhrakalpa) that has been crushed by the councilors and attendants of those possessed of perfected intellects.

If the *arthavāda*—which previously had another purpose and was established as a means of praise—were now being made authoritative independently, then there would indeed be a contradiction between the two sections. But this is not so; for it was stated first in a general sense for the purpose of establishing its status as a valid means of knowledge.
For some, it is said that their own purpose is achieved here, O fortunate one, through the mere awakening [to reality] by itself.

In all the Vedas, where the division is fixed into three parts, the sages have declared that even the four types of *arthavādas* are supplementary to the portion of the *brāhmaṇas*, by means of the distinctions of the injunctive (*codanā*) and other portions.
If it is argued that this statement regarding their being supplementary contradicts the Smṛti, know that the answer has already been given:
for this is a general statement, since it follows the subsequent mention of their distinction from both mantra and injunction.

Since the confidence in the scriptures is established for those of extremely refined intellect through the study of augury, astrology, and so forth—which are traditionally accepted as having faultless and fruitful results pertaining to this life—and also through activity directed toward the hereafter;
and since there exists verbal cognition regarding the supreme object which is free from defects and sublation; [therefore, the scriptures are authoritative].
Otherwise, how could there not be a repudiation of the path of the Naigamas? For that [object] is not, by its own nature, a source of pride (māna) therein.
This small section consisting of four chapters has been commenced to establish the validity of the undertaking of this treatise.
The two specific characteristics of the object [of knowledge] mentioned here are applicable, as they depend upon what is yet to be stated.
For in the section concerning causality, one would indeed say: "The Supreme is to be known through the teachings of the true Veda and other sources."
He will further explain such [qualities] as "bliss" and so forth in the chapters concerning the two genders and others.

When it is thus understood that [the Self] is not created within oneself or in another, and when it is established solely by the scripture as the cause of the universe, characterized by being the object of unconditional, supreme love—
then such a state may appropriately belong to both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, for they are not objects suitable for inference and other means of knowledge.
And since those two are untouched by suffering, the subsequent discourse proceeds in due order.

Because of its association with the secondary sense of "seeing," the observation of becoming many is not the primary meaning; nor does it appear here through examples and such that an inference would be established, for birth from such [a cause] is illogical.
Therefore, it is incorrect to claim that the word *sat* denotes the root-prakṛti, which is itself unevolved.
Because other [views] are refuted by scripture and by signs such as those that contradict what you yourself accept.
When one [element] is known, it is said that "everything is known"—this proposition is for the sake of establishing unity.
Furthermore, the triad consisting of clay, its effects, and so forth, is mentioned here as distinct varieties of that illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*).

Therefore, the claim that "thereby the inference of the unmanifest is stated" is a vain longing; for no reason has been stated, since the possibility [of the inference] is mentioned here only after the refutation of reasons such as similarity (*sārūpya*) and the like.

Through the words "Ādeśa," "Atman," and "Sva," which do not restrict the locus [of the Self], and through the teaching of identity with the suffix "-tvam" (thou), He— though devoid of ego— enters the multitude of non-conscious things along with the individual soul and its ego;
thus, by the statement "by the knowledge of One, all is known," and by the expression of identity with all,
the All-knowing One, whose form is the universe, becomes manifold even through the various branches of knowledge and other means.
If direct perception is desired, let it be so; however, that [perception] applies to the reality of the individual soul (jīva-tattva) which is appropriate for it.
For in the Sadvidyā, through three words, the identity of that [individual soul] with the Existent (Sat) above has been stated.
Now, Viśvakarman begins his discourse in order to pacify this [view] arising from such reasoning.
Herein is established the inner self of even the individual soul, consisting of unconditioned great bliss.
It is incorrect to argue that because the suffix *mayaṭ* was previously seen in the sense of "modification" (*vikāra*), it must likewise apply here at the end;
for its usage in the middle [of the passage] is observed to be otherwise. Here, the suffix should be understood as expressing abundance (*prācurya*), since any other meaning is precluded.

Furthermore, the abundance of bliss is established by the fact that the happiness of others has reached its limit in being minimal; this does not depend on the minimality of suffering, because it contradicts the nature of the Ruler, who destroys the misfortunes of others.

The statement "this very one is his Self" is said in order to express that this [Self] alone is not of another nature; and the mention of the "embodied one" (śārīra) with respect to Him would be an unrestricted application, because He is the body of all.
That [Self] is to be purified in accordance with various purposes; thus, for the All-pervasive Lord, there is merely the state of being propitiated by that [purification].
Upon reaching this [state], for the knower of the Supreme, there is an entry into the ocean of bliss in the form of attainment.

If it is argued that since this [Brahman] is bodiless and partless, it cannot possess a head, wings, a tail, or anything else, and therefore the statement "the tail is the support" refers here to the Supreme Brahman appearing as such—[we reply: if the designation of a "tail" is accepted, why would the other [parts] not be admitted? The mention of the Self as the support for Brahman must be understood as intended to declare its lack of dependence on any other substratum.

By the power of the vast accumulation of exceedingly infinite merit, there arises, according to the logic of Śakra and others, a continuous stream of lords who possess bodies endowed with the aforementioned abundance increased threefold.
Such a ruler of all men possesses greatness born from a divine form produced by [the ripening of] karma.
This very one, who was described as "he who is heard" within the eternally glorious solar orb, is indeed this single [Self].
The *Antarāditya-vidyā* states that [the Lord] has spoken to all the creators (*kalpakas*);

therefore, let there be a connection with merit for the Lord who grants permission for the remainder—do not say so. He is traditionally taught as one who is not to be commanded by another, whose fruits are self-dependent and for others; he is not merely this much.
The word *pāpman* may also be used for merit (*puṇya*), as in the passage beginning "even through the connection with auspicious marks, there is no good deed," and so forth.

That which is renowned as pure *sattva*, some indescribable, stainless substance distinct from the unmanifest (*avyakta*), is that very form— the divine form— which shines in heaven along with Śeṣa, the consumer of remnants (Garuḍa), and others. That God, who is eternally served by the sages and who never abandons His own essential nature,
transforms Himself for the sake of quelling the worldly existence of men through various manifestations preceded by His cosmic emanations (*vyūha*).

If it is argued that [the body] is non-existent because it possesses the nature of a body, because it consists of the seven elements and the three impurities, because it is a source of sin, existence, and suffering, and because it has parts—this is not so, for such an inference is contradicted by the subject (dharmin).
Contradiction would never occur regarding that which is known solely through scripture; otherwise, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) of the argument.
And as for that which he displays during his voluntary incarnations, even that is for the purpose of subduing the Asuras.

Although, by means of these three Vidyās, there may be a state of even greater transcendence than the unmanifest— the cause of all— and even than the individual soul (jīva-tattva), which comprises both the moving and the unmoving, sentient and insentient beings— nevertheless, in this chapter,

the author extols its attributes through a series of topical sections (adhikaraṇas), gradually restraining those who begin with mildness but end in cruelty, according to the different doors of emergence.

That singular Consciousness, which is designated as the Cause in the Upanishads by such primary terms as "Sat" and "Brahman," yet is conceived through various mental constructs— such as the practice of creative will— which are inconsistent with its true nature,
and which are expressed by names residing in the causal state that appropriately give rise to misconceptions of it being the elemental ether and so forth.
Having cast that away, he enjoys [the teaching] by stating the impossibility of the arising of the entire collection of scriptures remaining as mere footnotes.

however, the word *jyotis* (light), being conventional, denotes the Person characterized by divine splendor.

Subsequently, well-known words such as *indra* and others are restricted to that [Person] through a function based on those specific attributes. Thus, this section consists of pairs of words, following the sequence of the functions of words.

In this context, the ether (ākāśa) is seen in the *Sāman* as the ground of the origin and dissolution of all things; it is indicated by its own name in the *Taittirīya* as well, through the statement of its own birth from no other source.

Let it not be so, for this is a restatement of what is already established; moreover, since the state of being attained by the Supreme and so forth does not belong to that [ether], the Self is its creator. For it is well known in this world that the body and so forth are dependent upon the vital breath (prāṇa); therefore, its status as the cause [of the body], as stated in the Śruti, is firmly established by its conventional meaning (rūḍhi-śakti). in the third, intent on declaring "He is the Self who is the support of the universe," He is to be investigated through reasoning;

and in the fourth, the delusion arising from the recitations of the Sāṅkhya and other schools must be uprooted—thus some have declared the three quarters, and this too is for the mental composure of the listener.

Furthermore, according to the logic of the preceding section, self-restraint is appropriate here; thus, at the commencement of the discussion, the Great Sentence (Mahāvākya) unifies [the teachings] in accordance with what was stated in the introduction.

This is true; however, having granted the authority of the *Brāhmaṇas*, there may be a dispute regarding whether [the passage] belongs to a particular *Upaniṣad* or is to be imagined as belonging elsewhere.

Because qualities such as being born from That (*tajjatva*) have not been stated, and because various distinctions of attributes are observed, omnipresence and other qualities would indeed belong to the Self by its own nature; however, its atomicity (*aṇutva*) is assumed here for the sake of meditation upon the Greater One.

Even though it is taught in the Kaṭha Śruti that "the Self indeed is the enjoyer of food and the like," this [Self] might not be so, because of the statement regarding its dissolution through the swallowing of all things—both moving and stationary—drenched by death.

Furthermore, the exclusion of the individual soul (jīva) is known from the context; however, the designation of both as "enjoyers" may be due to their fixed roles as the impelled and the impeller, according to the analogy of the "umbrella-bearers."

The Paiṅgi-śruti, by distinguishing that "the knower eats the essence without eating," holds that the *sattva* is either the intellect (*buddhi*) or the vital breath (*prāṇa*). However, this is not true here; for if there were only one living being (*jīva*) who drinks between those two, then this scriptural mention of *sattva* would be appropriate for the living being as the enjoyer of karma, even while not eating. Do not say so; for the term *sattva* is properly applied to the living being as the enjoyer, yet it is "not eating."
This sequence of questions, intended for another purpose, was also spoken by those of former and later times.
If it be argued that this "Person in the eye" mentioned in the *Chāndogya* and other texts is either the individual soul (*jīva*),
or the deity of the eyes (the Sun), or a mere reflection— this is not so; for [the text] teaches,

"This indeed is the Brahman, this is the Immortal, the Fearless, this is the Bliss, the Void," and so forth, and because of the force of the established rule regarding its being the "Abode of All Desires" (*saṃyadvāma*) and other primary attributes, as well as the logic of the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*).

In the case of those scriptural passages that are elevated by [the principle of] independence (*svātantrya*), there is no doctrine that only that which bestows a fruit is an object of knowledge; for even the knowledge of the "vision of the auspicious" (*kalyāṇālokanādi*) possesses purposefulness by virtue of the force of an injunction.
Therefore, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is logical that the person within the eye is a reflected image.
This same method should be inferred as applicable, as far as possible, to the preceding and subsequent sections as well.

Do not entertain such a doubt. For [the knowledge of Brahman] is not limited by its constituent parts (*aṅga*); indeed, many aspects of it have been described as pertaining to those parts. Furthermore, the fruit mentioned here is stated to be in accordance with the knowledge of Brahman, whereas previously there was no mention of the vision of Brahman.

If it is argued that the Inner Controller (antaryāmī) is the individual soul (jīva), because of the statement that he conforms to the mental modifications dependent on various instruments and because of the scriptural declaration "there is no other seer," this is not so, because [the scripture] excludes any other controller.

Furthermore, the nature of being a "seer" and so forth consists essentially of the intellect (dhī) as structured by its respective objects; for these attributes are primary in the Lord alone, as evidenced by their mention in the Kāṇva and Mādhyandina recensions, and his very self is the body.

Because they occur in the same context, the two terms *ātmavijñāna* found recited in these two branches have one and the same meaning; thus, even when [the opponent] speaks of that, he is merely speaking of his own intellect, which is therefore meaningless.
For, by following what is well-established in common worldly usage and in the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*), these two [terms] are focused solely on the conscious [Self];
there is no sublation of this by anything, and through such passages as "there is no destruction of the existent" (*sataḥ... vināśaḥ*), there is a state of perfect harmony (*sāmarasya*).

The negation of "visibility" and other qualities occurs in the Imperishable (akṣara) which possesses transformation, due to its proximity [to the context]; let the "Imperishable" mentioned in the fifth case be that which is beyond each respective limit, namely the twenty-fifth principle, and not the Supreme. However, the first-mentioned Imperishable, characterized by omniscience and so forth, is the pure Brahman.
However, the soul and so forth mentioned later serve as the limit (avadhi) for that distinction, because they were spoken of by him [the opponent] as being distinct from it.

[if it is argued] "not so, because of the scriptural study of the *br̥hatī* [metre]," [we reply] that the word "fire" (*agni*) applies due to its connection with the body and the world.
Or rather, due to its specific distinction, the cognition of another [fire] regarding its own form, as well as the cognition of the Gārhapatya and other fires, is an auxiliary to the ritual action.

It is not the case that for the wise, the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) ever occurs through the vision of one thing in another; therefore, this Vaiśvānara is not something other [than Brahman]. [Objection: But the fruit is the attainment of food, success, and so forth—[we reply] it is not so. For here, by the very word "Brahman," which is joined with the vision of the other, the destruction of all evil is stated as the fruit; moreover, the supreme Brahman is the pervasive food.

Among these three [Upanishads], for those who worship here, that which is within the space between the eyebrows and the heart-cave is said to be the object of meditation; then, in the other three, that which is of vast and immeasurable extent due to its being the inner controller (antaryāmin) of the universe and so forth is to be meditated upon.

Furthermore, in the six [Upanishads], the words *brāhmaṇa*, *ātman*, and even the term *puruṣa*—by virtue of the restrictive context—bow down through their conventional application to the Cause of the Universe, which is distinguished from the field (kṣetra), the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), and the phenomenal world.

For it has been previously stated that everything arises from being produced by That (Brahman), and that the Lord’s nature as the inner controller of all and His having the universe as His body have been declared.

Therefore, the author of the Sūtras has here refuted, through sound reasoning, the entire web of trivial and drunken ravings that wander aimlessly in various directions, such as those concerning the contradiction of the oneness of the universe.
Abiding in every way through the state of being the self-dependent cause of the existence, maintenance, and activity of all beings;
having swallowed everything yet remaining eternally imperishable; possessing a universal body with fire and other elements as its limbs;
and being the object of the first definition as Vaiśvānara, whose limbs are the worlds beginning with the celestial realm.
In the second chapter, Śrīnivāsa, the crest-jewel upon the heads of the multitude of Śrutis, has been proclaimed.

The excellence of the Brahmins shall be established, and the delusion regarding the oneness of cause among the gods shall vanish.
In this chapter, exactly seven principles (nyāyas) directly converge as they relate to the subject matter beyond [the individual soul].
That Self, which is the support of all and the abode of its own majesty, is the ground of the intended meaning (tātparya) therein.
For the sake of establishing that [Self], the teaching and other [principles] have been stated here; they are interwoven with one another and should be reflected upon.
And the state of being the Lord of All is measured by the sixth method and protected by the final system.

This has already been established in the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* through the statement of the supreme Brahman and the mention of its distinctions based on differences in attributes; so why, at this inappropriate juncture, does he grind this flour into a paste once again?

True, the suspicion regarding a difference in procedure arising from the vivid attributes of the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) is addressed by means of words that establish recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), thereby uprooting it so that it never arises again.
If it is argued that he in whom the mind, together with the other groups of organs, is woven; who is manifold;

who is the support of the channels (nāḍīs); who moves within with the organs; and who is the enjoyer of karma [is the Self]—this is not so, because of his being the soul that supports the universe, because of his bestowing immortality, and because of the teaching that he is the object of delight for the liberated.
Because of the identity with the previously described process, and because of the manifestation accompanied by fasting, there is the attainment of another [state].

If it is argued that the eye is strung upon that [Supreme Self] which pervades all, then what of its birth? Its birth is said to be by His will; moreover, He exists as the supreme one in the form of the heart, being the navel of the network of channels (*nāḍīcakra*).

Or, there may be movement within Him who is immovably pervasive, through auspicious forms in this world, as in the case of the *Saubāla* recension; or this "movement" may be merely a figurative designation (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

To Nārada, whose grief did not cease due to his ignorance and longing for the Self, Sanatkumāra addressed these words regarding the vital breath (*prāṇa*): "This living being (*jīva*) is not fit to be harmed.
If it is argued that this very [Self] is indeed the one who possesses little opposition and infinite bliss, [we reply: no.
Here, that which is denoted by the word *satya* is taken as *hrū*, to be meditated upon as superior to that called *prāṇa*.

Let it be granted that the instruction concerning the Self under discussion finds its resting point in the vital breath (prāṇa), which is mentioned as something additional through the force of the answers and the questions regarding everything from Name up to Hope;
but let it not be so, for here the vital breath is described as having been produced from the Supreme Self, just like Name and the rest.

In the phrase "from itself" (*svasmāt*), it cannot be so [that the case ending denotes the ablative], because the case ending is natural (*svārasikī*) and thus not subject to grammatical modification.

If it be argued that the seer of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the "one who speaks beyond" (*ativādī*), and because he is impelled by repeating that [breath], he is a speaker of truth; therefore, the vital breath alone is the "I" in its entirety and the progenitor of all beings—this is not so.

Because the statement ends with "But this one indeed," the present speaker is distinct from the previous *ativādī*; for here, unlike the former, the status of being an *agnihotrī* is appropriate as his own abode of greatness, and thus the attributes of dharma are logically established.

In the passage concerning the "Bhūman," it is understood that the Prāṇa is the Supreme Self, the controller of all, who is Truth.

The statement regarding the heart being the size of a thumb-joint, which is the abode of all living beings, occurs in certain instances as a description of its measure within the context of human eligibility during the discussion of the Supreme Pervader.

In the context of praise (*stuti*), there may be a twofold function: one directed toward the virtues of oneself and the other toward those of another. Of these, the former is indeed worthy of respect; however, even in the latter case, the primary factor must be determined by those of sharp intellect as being merely a single part of the whole nature [of the object].
Furthermore, in that [latter] sense of "pleasing" (*rucy-artha*), there can be no act of pleasing through the speaking of falsehoods, for one who is not deluded would not do so.
"What praise could there be for that which is already an established reality?"—thus the Sage spoke in order to preclude figurative interpretation and the like.

How could those [beings] capable of attaining various bodies be unfit for the simultaneous presence of their karma in this world? When their respective histories exist, there is no non-eternality in the Śrutis due to their continuity.

The mention of an author at the beginning of the *Kāṇḍas* is restricted to the act of teaching, since the eternity of the Veda is established; thus, the Lord would teach the Vedas even during the creation of the phonemes, following the sequence of previous Kalpas.

If, due to the notion that the Vedas are the Lord’s [creation], you maintain that the restriction of sequence is intended to vary according to different *kalpas*, then the same would apply to the portions consisting of mantras; yet that is certainly not appropriate, because they are equal to the *vrīhi* grains, *soma*, and so forth.
Thus, whether the rule regarding sequence is considered as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) or as an optional one, such being the case—
This school of Akṣapāda has reached the pinnacle of the assembly of rival doctrines.

Due to subtlety, equal intensity of contact, simultaneous removal, obscuration, displacement, extreme proximity, extreme distance, suppression by a stronger force, non-arising, and impairment of the sense organs—

even present objects are not perceived; likewise, even the various well-known supernatural powers (siddhis) of the hosts of gods, resulting from birth, austerity, yoga, mantras, and medicinal herbs, are not perceived due to the power of concealment (antarddhāna-śakti).

It might be argued that, just as with a mere deity, there is worship of another alone; yet even so, one's own self would be the object of propitiation, where even one's own status is the fruit, and thus there is no qualification for this [worship].
Do not say so; those desiring liberation worship Him as the inner Self of all and as their own embodied soul.
Yet, due to desire, one revolves even from one's own station [as a god], with the fruit [of that state] lasting only until the beginning of a kalpa or an intermediate aeon (manvantara).

According to the path of the *Apashudrādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning Śūdras) as stated by Jaimini, there is no attainment of knowledge or the sacred fires for Śūdras and others; nevertheless, their eligibility for the practice of devotion to the Smṛtis is established.
This is because they can listen to the *Mahābhārata* and other such works, and because of their performance of duties appropriate to their own birth. Thus, [the objection] is untenable.
When the instruction regarding the Veda has been obtained, the initiation, the touching [of the body], and so forth are well known.
The hearing of the *Mahābhārata* and other such works by Śūdras is permitted for the sake of attaining the pacification of sins and other benefits;
for it is not the case that they would fail to gain a preliminary understanding of the meaning of the Vedas through them.
Furthermore, the Lord Murabhid instructed the eighteen branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) to the Pāṇḍava (Bhīṣma).
Since these are neither visible nor tangible, those of impaired intellect do not possess the qualification for worship.

The singing of Śūdras and others, as well as their exclusive devotion to the Supreme, is established through the religious duties appropriate to them; thus were Dharmavyādha, Tulādhāra, and Vidura perfected by the practice of previous births.
By addressing Janaśruti as "Śūdra," the speaker reveals his grief;
for his Kṣatriya status is indeed made more clearly known by signs such as his command over the Kṣatriyas and his royal prerogatives.
"Having shaken off [the body]"—here, the one previously mentioned in the preceding statement would be the liberated one named "Space.
First, he bears name and form during bondage, and subsequently, he abandons them upon attaining the state of Brahman.
This is illogical; rather, this very one who was previously mentioned must be understood as being taken up here by virtue of his essential nature (*hrupātta*).
The state of being a Brahmin is not found in the Vedas, nor are omniscience and ignorance simultaneously distinguished therein.

The Soul of the Universe, infinite in magnitude, the ordainer and sustainer, whose very nature is the object of enjoyment for the liberated; who consumes all things while being their own support; the ruler of all through His state of immeasurable existence;

the one to be worshipped by gods and others, served as their own Self by the deities headed by Vasu; the Lord who is not fit to be worshipped by Śūdras and the like; and the sole creator of names and forms—He was awakened here.

In the fourth quarter, the collection of statements determined to have another as their primary subject— though they clearly exhibit marks such as the individual soul (jīva) and so forth— is shown to follow the shadow of that [primary] meaning;
therein, by means of six and two methods respectively, he pacifies the doubts raised by the Sāṅkhya and Yoga systems.
Some have stated that "ghaṭṭau jāghaṭṭa" is thus the eighth conclusion (nigamana) that has been described.
By two [verses], the primary doctrine of Kapila is to be cast aside; then, by one [verse], the number stated by others is refuted;
by the fourth, the all-pervasive Lord is established as the ultimate limit through the function of the doorways;
and subsequently, the pure and impure souls must be excluded from the pair of substrates.
The remainder [of the refutation] is contained here in this eighth section of the fourth chapter, which effects the rejection of the Īśvara mentioned in other systems.

It is incorrect to claim that the *Kaṭhavallī*— having distinguished between the insentient, which culminates in the unmanifest (*avyakta*) such as the senses, and the *puruṣa*, the ultimate limit of the principles (*tattva*)— expounds the method taught in other supreme scriptures; for therein, various things to be mastered and the primary sequence are declared through numerous statements.
The Supreme Person, who is here described as Viṣṇu of peaceful nature, is made known through recognition.

The objects are not the nature of the senses, nor is this mind the cause of them; nor is it held that the intellect (buddhi) produces these [objects], nor does the Great One (mahat)—known as the intellect—arise from the Great One.

It is logical that "greatness" belongs to the enjoyer; for there could be no selfhood in the intellect. By process of elimination, the term "unmanifest" (avyakta) refers here to the body; thus, there is no recognition of the system of Kapila here.
The independent capacity of the unborn (aja) to produce everything is indicated [by the term] in certain passages, such as:
"Bound here, the unborn sleeps; then another unborn one leaves this [world] whose enjoyments have been experienced.

If it is argued that this is merely a Tantric usage and not a statement of the mere fact of being unborn, then the well-known lack of independence would not preclude even the act of creating from being prompted by another.

In the statement "in which [world] five," the twenty [puruṣas] enumerated by others are said to be increased by five; however, let it not be thought that the group of puruṣas mentioned here in the seventh [verse] is devoted to nothing else.
This is because space (ākāśa) is mentioned separately by its own name, and thus the power of the seventh case is not sublated.
The statement "the sixfold [breath] is here the support of all" is restated according to the injunction by means of the Brāhmaṇa and other texts.

In the *Nigama*, the compound "this [is] shame" (*hrayam*) has the designation (*saṃjñā*) as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). According to the rule of the seven seers (*saptarṣi*), there is a pentad consisting of the breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, ending with the mind (*manas*), which is determined by the context and known as the group of cognitive faculties (*dhīndriya*).
By the word "light" (*jyotis*), this is what is known in other recensions; however, the deficiency [in the number] is to be supplied.
The word "food" (anna) denotes the nose, while the word "life-breath" (prāṇa) denotes the tongue as well as the skin.

If it is argued that the Vedic declarations regarding "being," "non-being," and the "unmanifested" (avyākṛta) refer to the material cause of the universe, and that these terms apply to the "unmanifest" (avyakta) mentioned by others [the Sāṅkhyas], and therefore all other [Vedic] passages should be interpreted accordingly here [in the Upanishads], we say: no.
For where non-existence and so forth are observed, they are understood through the context [of the passage] to refer to [an opponent's view] such as omniscience and the like.
Although it has been studied that "the linga must exist," nevertheless, in this context, the word "ātman" and so forth remains uncontradicted.

In the statement, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent," only the state of dissolution is expressed; even such passages as "nothing at all existed" are likewise intent upon dissolution, since they negate the void and so forth.

Because everything is unmanifest due to the absence of differentiation, that which is the inner self of the multitude of substances in such a state is here denoted by terms such as "existent," "non-existent," and "unmanifest."

From the statement, "He whose karma this is, he is [that]," it is understood that [the Self] is subject to karma; thus, the claim that He alone is the agent of the transformation of what is created by Himself is refuted at the outset.

For Ajātaśatru, who was teaching Bālāki something whose inner reality he did not know, such a declaration of knowing that [Self] would be purposeless here; therefore, the word *karma* is used here in its primary sense as "action" performed in the world.

Thus, when the subject matter is restricted to that which is distinct from the individual soul (jīva), the mention therein of the "individual soul" and the "chief vital breath" (prāṇa) does not cause any harm here; for in that context, meditation is indeed upon [Brahman] as qualified by them.

Furthermore, according to the principle stated in the section concerning the "Horse-sacrifice" (vājivākya), even the vital breath and its enjoyer are mentioned as the substratum for the sake of making Brahman known—this is the universally established conclusion.

The Śruti reiterates that the husband and others are dear for the sake of fulfilling the desires of the Self; thus, it is understood from the context and other indications that the Self is the enjoyer of the fruits arising from merit and demerit.
Indeed, this proclaims the Lord’s dearness to those [beings] by His will, as He is the bestower of their respective experiences.
And this [Self] must be seen for the sake of liberation; here, it is made recognized through the collection of scriptural texts.

Through etymological derivation, the word *ātman* expresses the Supreme Brahman; or else, through its contracted meaning, this word *jīva* expresses the Supreme by means of a secondary function (*dvāravṛtti*). These are the alternative views. Āśmarathya [asserted their identity] on the basis of the unity of the individual manifestation; Auḍulomi [asserted it] on the basis of non-duality in the state of liberation; and Kāśakṛtsna spoke of the word *jīva* as having the Supreme as its object because the individual soul abides within that Supreme.

It is incorrect to say that this embodied soul attains the state of Brahman upon the removal of the limiting adjuncts of difference, because the perception of that difference persists as long as one has not transcended worldly existence; for the terms "equality" and "similarity" [imply a distinction], and the sequence of clay and its effects is contradicted by hundreds of scriptural passages. Therefore, the term "living being" (jīva) refers to the Lord.
Because he abides in that [Brahman], Kāśakṛtsna [held this view]; thus, this is the established doctrine of Vyāsa.

In this world, the potter and others are the distinct agents of the lump of clay and so forth; likewise, the Primordial Cause (Ādikartā) is not the material cause (*upādāna*), because it is devoid of modifications (*vikāra*).
It is not the case that [the Self] becomes a modification merely through the example of clay and the like, for such a modification would apply only to the secondary form (*svarūpa*) of the Supreme.
Because its activity has been shown to be like that of transformations such as the spider and the body-portal.

The Lord, through His own knowledge and other powers, becomes the source of what is produced by Himself and brings about His union with others; for when that union resides in material form, Primordial Matter (prakṛti) also serves as its instrumental cause due to its activity.
At the outset, the single One thinks, "May I become many," and this manifold becoming is established by the principle of Saubhari;
here, there is no contradiction between the scriptural texts on difference and non-difference, owing to the connection of the unity of the qualified [whole].
For when the effect is one, the proposition is established, and a corresponding collection of examples is cited;
thus the Śruti declares that [the Self] intended "May I be many" and became trees and so forth,
and says "He made Himself by Himself," thereby stating that He is the source of all beings.
Therefore, the Lord is both the agent and primordial nature, the inner self of all principles.

We know that there is no other cause for that [effect] apart from its material cause (*upādāna*) or its efficient cause (*nimitta*); it is illogical to claim that what is established as an efficient cause does not partake in the nature of a material cause.
This is because, through the distinction of desired forms and the integration of both [causes], this accords with both worldly experience and the Vedas.
Once [the goal] is accomplished, the crooked path of fashioning one's own arbitrary insignia is merely the ripening of the thought of cooking [what was already done].
Having thus described the dissolution of the other principles into darkness as being merely a state of oneness,

and having declared through Vedic and post-Vedic statements that primordial nature (prakṛti) and the spirit (puruṣa) are beginningless and so forth; the statement regarding their dissolution— that "these two dissolve into the Supreme"— should be understood according to the analogy of water merging into water.
Therefore, this creation of the universe, consisting of the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and so forth, is perfectly consistent with that [consciousness].

Some read as follows: "The dissolution at the beginning shines forth somewhere in one whose word is infallible; and when all its own effects have been swallowed up in darkness, it is Śiva alone"—this collection of such statements is for the purpose of suppressing the doubts that clearly arise regarding this matter.
With his mind solely intent on instructing his disciple, he extends by analogy the previously mentioned varieties of policy.
If Viśveśa (the Lord of All) is indeed the Lord of Śrī (the Goddess of Fortune), how could he have the authority merely to protect?
Having gone far away, he too would suffer; thus, by comparison with Fate and Śiva, this [world] would dawn like the collapse of a shopkeeper’s stall.

Do not say so! For our Supreme Person, whose prowess is limitless and vast, this is but a dramatic performance (*nāṭaka*) imitating his own glory, even while in states such as that of a fish. This is the case for the Lord of Brahmā, the Destroyer of Kāla.

Because it employs the methodology taught by the Sāṅkhya, because it accepts their theory of creation, because it adopts their system of *prasaṅkhyāna*, because it identifies the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*) as described by them, because it speaks of its own "sin" (*vṛjina*), because it attributes defects to its own fruit, because it distinguishes between the agent and primordial matter (*prakṛti*), and because it hears of multiple causes such as Druhiṇa and Śiva— the [Brahmasūtra] refuted what was stated in the first three quarters; however, by revealing the two-fold nature of the Vedas and Brahman, it protected [the truth].

Since the nature of Brahman— the embodied soul consisting of the stable and the moving, the conscious and the unconscious— is established as the object of inquiry, this natural direction of the words of the causal scriptures is well-expressed [by the Sūtras].
Those who, being Musalyas, describe here in various ways the sublation and obstruction of other extensive [scriptures]...
Let them be expelled from the other side, so that the stability of the Upaniṣads may be established.

Let it be that the desire to know [Brahman] is set aside for now, and let the statement of its definition, struck down by many obstacles, be tolerated; we shall even endure the prattle regarding the "source of the Śāstra," provided there be a declaration of concordance (*samanvaya*).
Yet, in the view of non-dual identity without distinction, these sūtras—with their clear meanings and specific statements—[do not hold].
How could there be a doctrine of difference between Prakṛti and Puruṣa through their own attributes, such as the primary faculty of seeing and so forth?

Although the attainment of satisfaction for those of great intellect, who are skilled in the methods of such various systems of logic, may be achieved through what has been stated, yet, fearing that those of duller minds might fall into the trap of mere rationalism,
[the author] confirms the status of Brahman as the cause by means of the "pillar-digging" method.
Whatever kind of effect-ness is understood by those who desire [to know], that is precisely of that same kind for that [effect].

In the second [verse], he avoids the repetition of the pair of feet (*pādadvandva*) for another reason; through the medium of the effect, the pair of other feet arises to pacify internal agitation, which would otherwise cause pain to the arms.

First, there is the breakdown of the connection of the cause here in the case of the Lord, because of its universal applicability; subsequently, that [avoidance] bears fruit by casting off what is eternally heard [in the scriptures].

When the primary meaning of the Upaniṣads has been suppressed by the shadow of the Tantras, another person now rises up today, claiming that because [the Upaniṣads] are weaker than the Tantras, one must follow them. This being the case, here [in our response], we shall cross the armies of those various Smṛtis and systems with [arguments] appropriate to each.
Having warded off [the attack] with counter-weapons, he makes firm from its very foundation the purpose that had been shaken.
It has been established in the *Karmakāṇḍa* that the Vedic scriptures possess immutability when the methods of the Smṛtis are set aside;

therefore, this discussion for the sake of proving that [immutability] would again be futile from the second pāda onwards. Do not say so. For one who perceives that following [the Smṛtis] is appropriate here—given their profound and difficult-to-comprehend nature as determined by the peaks of various Śrutis—through both the words of the authoritative ones and through reasoning, there can be no contradiction.
With two [verses], he removes the contradiction with Smṛti; then, with eight [verses], he removes the sublation by reasoning (tarka),
and thereby he confirms the Lord's status as the material cause and His agency—
these two being established through the principle of the simultaneous depression of one end of a balance scale and the elevation of the other.
One whose mind is intent on investigation within the category of doubt restrains partiality.

This sage Kapila, who is wise and celebrated in the Śruti itself as an incarnation of Vāsudeva, is renowned in the Rāmāyaṇa and other texts; he, whose intellect is skilled in profound contemplation, declares the reality of Vedānta.

Therefore, since that [truth] lies beyond our reach, its extraction must come from the very words of the Upaniṣads (the "head" of the Śruti). It cannot be established through the many faultless verses of Manu and others, for their purpose is not uniform, whereas the true meaning is established therein.
In the beginning, the Creator (Vidhātṛ) obtained the Vedas from the Blessed One; he is Vāgīśa, appointed over all branches of knowledge.
Therefore, one who holds the Vedas aloft experiences trembling at their violation or loss.
Let it not be so, for even for him, there is the sight of calamities such as the theft of the Vedas and the impairment of his own faculties, due to his state as a mere field-occupant (kṣetribhāvāt).
We resolve, as before, that error and the like may occur in cases where there is no other possible recourse.

It is argued that the universe must possess the three qualities (*traiguṇya*), because it has arisen from that which possesses the three qualities; for it is illogical that there should be no emergence from what is not so.
However, it is not tenable that there should be equality in every respect, as equality with something [in some respect] is accepted.
The systematic arrangement of causes and the equality of qualities appropriate [to them] are shattered in cases such as the scorpion produced from cow dung.
If the Lord assumes grossness by taking on the form of Prakṛti, then all objections are refuted.

When the objection was raised by those of dull intellect— that "I shall become many" (as read in the case of *sat*), which is observed in the instances of fire and water, implies that the world must possess similarity (*sālakṣaṇya*) with them—
the proponent [of the Sūtra] stated that this "seeing" (*īkṣā*) belongs to the Supreme Being in His respective forms; thus, he denied the existence of such a statement [in the opponent's sense].
The proponent here asserts that the designation "possessor of conceit" (abhimānin) is used in a general sense.

In order to dispel the defects of fraudulent arguments— consisting of mutually contradictory points and hollow pretenses— when those of dull intellect speak of the sequence of dogs and boars, asserting that "the universe must have atoms as its cause" according to the schools of Akṣapāda, Kṣapaṇaka, Kaṇabhuj, and Bhikṣu, based on their mutual agreement; ||| [this work is composed].
May the sun of the Vedānta shine for us, who, like a lion among elephants, destroys the mass of darkness consisting of false doctrines.

If even for that single body there exists one who is the sole experiencer of various pleasures and pains, then how could the body of the Lord— who is the universe itself— fall into the experience of universal suffering?
Thus, those who partake of the "sheath" (kośa) of the scriptures intend to ignore the boundary between the individual soul and the Lord.
May he who perceives both equality and inequality attain tranquility here, according to the policy of a sovereign and his servants.

If one says that the effect is something other than the causal substance—like a mat from its constituent reeds—and thus the activity of the causal factors would otherwise be fruitless, this is the assertion of the non-believer in persistence (the *adṛḍha-vaināśika*).

Let all this be granted even if there is identity of substance, on account of the difference in its intended states; for the non-existence of the effect is established by perception and parsimony (*lāghava*), and the identity with the world as taught in the Śruti is declared through the absorption of the universe into Brahman.

Those for whom the phenomenal world has its root in the Supreme Brahman, which is intermingled with the power of its own limiting adjunct (upādhi) consisting of Māyā— they too validate the scripture of non-duality here,

because [the adjuncts] are subordinate within that which is qualified by this or that [attribute], and likewise [they do so] regarding us, where the Inner Self is primary over Nature and the Person (prakṛti-puruṣa).
In this sentence, there is a connection between the gross and the subtle; thus, the non-differentiation of the world from [Brahman] is established.

Fools, however, vainly imagine that at the beginning of the universe there is an illusory transformation (*vivarta*), a partial modification (*pariṇati*), the birth of what remains as potentiality (*śaktiśeṣa*),
the manifestation of individual forms (*vyakti*), the emergence of diversity (*ullāsa*), or an unrestricted transformation (*vikṛti*) within the series of principles (*tattvapaṅkti*),
taking these to be the natural state based on fragments of various scriptural passages.
Those who know the reality, being devoted to the uniformity of all scriptural revelation, have set these [other views] aside.

If the position of non-difference (*ananyatva*) were asserted, then consciousness (*cit*) would also be subject to transformation; consequently, the identity of that [consciousness] with the individual soul (*jīva*)—as understood from such texts as "That thou art"—would be undermined, and the individual soul would become an ocean of suffering.
One who is not deluded does not create his own suffering, nor does he do so for sport. This is not so;
for non-difference is taught by way of coexistence (*tātsthyena*), since it is established that both consciousness and the unconscious are the body of That [Brahman].
When the agent and the material cause possess the capacity and the collection of instruments is present, they accomplish the effect;

therefore, one might ask: "What could that which is already existent and unitary bring forth as an instrument? [The answer is: this is due to the differentiation of non-existent capacities (*asac-chakti*).
One should find satisfaction in this by observing the examples of milk, the magnet, the spider, and the faces of the gods and sages.
By mere volition alone, the individual soul impels its own body, and likewise the Lord [impels] the universe-form.

If the Supreme transforms in its entirety as the effect, nothing whatsoever would remain; if it transforms only partially, then the scriptural teaching of His partlessness (*niṣkala*) would be contradicted—this remains true even if He is considered qualified (*saviśeṣa*).

If it is argued that [the Supreme] cannot thus be the material cause (*upādāna*) of Brahman, we say no, because this fault applies equally to your own positions. Since that [material causality] is grasped through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), accept that it is established by scripture, just as it is in the world.

For if one asserts that the effect called "conjunction" must occur between the all-pervading [Self] and the other [the body], or among atoms themselves, either in its entirety or by parts, that position is refuted; thus speaking, one would sink into the doctrine of emptiness (śūnyavāda).

The Sāṃkhya also declares Prakṛti to be all-pervading; how then could there be a creation of limited things from it? Such arguments apply equally to Māyā and the like. Therefore, the path proclaimed by our own scriptures remains unimpaired.
The creation of the universe could not possibly be for his own sake, as he has eternally attained all desires;

nor does the creation of suffering arise from compassion, nor is it a remedy for one who is omnipotent. Therefore, the claim that an omniscient being, satisfied in himself, is the cause of this world is a blind objection.
This [Lord] acts for sport like an ordinary person at the time of his own resolve, having attained all desires through the perfection of his will.
