If it were held that the playful activity (*līlā*) of one who constantly creates a universe that is both discordant and entirely composed of suffering would follow an improper sequence, then faults such as cruelty (*nirdayatva*) and the like would ensue.
This is not so, for [the Lord] possesses a beginningless flood of karma, which gives rise to the discordant succession of seeds, sprouts, and so forth.
Because he brings about such-and-such fruits for living beings, there is no abandonment of either compassion or equanimity.

If one were to postulate a distinction between the conscious and unconscious principles of the entire universe based on observed logic alone, there would be confusion regarding the necessary pervasion required to establish the presence of those very properties that oppose one's own desired conclusion.

However, when the existence of an omniscient creator is established from a scripture authorized to speak of matters entirely beyond perception, all properties are logically consistent, being supported by a valid cognition that is immune to sublation and other defects.

He refuted [the Sāṃkhya position] that had arisen on the grounds of its contradiction with the Smṛti of Sāṃkhya, its subversion by the doctrine of injunction (Vidhi), the dissimilarity of the effect, its being contradicted by various systems propounding a single object, the non-separation of the body and experience, the distinction between the material cause and the effect,
the subversion of its own benefit, the loss of the collection of causal factors, the contradiction of the inference regarding the whole and its parts, and the fruitlessness of action.

It is improper to say that one who is free from passion would repeatedly utter slander against others while remaining unshakable due to the absence of contradiction, when the Vedic doctrine of the Veda being the cause [of knowledge] stands firm; rather,
it is for the sake of pacifying the lingering doubts of many renowned Easterners at every moment.
The "neutralization by counter-argument" (prakaraṇasama), which is established through the delusion of equality, is to be refuted in the Tarka-pāda.
The Sāṃkhya system of the *Ṣaḍvaśālambin* is clearly recited in the *Mahābhārata* as being equal to Yoga;

for it is declared that "the twenty-fifth [principle] abides therein" as the inner self of all principles. Therefore, having established the *Seśvaratantra* as understood from the Vedas, [the author proceeds] with the aphorisms.
But he refutes that position which disregards the Lord, by means of arguments that entail severe retribution.
Establishing categories such as the Unmanifest through the means of inference, how could the Sāṃkhyas not find consistency in their own intellect within doctrines such as the thirty-six principles?
Examining the objections and solutions that are equally applicable to the conceptual constructions of those who are liberated from the constraints of Śruti, [one sees their lack of foundation].
They do not deny what has been perceived; they infer the minor [details] and expect the remainder from the scripture.
Some effects are seen to be produced by weavers and others, while everything else is heard to depend upon a creator; yet nowhere is there observed a contradiction to this dependence on another,
as in the cases of the lame man, the blind man, the drinking of milk, the ocean, grass, clouds, lightning, wind, and the magnet.
Through these examples, all that you desire does not bear fruit for us; rather, everything is presided over by a conscious being.

But surely, at the beginning of the treatise, it was stated that even insentient things depend upon an agent for their respective functions; why then does the supreme author of the Sūtras inquire after the inference of a creator?
Listen attentively: this question is not at all trivial, for [the opponent] cannot infer an omniscient creator.
And he thought that it could not be denied, because no restrictive rule governing both of those [alternatives] was observed.

Those who postulate the distinct substances such as *sattva* and the rest through the combination of the three *guṇas*, how could they explain their eternal omnipresence and the resulting states of equilibrium and disequilibrium? Furthermore,

how could the postulated mutual superimposition of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*— intended for the attainment of enjoyment and liberation according to the logic of "falling shadows" and so forth— be possible if both were insentient?

This fruit for men—beginning with worldly enjoyment and liberation—is all located in *pradhāna*; yet here, the capacity for seeing and so forth is attributed to the *puruṣa*, while the capacity for distinct perception and so forth is attributed to the *buddhi*.

The Sage composed the scripture for the sake of the liberation of one who is bound; thus, to say "I am eternally liberated" is a mutually contradictory statement. Let the devotees of the Jains mutter this at the marriage of a commoner!

Having stated that it is undesirable to postulate a single, supreme, and vast primordial material cause (*upādāna*)— based on the observation that the multitude of various atomic material causes possesses a body no greater [than its parts]—

he now refutes the theory of world-creation originating from subtle atomic substances and dyads, which is governed by a Lord (*seśa*), after having already rejected the transformation of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) devoid of the supervision of an intelligent being.

Long before the statement regarding "origination" (ārambhaṇa), the Kaṇādas' fabrication of non-existent substances concerning the object of negation now strikes down the various aspects of their causal process;
for when the cause is divided into three parts, those who rely on inference [must account for] each respective part as appropriate.
In this [work], he explains through the sūtras various states such as contradictions and the sequential progression of conceptual constructions.

Even those who, following the form of what is perceived, establish through inference that the produced atom is at least a binary atomic compound (dvyaṇuka), would not be able to assert its partlessness and so forth;
for everything is sustained within the subtle, which is the object of the light of the net [of reasoning] for those devoted to valid cognition.
Or one might proclaim those portions [of the teaching] as being without fruit; however, such a traditional teaching (smṛti) must be interpreted through indirect intention (anyaparya).

If there is no rest anywhere due to the infinity of the multitude of parts, and if it is argued that the mind would thus be equal to a mountain of black beans, then [we reply]: because of the gradation of their magnitude, there is a difference in the infinite as well; for a fixed inequality exists among things beginning with a fortnight and a month, and it is not undesirable even among those that are infinite.
And why has the priority and posteriority of two classes not been mentioned, given that they are equal in their infinity of individuals?

For those who resort to the path of the *śaktis*, nothing else—such as the grace of a deity—is seen [as the cause]; since it is distinct from that, its postulation at the outset has been rejected by the knowers of truth as requiring excessive effort. If one were to assume that even when effort is present, there is no dependence on further effort, then the same would apply to the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*).
Thus, in the doctrine of the unseen residing in the elements, the hypothesis of an unseen force inherent in the atoms that produce the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is here cut down.
Some have declared that relation is eternal, pervading all things as inseparably established;

others say it is eternal among eternal things but lasts only for the duration of life among non-eternal things. For those who speak of the fixed nature of each respective pair [of opposites], there would be no such systematic distinction by means of that [relation].
But the postulation of another [cause] would be cumbersome; how could there be no fault of infinite regress for those who accept [such] additional factors?

If the category of substances—consisting of both composite wholes and atoms—is shaken off by the authors of the Sūtras, then the universe, whose sole defining characteristic is pervasion, would either be the "Supremely Great" (the Infinite) or else non-existent as a substance.

Let it not be so; for the perception of atoms and their aggregation, as well as the establishment of the relationship between those two, remain uncontradicted. Furthermore, scripture also proclaims that the world originates from adventitious elements such as earth.

In this first pāda, the Guru refutes that portion of Jaimini’s system concerning the practice of rituals— which was rejected by him on account of its contradiction with the Vedas— and instead establishes the portion concerning the ultimate reality as reasoned by them. Having previously discarded the views of the semi-nihilists (Ardhavaināśikas) through unconditioned principles of logic,
he now proceeds to destroy the positions of the nihilists (Vaināśikas) by refuting the doctrines of the Buddha and Śiva.
Śrīdhara, in his own treatise, has calculated that Buddha, along with his own incarnations, is indeed omniscient; he would not for a moment wish to deceive anyone throughout the entire land of Suhma.
Therefore, if it is argued that the Sāttvata and other systems fall into inconsistency when confronted by the refutation of what was spoken by Buddha—this is not so.
Because [the deity] engages in delusion and other [afflictions] with the intent to crush those who oppose his own desired object.

The desire to delude is irresistible even for the Creator of all beings; otherwise, how could there be delusion for us? Therefore, He bestows either the fruit corresponding to one's karma—whether it be the realization of truth or delusion.
This is established by His own words and other evidence. He is not partial toward anyone without cause; therefore, His speech is impartial.
Out of compassion, He does not intend to deceive, nor would the fruit be devoid of sin if it were not dependent on Him.

Some who know the Sugata’s doctrine maintain that the Buddha is to be conceptualized; some say he is directly perceived within the mind; some say he is to be inferred from the form of cognition; and some declare that the object of awakening is false.
By the same logic, others have stated that even the intellect is established as being merely conventional.
Today he subdues all those teachers of the Daityas, such as the Vaibhāṣikas and others, by means of reasoning and valid cognition.

The Vaibhāṣika has asserted that the manifestation of aggregates such as the earth and the body arises either from atoms possessing one, two, or more natures, or from those possessing a single nature each.

In that case, because of the momentary disintegration [of the atoms], the functions of cognition, grasping, and so forth, as well as the relationship between the object to be known and the knowing intellect, would not be established; furthermore, unimpeded recognition—which destroys inferential reasoning—would also fail. The rest has been well stated elsewhere.

May the one known as a Sautrāntika attain tranquility, having been subdued by his own fellow schoolmates who are skilled in instruction— those who, by speaking at length of contradictions and the excessive weightiness of their claims made before and after [the perception], silenced him as he argued that "the previous object, while projecting its own internal variety of forms onto subsequent cognitions, is to be inferred from that diversity; it is never directly perceived at that time."

Neither the grasped nor the grasper exist anywhere; rather, today, at the transcendence of the state of worldly existence, the nature of the intellect—which is variegated by diverse beginningless continuities and possesses a threefold nature—shines forth by its own self.
Such is the statement of the Yogācāra: the sublation of the object and the subject is identical within cognition.
Or rather, it should be avoided by those who consider that the differentiation between self and other can never be established anywhere at all.

The identity of the object of cognition and the cognizer through the intellect is not possible here for you, whether they are real or otherwise, since you admit that distinctness entails a loss of the defining characteristic of the grasper. Nor is there any wonder in their identity;
for no one knows of a "wonderful" substance or quality that possesses both a distinct and a non-distinct form.
Therefore, let the theory of self-manifestation (ātmakhyāti) here abide in the mere fact of self-luminosity.

Whether existence, non-existence, both, or the avoidance of both—since all these lead to undesirable consequences, everything is empty and transcends the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*). This is because it is not [established] through one's own desired doctrine. That ultimate truth is unshakeable; if that were abandoned, conventional reality would be non-existent and no purpose would be accomplished.
Therefore, such a baseless negation, never seen anywhere, should not be postulated here.
If an entity were non-existent before and after its production, it would likewise not exist in the middle, like a flower in the sky; nor could there be an effect.
But since it is indeed perceived therein, how could such terms as "middle" or "effect" apply?
Furthermore, the inquiry as to whether the cause at the commencement of an effect is itself subject to transformation or not is likewise futile.
Since the accomplishment of an effect results from a causal complex, the regressus ad infinitum of causes does not constitute a defect.

If the probandum, the reason, and its members were established merely through conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) in accordance with this statement, then how could defects such as "unestablished" (*asiddha*) not arise here?
If you say that there is no cognition of validity in that regard,
and thus it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) according to the actual state of things (*vastusthiti*), then this applies equally to the one who establishes your own position as well.

Non-apprehension (*akhyāti*), misapprehension (*anyathādhī*), cognition devoid of an object (*viṣayarahitadhī*), cognition without a substratum (*anadhiṣṭhānabuddhi*), the association with the form of an external object (*bāhyārthākārayoga*), cognition of what is existent, non-existent, or other than those two (*sadasaditaradhī*), the cognition of emptiness (*śūnyadhī*), and the cognition of the self (*ātmadhī*)—
these various positions (*pakṣabheda*) favored by proponents of different systems regarding error are generally accepted;

however, for those learned in the Vedas, cognition is usually considered to be of an object as it truly is (*yathārthā*), though in some cases it is held to be due to the non-apprehension of difference (*bhedāgraha*) and so forth.

If, because of agreement in some portion, the remaining part of the words of the Jina and his disciples were to be authoritative, then the Upaniṣads would be sublated by them; thus is the vain hope of those who pluck out their hair. Since even discrepancies are observed, let it be that the word of the Sugata alone is the truth.
Therefore, because they mutually exclude one another, our Vedic revelation is unshakable by human speech.

Truth and untruth, along with their two-fold combinations and the further addition of the aforementioned [negations], are proclaimed by those whose speech has cleared away the sky of [false] assertions such as "it exists" and so forth; this is the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*). If contradiction is accepted by them, it is a violation of their own system; if it is not accepted, it is a flaw in the opponent's statement. Furthermore, there can be no connection with non-existence or the like anywhere that is devoid of limiting conditions (*anupadhika*).

For this [merit] increases according to its fitness within each individual body of living beings; upon the destruction of the body, it becomes a celestial mansion in liberation, characterized by eternal upward motion and so forth due to its heaviness, while the earth and other elements possess eternal downward motion.
Its pervasiveness arises from dharma alone, like the sky, or else such is its nature as a *pudgala*.
Those who construct theories through fallacious arguments must be driven far away by those skilled in the methods of the scriptures.

"Rudra knows everything; he is honored in the Vedas, seen as a speaker of truth, and his vow is famous in certain Upanishads—let his word be authoritative. Do not say so. For this very Rudra, commanded by the Lord—who delights in crushing the Daityas—to compose "delusive scriptures" (moha-śāstra) and the like, composed his own Tantra; therefore, it is not to be relied upon by the learned.
Indeed, in the discourse of Prajāpati, the Upaniṣad clearly proclaimed the doctrine that the body is the self;
that Lokāyata system was composed by Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, who resorted to delusion;
and even in the Mahābhārata, the preeminent followers of the Lokāyata are celebrated as being in the lineage of Kaṇva.
Therefore, in this case, the deception on the part of the Lord of Creatures is likewise justified for the sake of the task at hand.

The tradition of Paśupati is fourfold through specific designations such as Śaiva and others, or otherwise; here, the mutual contradiction with the Veda is clear, and thus it is said that those who enter it deserve the curse for being corrupted by it.
Those who follow the Vedas remembered those who had entered [the heretical systems] as unworthy of instruction and worldly-minded.
Even regarding this reality, there is a deviation [from it] due to the subsequent statements concerning the doctrine of the Sugata, the Victor, which have been received in succession.

If it is argued that another tantra is also honored like the Veda in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts—based on statements such as "Nārāyaṇa is the ultimate end of all," the declaration of its indestructibility by any cause, and the description of its authority—it follows that there is no refutation of it as there is of the Buddhists and others; this is true in part. However, while there might be sublation in certain respects, such [sublation] does not exist anywhere in the *Pañcarātra*, and thus its acceptance here is equal to that of the Veda.
Indeed, conventions are seen to be adopted in the world, and they must be upheld by the king;
therefore, the objection that partiality toward us is somehow improper is a charge fit for children.
Let others be deceived by others, but let the statement regarding the protection of convention remain consistent with righteousness (*dharma*).
The statement regarding the identity of the final goal is intended to refute other [erroneous] graspings, since such a view is seen to be contradicted by statements to the contrary.

If it is argued that the authority of the Sāttvata [Pāñcarātra] is established by the force of the logic of the *karmakāṇḍa* and the *smṛtis*, and that there is no connection for it with this [third] chapter because it does not subdue rival systems, we say: no;
for the hostility of the Pāñcarātra must be refuted by removing the delusion of contradiction.
By means of the statement arising from false reasoning and so forth, its establishment is demonstrated as being continuous throughout other times.

If it is argued that the Sage’s censure of the Veda in this [text] indicates a lack of devotion to the Veda on the part of the Sāttvata, do not say so; for in a statement intended primarily to offer praise based on clarity, there is no loss of Vedic affinity.
Indeed, the Blessed Lord, compassionate toward His devotees, composes this work while condensing the essence of the Śruti.
And just as in the case of the Śrauta, Smārta, and other rites, the All-pervading Lord here divided the Vedic [path] into the Vaidika and the Tāntrika.

Since the authority of the Vedas is declared, and since [the Purāṇas] state that they themselves are rooted in those [Vedas], their distinction from the heterodox Āgamas is evident; thus, the statement that they possess a status equal to the Vedas is not the word of a Seer (Ārṣa).
What loss is there in [the Purāṇas] being variegated by minor sciences, just as it is in such portions of the Veda?
However, for the sake of providing a means toward liberation, the various distinctions of spiritual accomplishments were enumerated within the Sāttvata system.

[The opponent argues: "The Pañcarātra is not an authoritative source, for it describes the birth of the individual soul (jīva) and proclaims that the mind is produced from the principle of the soul; furthermore, it designates that [mind] as the cause of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).

[The author replies: "Do not say so. The words 'soul' and the like do not denote the birth of the omnipresent Lord; rather, because He manifests through various emanations (vyūha-bheda), those specific designations are applied to Him within those [emanations] due to His assumption of the respective principles (tattva-abhimāna), thereby attaining their fixed limitations."

Since it is stated here that the *jīva* is without beginning or end, the position that it is produced is certainly not accepted; nor does the word "Saṃkarṣaṇa" and so forth apply in any way to the *jīva* alone.
Furthermore, the sequence of creation as taught in the Śruti was not recited by [the author] himself, and one should not postulate anything contrary to it.
Therefore, there is no contradiction here—whether between the words or between them and the Śruti—since the intended purport is seen to depend upon those respective authorities.

The Sāṃkhyas and Vaiśeṣikas desire that dharma which is recited in the Śruti as the truth; however, the principles and practices found in the teachings of the Buddhists, the Kṣapaṇakas, and Paśupati are devoid of the Śruti.
In the Tantra known as the Pañcarātra, which is as infallible as the Viṣṇusmṛti that embellishes the Vedas, [dharma is likewise established].
The reality established by the three Vedas, as well as the conduct, are accepted equally according to the principle of the distinction between the various schools.

The five sacrifices are remembered even by the sages as being performed for a Śūdra with the mantra of salutation (*namaskāra*); therein, terms such as *haviṣkṛt* and others are studied, so that he possesses a partial entitlement here as well.
Regarding the distinctions such as *abhigamana* and the rest, the sequence of time mentioned by Dakṣa should be applied as stated.
Having synthesized everything through reasoning, beginning with the animal sacrifice, the *iṣṭi*, the Soma sacrifice, and so forth, by means of the *grāhya* [the object to be grasped].

The term "Ācārya" is used in some instances as a generic designation for one born into that status; however, in such scriptural injunctions as "The teacher is God," its application is restricted by the definitions established in the Smṛtis.
Similarly, in cases where no other recourse is available, such as with the term "Sāttvata" and others, there is no fault in breaking conventional usage (rūḍhi).
Furthermore, the presence of Brahmins and others in this scripture is well-known in various ways throughout the Mahābhārata and other texts.

Those who followed Sāṅkhya were driven away by Yoga; those who followed Akṣapāda were subdued by Kaṇacara; the intellects of the Lokāyatas were stolen by the crushing of the Buddhists; and those who arose from the Jains were defeated by their own contradictions.
Thus, when the Lord’s power was manifested in the *Tantra* of the Paśus, they remained fixed in such base persistence.
In this [work], those of wrong views have been destroyed along with their reliance on fallacious reasoning and scriptures that resemble [the truth].

In this chapter, the Seer of the Fifth Veda, having cast aside the objections raised by the followers of Kapila, the adherents of Kaṇāda, the elder Vaibhāṣikas and others, those called Yogācāras who have fallen into the nihilism that destroys the doctrine of the Sugata,
the devotees of the Arhat-siddhānta, and those established in the system of Paśupati,
has declared the *Pañcarātra* as the path of the Vedas.
The Sāṅkhyas declare everything to be eternal, while the Vaibhāṣikas and others maintain that everything here is momentary;

the followers of the Jina recite the sevenfold predication (saptabhaṅgī) regarding all things as both eternal and non-eternal. Even the Vaiśeṣikas and others, having analyzed the eternal and the non-eternal, speak of them by reversing [the order]. Now, obstructing those views arising from the Śrutis, he joins the sections on Space (viyat) and Vital Air (prāṇa) with the Śrutis themselves.

Regarding the previous [section] on the qualification of the person (*puruṣa-adhikāra*), some say that because the word "born" (*jani*) was used there to express eternality, it is established that the same applies to the production of space (*vyoman*); thus, they claim there is a contradiction between the two statements. The proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) replies: the creation of space is measured by hundreds of Vedic passages; its establishment cannot be otherwise.
He states the inconsistency of the argument by saying that the assertion of wind, space, and nectar is contradicted by the rules of birth.

If it is argued that the statement regarding the origination of space (*vyoman*) must have a limited scope—just as in the case of the Self (*ātman*)—because of its mention immediately after fire (*tejas*), because of the expression "immortal" (*amṛta*), and because it is a substance without parts, we say no.

This is because "firstness" (*prāthamya*) is not explicitly heard [in the text]; if one were to assume it based on its position in the sequence of recitation, that assumption would be sublated by other evidence.
Furthermore, the term "immortal" here is equivalent to the expression "not dying," due to the uniformity of intent across multiple passages.

The doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) is logical and is endorsed by the Śrutis; there is no composite whole (*avayavin*) to be produced, for the doctrine of creation consists in various substances assuming different names while remaining in a state of coexistence.
Furthermore, states such as sound and so forth are accepted by you even within the category of partless substances;
therefore, the origination of space mentioned in the Śrutis—being equal to the origination of other things—is not to be rejected.

From the immutable Brahman, this entire universe arises according to the logic of sons, grandsons, and so forth; from this [Brahman], the passage beginning with "prāṇa" (breath) is also easily understood here, and thus there is no delusion regarding the application [of these terms].

Because of the risk of over-extension if one were to cause confusion by following the sequential order of the recitation of "prāṇa," "svānta" (mind), and so on, [the text] shows that, like the first, the Supreme creates each respective body in accordance with the thread of its own creative vision (īkṣā).

Since it has already been stated that all substance is eternal through the refutation of composite substances, why does the author of the Sūtras state eternity once again with respect to the Puruṣa? True; he here dispels the notion that [eternity] belongs to a conscious entity that is subject to limiting conditions (upādhi) and thus deserves a different name.
Thus, here the two attributes of inwardness and consciousness are established as eternal, even for the knower of the field (kṣetrajña).
The doctrine that "everything possessing birth is distinct from the meaning of the word 'Real' (sat)" is established by such texts as "all this has that as its self" (*aitadātmyam*);

thus, creation is declared [to be illusory]. Furthermore, the theory of the partless nature [of the Self] has been refuted in the case of space and so forth. The idea that the individual soul (*jīva*) might arise from That [the Supreme Self] is not tenable, because it would entail the fallacy of the acquisition of what was not previously done (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and other defects; moreover, despite explicit scriptural statements regarding its eternity and non-birth, its "birth" is merely its conjunction with the body and other limiting adjuncts.
If the body were the self, there would have to be birth [of desire]; yet that is not possible here for one who has just been born, because of innate attachment.
Even the theory that cognition arises from the process of fermenting grain (*kiṇva*) and so forth, or like a variegated cloth made of clouds and stones, is untenable in this case.
The sense of "mine-ness" regarding the body is as natural as it is toward a house; the delusion of identity arises only from defects.
And the inference for unity is set aside by the stronger inference derived from scripture and from reasoning.

Those who maintain that the living being (*jīva*) is like foam upon the ocean of reality— which is subject to unerring transformation— thus desire the body to be distinct from the body, and the stream of consciousness (*dhīsantāna*)— which consists of the vital breath, intellect, and senses— to be eternal, persisting until liberation, yet dissolving at the time of cosmic dissolution; while [they also hold it] to be stationary.
Here, [these faults] have been shaken off far away by those scriptural traditions which are free from the defect of contradiction, unlike other [traditions].

Some have asserted that the Self is merely consciousness; others, however, maintain that its nature as a knower arises from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). In this regard, various contradictions with the scriptures (*āmnāya*) and other authorities are set forth by such sūtras as "Therefore, [the Self] is a knower" (*jño'ta eva*).

Since the principle previously established applies here as well—to this eternally conscious Self which is devoid of birth and dissolution—the statement regarding its modification (*vikṛti*), which would otherwise imply contraction and the like, must be understood as occurring only through an indirect medium (*sad-vāraka*).

The scriptures declare both the state of being a knower and the nature of knowledge; we do not fall into error here on this view. Why should the Self not shine everywhere? For it is established by the Vedas that the embodied soul is atomic.

Since its own form is self-luminous and its light is always present though indistinct, its manifestation is accepted as constant; however, due to the contraction of the intellect, there is merely an obstruction to its distinct delineation during states such as deep sleep.
If the particle *eva* is restricted to the property (*dharma*), then its exclusionary function would be threefold:
it would apply to the locus (*dharmī*) when there is a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with this [property], and it would entail the negation of that property in the domain of its opposite.
Thus, in the statement "he certainly knows," the insentient one is not the knower; the mere expression of "knowing" excludes dullness.
This very particle "eva" attains a scope that is consistent with such statements as "the non-loss of knowledge" (jñānālopa).
From the scriptural statements regarding the soul's departure, its vibration, and its atomic size, it acquires power through its subtlety;
yet, due to the abundance of its intelligence, there is simultaneity in the perception of multiple forms according to the theory of parts (*avayava-naya*).

Where omnipresence is taught, this refers to the Supreme Self, as indicated by the marks of the intended meaning (*tātparya-liṅga*); the doctrine of pervasiveness regarding the individual soul (*jīva*) has as its purport either the greatness of its intellect or its extreme transparency.

Let it be that the person possesses the nature of a knower in this way; nevertheless, agency cannot be established for him, because agency is negated by the Śrutis and other authorities, and because he is devoid of modification (*vikṛti*). This is due to the sublation of false views. For the denial of agency and the statement regarding his lack of modification have been declared to have another meaning (*anyaparyam*).
[Objection: "The agent [is the self], because the scriptures would otherwise be purposeless. [Reply: Therefore, there can be no injunction (*niyoga*) here for one who is not a cognizer.

Furthermore, if the negation of the agency of the "I" spoken by the proponent is refuted by his own statement and so forth, yet this negation applies to an "I" other than the referent of the word "I," then for one who knows the Upaniṣads, this is merely proving what is already established. Moreover, if there were also an absence of the state of being an enjoyer (the self as subject), then the scriptures concerning bondage, liberation, and so forth would follow as being futile.
Through taking life, through dwelling [in a place], and through the yoga of thinking "I am superior to my nature," one becomes a doer.

The application of effort for the sake of pacifying the desire for knowledge regarding activity is weak when the task depends on a collection of causes; the engagement in what is to be done, whether by means of scriptural injunction or otherwise, is established in the world.
That state which is fit for scripture is one regulated by destiny through the teaching of beneficial speech, along with its purpose.
Thus, this person here appears as the knower, the agent, and the enjoyer through all means of valid cognition.
An agent is certainly not dependent on another; likewise, Pāṇini [is independent].
If it were otherwise, then the command "one should act" or "one should not act" would be like ordering a prisoner to run while he is already in chains.
Do not say so; for agency and its fruit belong to one who is subject to the power of karma, the senses, time, and primordial nature (prakṛti).
Having accepted that the Lord is solely the Self, as known through hundreds of scriptural texts, such hatred is thus endless.
The all-pervasive cause is common to all the sprouts of effects, like water; yet there is diversity from Brahmā downwards due to the seeds of the karma of living beings, which yield specific fruits.

Equality is its own song, heard even here; nevertheless, the distinction between those who wish to lead others downward and so forth results in fruit corresponding to such karma—this beginningless stream is thus determined.

In due time, the Blessed One, who relies upon mere expedients, generates that very compassion of one whose mind is intent on the welfare of others— the desire to bring about the cessation of suffering— which pacifies suffering.
He bestows the union with the body and so forth, instructs in the Vedic injunctions, and speaks the essence of Vedānta.
By that very [power], she brings forth for men at the time of death a yoga of boundless bliss that is free from substrate.
If it is argued that there would be the fault of partiality (nigrahāṃśa) in the punisher, we say no, because [the Lord] cannot be subject to affliction;
for His own disadvantage does not accrue to the Lord, nor is He opposed to the disadvantage of others.
Compassion has its scope in certain cases, and His status as a witness and so forth is well-established.
And when this intrinsic nature is perceived, it is appropriate to take refuge in it with the thought that it is the bestower of fruit.
For those who possess valid cognition, the inner self (*pratyag-ātman*) is the referent of the "I" (*ahamartha*), as well as the agenthood and so forth;
because its activity is preceded by its own will, this [self] is distinct from non-conscious matter and is equal to the Lord (*īśvara*).
However, the Lord exerts effort solely through His own will, whereas everything else is dependent upon Him.
The activity of the three [factors] occurs with a specific destination determined by the sequence beginning with the charioteer.

Agency might exist at times when there is an instrument, provided it is independent of the instigation of another; otherwise, how could there be its restraint and so forth? If you say this is not so because it applies equally even to our own position, [we reply]: for those who are compassionate would certainly not cause that which has already engaged in unwholesome activity to engage in it again. If that [agency] arises from its own nature, then why would the other [lack of agency] not do so as well? Thus, the destruction of what was studied is fruitless.

The inequality of the embodied souls (kṣetrajña), though they are equal, arises from such a diversity of unseen merit (adṛṣṭa); no other unseen force is required, for there must be a Ruler who ordains it through His sovereign will.
Furthermore, the Lord’s role as an impeller—established by the consensus of the Vedas and His status as a witness—is not contradicted;
even a small portion of this truth should be accepted by those whose minds are attentive, as found in the Bhāṣya and other texts.

It is incorrect to say that the Lord is the agent of fruits but not the impeller of the instruments; for this contradicts all the Śrutis and other scriptures. Nor is the fruit [produced] by action alone, nor is it the result of sinful conduct. Indeed, even reflection and the like depend upon action for those who sustain existence, as stated by the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra); and he will likewise declare that for living beings and even for deities, [action] is presided over by the collection of instruments.

The author of the Sūtras has declared in many ways that the Supreme is absolutely distinct from the individual soul; by means of the scriptural passages that reconcile the texts on difference and non-difference, he has also dispelled the objection raised by his opponents.
Indeed, there is no further reason here, even in the resolution of the stated objection, for [the opponent's] position to prevail.
This investigation of the degrees is for the purpose of refuting the opinions of many wicked-minded scholars who employ arguments such as "a quarter-part" and so forth.

The status of being a partial incarnation (*aṃśatva*) in those such as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa arises from their authority over specific portions of the Divine Form; however, the statement that the individual soul (*jīva*) is a portion of Brahman is not tenable, for it is impossible for the speaker to refer to Brahman as being possessed of parts, since Brahman is partless.

Furthermore, it is incorrect to claim that Brahman and the like are a collective totality of consciousness (*citsamaṣṭi*) and that each individual possesses a portion thereof, because the oneness of the creator of the universe—who meditates on becoming many with the thought "May I become many"—is established.

It is incorrect to argue that the single ether becomes manifold through various limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as pots and the like, and that similarly, upon the removal of those adjuncts, the soul (bhavabhṛt) returns to its state of being Brahman; for [the analogy fails] due to the difficulty of the self-initiating of its own non-existence, the non-observation of the recognition of specific qualities, the manifold contradictions arising from the consideration of parts as both severed and unsevered, and because the term "samya" (equality/identity) implies liberation.
Some proclaim that in the shoreless ocean of Māyā, within its illusory waves, the reflection of the moon of Brahman constitutes the individual souls (jīvas); this is but the song of a madman.
For the seer of Brahman does not perceive them as such even in the slightest degree; nor can the soul be postulated by itself prior to its own conceptualization.
Since it would lack its own selfhood before being imagined, one must seek a third party as the postulator in this matter.

Brahman here is pure Being (sanmātra), which pervades all; moreover, some say that there are three eternally established parts due to the distinction between the individual soul (jīva), the Lord (īśa), and consciousness (cit). This [view] need not be raised [as an objection]. Because the persistence of pure existence alone is taught, and because the Lord is said to possess a body superior to that [existence], the statement regarding the threefold nature of Brahman must have another intention, since Brahman is determined to be partless.

In the view that accords with the scriptures, the statement regarding partiality (aṃśatva)—as in "Kiraṭa and others are portions of Me"—is intended to be understood as based on similarity and smallness, since [the parts] are eternally distinct according to that logic.

Thus, the designation of "portion" would be non-primary; for to those of subtle intellect, it refers to a single part of one and the same reality. Therefore, the individual soul (jīva) is called a "portion" in relation to the Lord who possesses all attributes, being a mode (prakāra) of Him through its possession of qualities.

It has already been stated previously that the undesirable consequences in the opponent's view—beginning with the impossibility of constant perception and so forth—have been extensively discussed here as well; why then speak again of such things as the confusion of enjoyments?

Do not say so; for while previously [the author] quelled those who extended their arms [in opposition], now he does so out of compassion to ward off the wicked views of those arrogant in their pride regarding the Veda, and this shall also apply to future doctrines.
For the living being who is whirling like a constellation in the wind-wheel of false knowledge and the like, [the author],
in order to effect the abandonment of worldly existence through the awakening to the reality of the inner self— a process uncontroverted by any philosophical system—

proceeded to purify once more the soul whose form was established at the commencement of the Mīmāṃsā inquiry; for he was about to explain the distinction between the worship of the Supreme and the distinction of the limbs [of ritual], which contain within them the knowledge of the pure Self.

O All-pervasive Lord, even regarding the creation of the ether and other elements, as well as the successive stages [of evolution], there are seven points established by the removal of mutual contradictions among the various scriptural traditions (Āmnāyas): namely, that the soul’s birth and dissolution are merely adventitious (aupādhika) due to its being qualified by prior categories; that its nature is a mass of consciousness and pure subjectivity; that its agency is dependent on another; that it possesses a body composed of the [three] qualities (guṇas); and that it is a portion of the Universal Form (Viśvarūpa). These are the seven matters to be accomplished in the "Sky-foot" (Vyomapāda) section.

If it is argued that there is no fruit in the non-mention of the origin of the dice and so forth, and that any further suspicion here is trivial, and that even the investigation into their number and such is like an inquiry into the teeth of an elephant that has already eaten its fill—this is not so.

For those who state that there is some purpose for these [passages] other than the Brāhmaṇa rites, they possess meaningfulness through sublation; thus there would be a direct connection with them, since the middle ones follow by implication from the first and the last.

There are eight topics here. First, the method regarding the elements (viyat) has been stated; [the second topic] strengthens the method regarding fire, water, and food mentioned previously during the creation of individual distinctions.
Even in the considerations of number, measure, and so forth, there may be fruit through meditations and the like based upon those [elements].
This chapter is also intended to clarify that the cognizer is distinct from the vital breaths and the other [faculties].
The Veda, speaking at the beginning of the existence of the sages, declares their state as living beings;
here, it is not the Brahman alone that is to be denoted, for that would destroy the plural number, and thus the eternality of the *akṣa* [the individual self] is established.
Do not say so; because of the firmness of its creation, this plural number is to be understood according to the rule of the "noose" (*pāśa*).
For [the status of] being a vital breath and a seer is indeed easily established even in the Supreme Self, due to the similarity in their etymological derivations and other such characteristics.
It has been stated that "seven vital breaths move," and these have been specifically designated as such even in the context of yoga;
therefore, the claim that there are seven sense organs (*indriya*) is an incorrect statement based on a superficial view, for here [in this system] they are understood in another sense.
Their defining characteristic is their nature as substances evolved from the *sāttvika* ego (*ahaṃkāra*), which is common to them all.
The statement of distinction regarding the mind as the primary [organ] is fruitful [only] in comparison to the organs of action and cognition.

Some have declared that there is a single sense organ pervading the body, while others say it is divided into parts with distinct functions; some, averse to the path of the Vedas, have discarded the organs of action through petty reasoning.

Some say that the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is accompanied by the entire group of instruments including the intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṅkāra), and mind (citta); others have proclaimed him as being devoid of the mind. Thus, I shall here refute them according to their actual meaning.

If it is argued that the pervasiveness of the sense organs is established because all [scriptures] speak of their infinity and do not state any restriction regarding their limited size, we say no; for [the senses] depart from, move toward, and return to the entire body. The cognition of distant objects occurs through the functioning (vṛtti) [of the sense]; the mention of "infinity" in passages concerning the ritual of worship refers to [the soul's] own effects.
And because those things situated in the bulbous root (kanda) undergo transformation within their respective bodies, there is expansion.

Prāṇa has been established as being produced by another according to the principle previously stated; it is either merely air or its activity within the body. Since there is no doctrine of its separate origination, it is appropriate that its substantiality be included in the category of substances along with them. It would not be a distinct reality, for just as one does not abandon the state of air when it becomes fire, so too here, its abandonment [as a substance] is never possible.

It has been stated that the vital breath (prāṇa) is equal to the three worlds; however, it is incorrect to conclude from this that it is all-pervading (jagadvyāpaka), because that would contradict its departure (utkrānti), movement (gati), and so forth, which are mentioned in the same context as the individual soul (jīva). The scriptural statement regarding its equality with everything is for the purpose of praise, intended here to show that it is the cause for sustaining the instruments (karaṇa) and the field (kṣetra).
Within the body, it provides manifold assistance, manifesting in ten ways through its various functional modifications.

Even for the deities who are enjoyers, their presiding over bodies and instruments is not independent of the Lord, because He grants them that sovereignty; therefore, all embodied beings are indeed His body.
For if there were absolute independence [on their part], the principle of the vassal king would never apply anywhere.
According to the principle of vital breaths, sovereignty here belongs to sentient beings over their own capacity, yet it is dependent on another.

Prāṇa might also be considered a sense-organ (*indriya*) because it is an instrument (*upakaraṇa*) and because it is declared to be the chief among them due to its role in departure from the body and so forth; yet this is not the case if one does not accept a separate verbal designation for it, as its distinction [from the other senses] is explicitly stated.

Since its status as a sense-organ is directly mentioned, the logic of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*) applies to the mind (*manas*), but not to prāṇa. Furthermore, its being a modification of the sāttvika *ahaṅkāra* is weak, as it is based merely on a similarity of terminology.
He is remembered by Manu and others as the primordial creator whose name begins with "Sarasija-vasati" (the Lotus-dweller);
it is also stated that he entered [the world] through the individual soul (jīva). Therefore, the sequence of his delegated tasks is established here.

Thus, it is not the case that there is only one enterer; for it is studied in scripture that He, having made the threefold [world], differentiated it. That Blessed Lord, as the inner self within each respective soul, creates such a multitude of effects.

Even this scriptural passage, "by means of the living self," does not state the identity of the Brahman and the individual soul (jīva), because it has already been declared that there is a distinction between their stable natures in the statement, "The one is the inner self; the other is the body.
Therefore, the Lord, being qualified by that [individual soul], is the agent even during the entry [into the world] by way of having that [soul] as His instrument.
For if the soul were its agent, the scriptural statement "it [breathes] by the prāṇa" would not be tenable here, because of the difference between the agent and the instrument.

It has been stated that fire resides within the center of the cosmic egg, and that its threefold nature (*trivṛttva*) is clearly taught through the mention of the consumption of fire, water, and food by various forms; therefore, the Creator (*vedhas*) must have made it threefold.
Do not say so; let there be the creation of the cosmic egg (*brāhmaṇḍa-sṛṣṭi*), but how could this be preceded by a threefold transformation?
The transformation of food and other such things when consumed is said to be threefold; the perception of other [objects] arises from their proximity.

In this [Prāṇapāda], they have declared: the number and measure of the births of the senses; the nature of the vital air (prāṇavāyu), its subtlety, and its presiding deities; the dependence [of the senses] upon those two objects;

the non-sensory nature of the prāṇa; and the manifold names of the individual [entities] consisting of sentient and insentient matter, starting from the first five-fold combiner (pañcīkartṛ) who is enveloped by the armor originating from his own navel.
[One attributes] eternality to space, wind, and atoms; to the Person (puruṣa), qualities such as ignorance;
to the auditory organ and others, the nature of being elements; to the mind, omnipresence and the status of being a distinct eternal reality;
to the vital breaths, the state of being the Self and so forth; and to the host of celestial beings, independence in governing their own domains.
Even for the Creator, there would be a fracture in his pair of feet were he to describe the sequence of the machine's release here.

If it is argued that no contradiction is established by explaining through reasonings that are true only at first sight, then a contradiction would indeed be established according to the actual state of things as perceived by those who possess right knowledge; in that case, one's own self-conceit would be thwarted.

Therefore, this chapter, which serves to pacify contradictions, is opposed to the friend of the Buddhists (the Sautrāntika); for the "unestablished nature of reasoning" (tarkāpratiṣṭhā) should be applied only to the independent doctrines of those who turn away from the path of the Śruti.
Śrī: Introduction.

If liberation were not something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), then the practice of meditation would be fruitless; yet if it were something to be accomplished, it would be perishable—how then could there be final liberation (*apavarga*) devoid of rebirth?
Do not say so; for one who is devoted to the Supreme, that experience of Brahman—which was previously unestablished—is indeed what is to be accomplished.
The destruction of the contraction of the intellect occurs, and this [state] becomes transcendent, having passed beyond all limits.

First, through his two feet, he generates in them the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman; thereafter, with both [feet] together and along with all its auxiliary limbs, he declares that manifold [knowledge].
He [fosters] detachment from sovereignty and the like, and longing for the Person of boundless glory.
He also describes, in successive quarters [of verses], the various types of spells (*vidyā*) and their respective implements (*upakaraṇa*).

A living being whose mind is distressed by *saṃsāra* exerts itself here in this section concerning the body (*śārīraka*) for the sake of dispassion (*vairāgya*). But why was this quarter composed by the authors of the Sūtras?

True; however, placing other attainments on the scale against the multitude of hells would be appropriate at the commencement of the means to liberation; indeed, one who is hastening here must possess clear self-awareness.

Since bodies and the like are to be experienced according to the law of enjoyment, they are obtained right there—whether in heaven or on earth—by means of the subtle elements such as breath; so why here [in this life] cling to a former body already grasped?
Furthermore, the Lord himself brings about the movement of the minute soul through the process of vitalizing breath.
Do not say so; for it is improper to speak with such reverence regarding an arbitrary action that is not constrained by the authority of scripture.
People designate a collection of various kinds by the name of its predominant part; thus, because of their abundance, this group of elements is called "water-like" (āpaḥ puruṣavacasaḥ).

For that all-pervading Lord creates [the world] with those [elements] both in their unevolved (avyākṛta) and evolved (pañcīkṛta) states, and furthermore, he establishes a gradation [of their proportions].
In this context, the word "śraddhā" denotes water, because it is so designated in the Veda, as is indicated by its specific name.
Having thus conceived these five fires— namely, the sky, Parjanya, the earth, man, and woman—

the scripture declares that the winds offer as oblations into those five fires, along with their attendants, the subtle element called faith (śraddhā), which, through a gradual transformation, takes the form of moon, rain, food, and semen, and which consists of the living soul (jīva) assuming a body.

Whatever auspicious karma, such as sacrifices (iṣṭa) and charitable works (pūrta), a person may perform here while embodied, they must experience its entirety before returning to earth at the end; this is because the scriptural view is contradicted by what is actually seen.

Since it is not heard that the fruit is experienced "in its entirety" (kārtsnyena), and because there are scriptural teachings regarding differences in birth and so forth resulting from good deeds, therefore the traveler to heaven returns accompanied by the remainder of his prārabdha-karma along with other [unexhausted] karmas.

The man of action, having died, goes toward the smoke, the night, the fortnight, the month shrouded in darkness, the southern solstice, the worlds of the ancestors, and even the sky where the moon resides. But upon his return, from the moon he proceeds through the sky-path to the smoke, the mist, and the cloud.
Then, having entered rice and other grains as semen, he becomes a sovereign of the wheel of torments within the womb.
The goal of the *ācāra* portion would consist of conduct, livelihood, and so forth, derived from the word "conduct" (*caraṇa*);
however, since action (*karman*) and conduct (*ācāra*) are distinguished by scripture, such a statement is not correct because there is no valid basis for it.
For, according to the primary sense of the term, even in the context of action, one should not restrict [the meaning] to a single part as if it were merely conduct.
Since birth and so forth are understood to arise from the differentiation of karma, it should be considered that [the distinction between] conduct and its accomplishment [is likewise established].

The sages have recorded in every step the transgressions resulting from the violation of established conduct, as well as the destruction of ancient sins and the fitness for meritorious deeds through following that conduct;
therefore, there should be no suspicion of abandoning it with the thought that heaven is attained by mere virtuous action alone.
For one who has not abandoned improper conduct, the collection of Vedic hymns does not purify him, being like water in a dog-skin bag.

If it is argued that for all [beings] upon the fall of the body, the attainment of the Moon is stated as a rule, and therefore for those burdened by sin, that [attainment] is preceded by a journey to hell—this is not so;

for the word "all" would be restricted by the scriptural statement, "The world is filled with them, but not the other. Consequently, at the end of their respective torments, they suddenly enter a contemptible womb here [in this world].

The attainment of birth in the womb and other such places will be manifold due to the ripening of karma through a great abundance of merits and sins; yet, like one without a face, it requires a fifth oblation.
Similarly, upon the fall of the body, how many times does the path of smoke and so forth occur through intense auspicious deeds?
Having instantly attained divine forms, celestial chariots, and the like, they became renowned for having departed [to higher realms].
The fact that the two oblations possess a body is beyond dispute in the case of the first and the last;

however, the claim that birth [occurs] in ether, air, and so forth because of the presence of the verbal root *bhū* (to become) is without substance. It is merely a matter of their being unfit for separate sacrificial offerings (*abhisarpaṇa*). The intention of the text is that they are not to be treated as distinct recipients of the offering.
The fruit to be accomplished through merit in the two worlds [of heaven and earth] is taught here; there is no [fruit] in the midst of worldly enjoyment.

Because the specific designation "for a long time" or "not for a long time" regarding the state of abiding in space and so forth would be lost, and because it would result in the loss of the state of being "white," there would be no fixed rule; yet this is not due to an inherent natural tendency, for it is heard in scripture that [the soul] is "difficult to deliver from rice and the like. Therefore, previously...
It is understood through the power of the statement that there is an immediate abandonment of each respective [object] by that [perception].

If it is argued that the birth [of beings] is heard of here under names such as "rice" (*vrīhi*) and so forth, and that this might be like the status of gods and humans, and that those who know the Vedas do not establish the selflessness of stationary things (*sthāvara*), we say no;
for when the fruits of merit alone are being enumerated, it would be inappropriate to speak of them as "stationary."
Like two bulls in heat, the semen and blood move toward the womb even within a stationary body, even though it is another's body.

It is also incorrect to say that even a rite such as the *iṣṭi*, though enjoined by the Vedas and performed according to rule, is impure due to its connection with violence, and that the virtuous person experiences a portion of that sin starting from the state of being rice and so forth.

For it has been stated through the *mantras* and *arthavādas* that the animal sacrifice is for the benefit of the animal; like medical treatment, this killing in the sacrifice is declared to be "non-killing. Thus Manu praises it, while the censure mentioned here refers to something else entirely.

"The slaughter of an animal here would point to the fault of the performer; it might benefit that sacrifice, therefore they—the followers of Sāṃkhya—declared that this is a prohibition and not a prescription.
When the uselessness of the animal sacrifice has been refuted, such a view is certainly not appropriate; rather, there is the alternative of using a flour-made animal and so forth.
Since it is restricted to specific individuals according to their respective times, there can be no contradiction anywhere.
Furthermore, for one who abandons here the sequence of general rule and exception, what kind of "constant non-violence" could there be?
Indeed, for you, no pure [action] can ever be established, since every prescriptive injunction clearly entails the negation of its specific opposite.
For instance, where untruth and the like are prescribed as medicine, a subsequent expiation is enjoined on that very account.
In that case, it would be so by way of necessity, as in other instances, or else it would be merely for the sake of that [necessity].

Some say that the possessor of the field (kṣetrajña) is unattached, like the sky amidst pestles during a battle; they say he is the non-doer of action, and likewise that the fruit of action resides solely within the distinctions of various limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
They describe him as the liberation of the unmanifest, yet as one who experiences worldly existence, and as being by nature eternally liberated from the beginning.
This chapter on detachment has thus cast out their such thoughts by means of these logical arguments.

In this [fourth] quarter, however, there are six topics: one should abandon the body here along with the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*); having experienced heaven, one would descend accompanied by residual karma (*anuśaya*), following a path differentiated by its measure;
there would be no attainment of the moon and so forth for those who have taken the path to hell; and there is similarity [of form] in the intermediate space and other realms.
Therefore, descent into another body is swift, whereas union with the body of rice and the like takes a long time.
In the two preceding chapters, the Brahman itself spoke in many ways through its own inherent natures; why, then, is it drawn here into the midst of the chapter on the means (*sādhanādhyāya*)?
Do not think so, for that [Brahman] clarifies the supreme [Self] by breaking it down, because of the distinction in its forms.
And it proclaims the state of being the perfected means and so forth of the All-pervading Lord, for the sake of expanding the thirst to attain Him.
If Brahminhood consists in the absence of qualities (*nairguṇya*), then the distinction between Brahmins and non-Brahmins based on qualities is false in this world;

if you say that this distinction is merely imagined through these [qualities], then there is no obstruction to tranquility (*śama*) here, nor even the sequence of [empirical] perception. And if you say that it is eternally free from defects, then the effort to pacify defects is in vain.

If it were something to be conceptualized, there would be the fault [of infinite regress]; this quarter [of the verse] is intended to refute the opponent's position that [the cause] is the primordial nature (prakṛti).

Furthermore, how could there be at the outset the state of being conceivable, the status of being an object of valid cognition, self-luminosity, the nature of bliss, and the state of being the substratum of the universe— along with the thought of becoming many— for that which is devoid of distinctions?
[Otherwise,] there would be the abandonment of the meaning of all scriptures, contradiction by one's own words, and subversion by all means of knowledge.
Thus, for those possessed of deceit and insolence, the section on the meditation upon the qualified state (saguṇa-daśopāsti-pāda) is also difficult to establish.
If it is argued: "How can the contemplation of states such as waking and dreaming fit within this [system], which is free from defects and rich in virtues?"—it is not so;
for [this system] is intended to establish the manifold greatness of Brahman through the manifestation of the objects of dreams.
This is presented here in order to demonstrate that this living being is subject to a state of dependence regarding its own liberation.
Some have recited the first half of this verse as the remainder of the preceding quarter-verse,
and the latter half as being directly connected here because it describes various qualities for the purpose of worship.
This is not at all a grave error, since the skillful method of describing a variegated subject (śabalita) has been inverted.
In the statement of the Brāhma [Sūtra], the "seizing of the fault of the living being" (jīvadoṣagraha) refers here to the mouth of that which is the opposite of the intellect.

Let there be unreal objects created in dreams; nevertheless, even here, the manifold delusion is difficult to abandon because it is experienced as being present now, just like the waking state, and because of the persistence of errors such as the memory of what has been destroyed.
It is true that creation exists merely as established by scripture and other authorities, since it is impossible to reject what has been heard in the scriptures.
For we do not discard even an error, such as that of a dream, provided it is sublated only in part, just like a waking experience.

Some, by the power of yoga, having emerged from their own bodies according to the principle of moving at will, enter the bodies of others; first leaving their former bodies, they subsequently take possession of another form.
Others likewise experience such a state of events even in dreams, sustained merely by the movement of breath.
This is established by the logic of Saubhari, who assumed other bodies through the expansion of the power arising from his mind.
It was said by the Lord of creatures: "O lady, [the soul] possesses from birth the power of true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpatā*) and so forth;

he is the creator of sons and the like, and here in this world he creates objects as if they were his own dream. This is not so, because such qualities are mentioned in reference to liberation, and it is impossible for him to produce things that are not desired and so on.
Furthermore, because dreams are indicative [of future events], this creation of the Creator of the entire universe is likewise [indicative].

Even the suffix *ṇamul* in the expression "vidhātety api" (even while intending) is prescribed when the subject is being referred to; thus, this [Lord], though waking even while others sleep, is clearly understood from the statement regarding his embrace. How many distinct purposes, determined by their respective times, exist even during his wakefulness?
It has also been stated by the authoritative teachers that the bestowing of fruits occurs in accordance with each respective action.
Having obtained the designation "mere illusion" (māyāmātra), the Sugatas have declared the entire universe to be false;
therefore, that which was stated by them at the commencement of their treatises is here [in our system] untenable due to its inconsistency and other flaws.
[We reply: The word *māyā* is not a synonym for "false"; since it is used figuratively (*upacara*), what could possibly follow from that?
Because it is applied to truth, the scriptures, and so forth, according to appropriate rules, this [term] has the sense of "wonderful."

The scripture declares, without restriction, that the place of a living being during deep sleep is either the channels (nāḍī), the pericardium (purītat), or the space within the heart (hārda/brāhma); therefore, let there be an option (vikalpa) here due to their mutual independence.
That is not so, for they are joined by other auxiliary functions, like a bed placed upon a palace.
In every alternative, an option involving a sequence of four faults is not tenable.

This deep sleep (suṣupti) is such that it possesses a multitude of pleasures, including liberation, purity, and joy, as is declared by the Śruti itself; therefore, the embodied soul waking up from it must be different from that [state]. Do not say so, for because of the persistence of karma, the necessity of memory, and the word "pūrva" (the very same), he is indeed the one who was there before.
Because he teaches the means to liberation and so forth, and because he reiterates his own position, he is indeed the enlightened one of the ancients.
The beginninglessness of souls has been stated; the imitation of stone will be refuted at the time of liberation;
the engagement in activities for the sake of heaven and so forth is known through the method of the Śruti; and the Buddhists and others have been defeated.
Because unity is taught even at the end of a kalpa, and because of the grasping of names and forms, [the doctrine] is restricted in its scope.
Furthermore, there is the thought [of the Self] for the sake of attaining the desire to emerge from deep sleep and from states equal to dissolution.

If it is argued that waking and dreaming are not devoid of cognition, while deep sleep is filled with breath, and therefore the state of being "half-asleep" (mugdha) must be immortality because the group of senses and vital breaths has been stilled—
this is not so; for there is no distinction in cause regarding death and the like, and because there is no certainty in arising from the states of remaining [in sleep] or dying.
Having begun to die, one ceases midway due to fate; this is the state of the fourth half.

The calamity that is shown to living beings during states such as waking and so forth— that very [calamity], even when in those respective states, is here purified by the yoga of the stainless and auspicious *brāhma* [state].
Thereafter, through the union of association and so on, one abandons the categories of defects by means of both [the *brāhma* state and the practice].
By means of a pair of methods, the leader removes both inferiority and the loss of magnanimity.

The statement that [Brahman] is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) is for the purpose of expressing its freedom from attributes; here, the description of its qualities is a figurative eulogy (*arthavāda*) regarding the nature of ignorance.
In reality, its state of being free from defects (*nirdoṣya*) is the truth, while everything else is equal to the enjoyments of a dream.

Thus, those who are deluded by the deceptive doctrine that robs the individual soul (*jīva*), the Lord (*īśa*), and the Infinite (*bhūman*)— [Please provide the remainder of the verse to complete the translation.]
Now begins the chapter "Not even from our standpoint" (Na sthānato 'pi), which possesses many peaks.

An object to be abandoned is that which, by its very nature, exists here as a cause of suffering; it must be relinquished even against one's own will, for otherwise its status as something to be abandoned would not exist.
This is because there can be no abandonment of that which is inherently undesirable.
Nor is it blameworthy, just as in the case of sentient beings who possess eternal sovereignty, for [the abandonment] occurs through a change of state.
By scripture alone, one understands the purity and impurity of the supreme self and that which is other than it within a single body.
Though omnipresent, the Self dwells within the bodies of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and others as an atom;
being designated by various terms according to those [bodies], why then is He not subject to their respective commands?
Do not say so; for He is not made known [as such] because He is devoid of ignorance, and because He is the Ruler, He is not one who is to be ruled.
One who knows only a little and is dependent on others is urged toward enlightenment by those who know how to bring benefit to the world.
Those who know the principles of logic certainly do not tolerate the subversion of a general rule by an exception.
Therefore, with respect to qualities such as the sacred syllable *oṃ*, a prohibition must remain within its scope without overstepping the domain of the injunction.
Thus, when the conflict is resolved, there is no establishment of the principle of "cutting off" (apaccheda) where the subject matter is equal.
Since a constant negation of the other [the self] is observed here, from that follows the principle of the commencement [of the inquiry].
The study [of scripture] protects the reality of the effect by considering how the existent could arise from the non-existent;
for the word "clay" alone removes any notion of a different substance in the effect.
Because the world is included within the distinguished Lord, it is appropriate that there is "neither diversity nor plurality" here.
The statement "it is led to the Supreme" serves to pacify the doubt that its extent has been fully specified.

The Supreme Self is fully visible in every region of every object by virtue of its possession of all attributes, yet it is devoid of distinctions such as increase or decrease; this is indeed the teaching through the analogy of the sun and its reflection in reservoirs of water.

If it be argued that there is no touch or heat [in the reflection], then the logic of the examples of the space within a jar or a water-pot does not hold; therefore, the position of the Vedānta is that the Brahman possesses two forms and a twofold manifestation.

If it is argued that the production of the world from the Omniscient Lord involves suffering for Himself, and that His lack of consciousness cannot be postulated even in part—since clay, its effects, and so forth are here naturally and extensively cited as examples along with their respective propositions;
and therefore, the unmanifest (avyākṛta) and other states must necessarily be subject to transformation—[we reply: no.
The Blessed One sports while manifesting his own portion as the deluded [individual soul], because of the removal of misfortunes.
Some say that Brahman is an eternal, insentient portion characterized by various transformations;
others, according to the analogy of foam and so forth, [say it is] due to its undergoing transformation; some [say it consists of] portions that are conscious, unconscious, and omniscient;
and a few here maintain that the world and Brahman share a single nature, according to the analogy of moonlight and so forth.
All of them, having lost their natural course through the sound of all the Vedas, must be terrified here.

Because of the statement regarding the measurement of knowledge after crossing the bridge (*setu*), because of the mention of a connection with that which is to be reached, and because of the scriptural declaration of another's superiority, the Cause must be the attainer; however,
it is incorrect to say that the object to be reached would be something else, for since the state of being "reached" is predicated of the limitless Cause,
one should accept that the nature of being a "bridge" and so forth is uncontradicted in this context by many [scriptural passages].

The designation "bridge" (setu) is appropriate here because it is like a bridge, due to its function of supporting or binding; furthermore, even though this [Brahman] is all-pervasive, the description of it as limited by adjuncts (upādhi) was meaningfully formulated previously in the Sūtras.
And the fourfold nature of that [Veda] is conceived according to the respective capacities of various intellects, despite its infinite magnitude.
Or rather, "of the immortal" (amṛtasya) may refer to liberation itself.

In a discourse concerning the superiority of one thing over another, that which is observed to be the ultimate limit (*paramāvadhi*) is the cause; in such a case, the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*) and so forth serve as that limit in relation to others, and thus they are "supreme" (*para*).
This is because it would be illogical to speak of something as "supreme" (*tatpara*) regarding a subject already stated to be beyond which nothing else exists.
Thus, let there be a restatement of what was said before, or else let it be joined with the pervader as the case may be.

He is to be propitiated by the multitude of eyes fixed upon the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa); he is the presiding lord of the rites established therein, and the deity whose majesty is beyond all conditions, arisen from the middle section (madhyakāṇḍa).
Even here, by this much being said, he alone is the goal for those terrified by the fear of worldly existence who seek protection.
It is established that it bestows the fruit appropriate for each respective beautiful meaning; thus, it is exceedingly noble.
The fruit of agriculture and even of crushing [grains] arises either through an intermediate step or otherwise;

that dharma-s serve as means is understood from the Śrutis, which are free from defects and sublation. Therefore, if it is argued that the statement "the fruit comes from the grace of the Lord" is merely for the sake of praising Him, we say no.
Because it is impossible to postulate a novel [causal] capacity that does not produce the grace of the deity worshipped in the Śruti.

Although the root to be propitiated is the very fruit [of the action], and even when the fruit has ripened, there is still a dependence on ritual action (*karman*) in the performance of the deity’s office;
nevertheless, having observed the supreme qualities of the deity— such as its witnesshood, indifference, and so forth— one engages in pleasing it and the like.
Now, with your words of such noble generosity, you are able to restrain those who are held back by the terrors of doubt.

It is only fitting that sons, whose differences of inclination are fixed, find from their sovereign father— who is compassionate, a knower of what is appropriate, impartial, and generous— the various objects they seek;
for therein lies what is to be attained by themselves, from which comes the removal of whatever is adverse here, and from whom comes its pacification.
Whatever is to be given should be done without distinction; likewise, even the act of subduing should be carried out here according to worldly custom.

In that pure bliss, in that ocean of auspicious qualities, in His own body which is true and eternal, in that manifestation of playful enjoyment shining with the ornaments and weapons of the Goddesses—
[all this] resplendent with manifold enduring relationships such as being the Remainder (śeṣitva) and the state of being the Support (ādhārabhāva).
May our Vedic revelation be unwinking toward Hari, who brings forth both heaven and liberation.
In the *Pāda* [section], He is described as the cause of the objects seen in dreams; here, in the *Suṣupti* [section], He is the excellent protector;

in the *Mugdha* [section], He is the awakener and so forth; and in the *Udbodha* [section], He is the possessor of sinless and auspicious qualities, the one who possesses non-conscious parts through His own bodies. He is said by those of vast devotion to be the ultimate limit of supremacy and the bestower of all fruits.
In truth, one should consider the distinctions of form and so forth in the case of qualities such as shame and in the subsequent devotion.
