To those who proclaim that for one about to be liberated, there is nothing further to be accomplished by the wise once the realization of reality is perfected— thereby declaring that which is most beneficial, sinless, and permeated with the knowledge of reality, while casting off the delirious ravings of the great fever of logic and the chronic affliction of doubt regarding the truth; [To them, this work is addressed.]
He declares that the worship of Murāri must be practiced throughout one's entire life for the sake of attaining liberation.
Fearing the terrible torments and the return from the path of the ancestors, one marries thirst to the nectar-ocean of Kṛṣṇa; as much as has been said is for that purpose.
Having thus obtained authority, one exercises supreme authority over the practice wherein all its limbs are complete.
In this case, it causes a great deal of confusion regarding the distinction between the two types of *para* (the subsequent).

In this very system, the application of the methods (*naya*) is restricted to a single aspect; there can be no simultaneous deliberation upon two [contradictory aspects], for neither difference nor non-difference could here constitute a single object, as that would entail the loss of the other.
Therefore, when an objection is raised against this work—that the expansion of methods is merely scattered—it is answered as follows:
This [Brahman] is the regulator of knowledge as delimited by the objects of knowledge; thus its significance is established.

The authors [of the sūtras] have declared this fourth quarter [of the Vedānta-sūtras] as a summary of the qualities for the purpose of establishing the identity of the knowledge [of Brahman]; thus, the consideration of differences arises here by way of refuting that [identity].
To dispel the doubts of those desiring to hear [the truth], the commentators have spoken in this manner.
The investigation into their difference and non-difference is the subject matter here, and it is stated that this [subject] continues [throughout].

If one’s aspiration here were not divided by various branches of knowledge, yet there were attainment even in part within that mass of infinite, unconditioned, and boundless qualities— the blissful channels beyond all limits— let it not be so; for the one whose desires are fulfilled by those very dharmas, together with their opposites, [the attainment is] complete.
The goal to be attained is Brahman alone and no other fruit whatsoever; therefore, the principle of "as is one's intention, so is one's attainment" (tatkratu-nyāya) is established.
In the second [section], the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*), differentiation among injunctions is regulated by means such as distinct words;
however, due to the unity of connection and so forth, it is otherwise when combined with what is fixed. That same principle applies to the [injunctions] regarding knowledge (*vidyā*).
Therefore, at the outset, the method for other recensional branches (*śākhāntara*) was stated by that very same [principle], because there is no difference in the impulsion (*codanā*) and so forth.
Having first raised [the objection] by means of scripture itself, he then refuted it by stating that those [passages] have a different meaning intended to establish difference.
In different branches (śākhās), there is a different method of treatment, and moreover, the same [text] is heard without distinction;
therefore, it might follow that there is a difference in the knowledge (vidyā). However, both of these [arguments] are untenable because of the difference among the students.
Since the scriptural statement says "of those very [students]," any suspicion of difference arising in some cases is unjustified.

For here, in the context of private recitation (*svādhyāya*), the term "Brahman-knowledge" (*brāhmī vidyā*) must apply, because it is stated that [the result] follows from that specific vow (*vrata*).
If identity is established through the identity of form, what else remains to be integrated? If there were another quality, there would be no difference;
therefore, why this fruitless deliberation here? If it is argued thus, we say:
no, for while the identity of the object's form indicates identity, some further limb [of the text] is drawn in.
In the case of action as well, it is exactly the same: the object of the verbal root is that which is distinct from the aspect of differentiation.

Even though there is a division of branches (*śākhā*), the *udgītha-vidyā* would be one and the same—just as previously stated—because the injunctions (*codanā*) and other factors are identical, which would eliminate the distinction; however, that is not so, because a difference in form is perceived in both cases.
For a disparity is established: in one case the singer (*gātṛ*) and the song (*geya*) are complete, while in the other they are incomplete.
Even the non-difference of the remainder does not establish non-difference; however, difference would be established even when there is unity.

The word *udgītha* in the Chāndogya refers to the whole [Sāman], because it is established by its initial context; however, for the Vājasaneyins, it would denote only a part of it due to the absence of such contextual restriction. Furthermore, their mention of the *udgītha* as being in the singer is not figurative, as it stands at the beginning of the section.
For that [cessation] is to be accomplished by the agent; there is no contradiction in stating that the pacification of the enemy is its result.

Although the non-Vedic sciences (*abrahmavidyā*), being motivated by worldly aims such as the humiliation of others, are not to be accepted in the treatise on liberation (*mokṣaśāstra*), some maintain that even these are to be examined with equanimity.
For even the sciences pursued for specific desires (*kāmyā vidyā*) are useful for the Vedic sciences (*brahmavidyā*) by way of removing what is undesirable.
Others say that there is a corresponding observation based on the various distinctions of those respective objects to be accomplished.
How indeed could one who does not know the true nature of the heart reflect upon it anywhere as being seen within the heart?
Therefore, for such people, there would be no occasion for investigation here;
rather, they might [merely] attribute an excess of potency to ritual acts in the bestowing of their own fruits.
That [result] is required for the present context because it generates an excellence in the purposeful action of meditating upon the Brahman.

If it is argued that because of equality in terms of being the "eldest" (*jyeṣṭha*) and "most excellent" (*śreṣṭha*), and so on, the *Vāsiṣṭha* version appears in some places to be superior, and therefore the knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇavidyā*) found in many Vedic texts should be distinguished due to such differences in form—
this is not so; for there is no difference in the description of how speech and the other [senses] are subject to their respective qualities.
If speech and the other [senses] do not perform their respective functions, there would be no difference [between them] based on that alone.

Indeed, [the author] will state that "due to the difference of various sounds and so forth" the Brahma-vidyā is distinct; for the form of one vidyā read within a specific context should not be applied elsewhere.
Therefore, those qualities beginning with truthfulness and their opposites must be established as being restricted to their respective contexts.
Do not say so; for here it is the understanding of the true nature of Brahman that is required in all cases.
Reality (*satyatva*) resides in the cause of the universe due to its abandonment of the manifold web of transformations of the conscious and the unconscious;
knowledge (*jñānatva*) resides in it because of its nature as a knower, and because of its self-luminosity through an abundance of light.
Here, everything else is measured by the three, two, or one determinations (*paricchitti*), while Brahman is other than that.
Its infinity arises from the perpetual separation of that abode of stainless bliss from even those three.

It may be argued that since the status of being the cause of the entire universe was stated in the *Janmādi-sūtra*, the nature of Brahman is already understood through that alone; therefore, the mention here of "truth" (*satya*) and so forth is redundant. This is not so, because if the Lord were merely the cause, there would follow the contingency of Him being subject to the various defects inherent in other causes.
For when [the mind] is mounted upon doubt, its success is achieved through the gradual differentiation of the alternatives.

But surely, meditation (*ādhyāna*) can also occur by means of "beloved ones" and so forth, taking the form of a head, wings, tail, and so on? Certainly; in that case, the understanding [of Brahman] occurs through those "beloved ones" and the like, for they are present in all [beings].
However, let there be no [meditation] by means of parts such as a tail in that which is partless, nor is there the perception of that [partless reality] in a superior principle.
Therefore, just as in the case of the commencement with the funeral fire (cityāgni), the description provided here in the Brāhmaṇa should be understood accordingly.
Some here understand the word "ānanda" in the Sūtra as primarily denoting bliss; others see it as naming the bliss of dharma, or as expressing both.
And when there is a mention of knowledge, this is likewise so; one should not entertain doubt as long as there is equality with the other.
For that long, the practice of the Dharma is established here among many inhabited lands, O Brāhmaṇī.
One might argue that the injunction "one should sip water" (ācāmet) here prescribes a previously unestablished act of sipping for one who possesses the knowledge of the vital breaths (prāṇavidyā).

This is not so; for such an act is already established by Smṛti and other sources. What is enjoined here is merely the contemplation of the vital breaths as being one's clothing, which is not otherwise established. Furthermore, even an injunction that rests upon an already established verbal root-meaning—such as "one should eat"—is logically consistent with this context.
The science of breath (prāṇavidyā) previously mentioned is now considered here as an ancillary limb of that [science], at this opportune moment.

The wearing [of the garment] at the beginning and at the end is declared to be the "enclosing" (*paridhi*); moreover, the *mantra* seen here is for the purpose of pleasing one who is to be propitiated. It would not be a hymn of praise intended to celebrate the attainment of a [new] state of existence.
Furthermore, because it is something not previously established, the intention of the injunction is that one should "put on" [the garment] by means of the word.
The vital breath is to be honored; one who is clothed in garments is joined by the virtuous with waters.
When there is identity of the branch (śākhā), there can be no difference in the students, nor is any other quality to be enjoined;
therefore, why should the hearing of the aforementioned non-distinction not here again divide the knowledge?
Do not say so; for although it is a restatement (anuvāda) and does not serve to enjoin a new quality, nevertheless—
For the sake of clarity and ease of understanding, and because their unity is established through the principle of the resolution of calamities, [the individual instances] are treated as one.
The Śāṇḍilya-vidyā clearly appears not to have been recited by the Chandogas and the Vājasaneyins;
why, then, was the reflection upon difference and non-difference not demonstrated here by the authors of the Bhāṣya? To this we reply:
wherever there is an additional recitation, there [the inclusion] of those additional [elements occurs].

This is because it is stated in common [regarding all categories] that [the inclusion of one in another] may be either more or less than [the original], depending on whether it is joined with internal inclusion (antarbhāva) and so forth.

If it is argued that because the *Śāṇḍilya-vidyā* is studied in two locations—one devoid of powers such as *vaśitva* (mastery) and the other endowed with them—a distinction between the two must be postulated here, we say no. For even the powers like *vaśitva* mentioned in the *Āraṇyaka* are indeed an expansion of the quality of "truthful resolve" (*satya-saṅkalpatā*);
and since the version studied in the *Agnirahasya* lacks these additional qualities, there is no sublation of the identity of the *vidyā* here.
Worship of the Blessed One, who is indicated by the eye and the sun, would be one because there is no difference in the injunctions and so forth;
therefore, there would be no restriction regarding the names. This is not so, because of the difference in form due to the location.
The location is taught for the purpose of the cognition of being situated therein; if it were not so, there would be no extension of the form.
Therefore, from the conjunction of the sun and the eye, those two names, "Ahar" and "Aham," should be established.

If it is argued that the multitude of qualities beginning with "accumulation" (*sambhṛti*) should be connected to all meditations (*vidyās*) because they are not mentioned in the specific context of each, we say no; for in some cases, they are established by indicative mark (*liṅga*) where there is no other way.
In meditations occupying a small space, the qualities whose nature is not yet fully integrated function in their own appropriate place;

however, in the case of the meditation on the heaven-pervading one (*dyu-vyāpti*), because of its recitation together with a single mantra, the other qualities occupy the same position as that [central] one.
It is incorrect to claim that there is no difference between the two knowledges concerning the Person because of the identity of their designations;
for here, due to the arrangement of forms such as sacrifice and so forth, a distinction in form is well-established by their dissimilarity.
Furthermore, since they have that same purpose, liberation—the fruit of supreme devotion—is restated here just as it was in the Taittirīya.
In the Chāndogya, however, the fruit is said to be a full lifespan; thus, there appears to be a difference in the connection between these two [texts].

If it is argued that since the distinction between the forms [of the mantras] and so forth is clear, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the identity of the person and the knowledge (*vidyā*)—based merely on the similarity of names and such—is weak, and thus the application (*adhikāra*) is fruitless; we say no.

For the *nyāsa-vidyā* recited in this context is indeed distinct, as its primary purpose is the injunction for that [application]. Therefore, the differentiation between these two is highly meaningful for the sake of establishing their independence and other attributes.

If it is thus argued that the vision of sacrifice (*yajñadṛṣṭi*) is enjoined regarding the Person who knows the Supreme (*paravid*), then how is it that various elements not belonging to the limbs of the sacrifice are imagined here and there in connection with that [Person]?
Therefore, some say that this is appropriately a praise of the knowledge under discussion; others say otherwise.
Let this matter rest; for even in both ways it is easily established, yet the tradition itself must be considered.

The mantras beginning with "śannaḥ," which are recited in the vicinity of the Brāhma-vidyā, would apply to all vidyās because they serve that purpose; this is not so, however, due to the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that they are subordinate to the study [of the specific vidyā] mentioned therein.

Otherwise, other mantras such as "śukram pravidhya" and the like—which are recited in proximity and serve that same purpose—would also [apply to all vidyās], yet this is not tenable because [the former case] is weaker than the indicative mark.
Two branches declare that those who possess liberation abandon both merit and sin at some point;
another states their entry [into the Self] at the time of the transition of the legacy for the beloved and its opposite;
and in some places, it is taught separately as "forsaking" (hāna) and "taking up" (upāyana)—thus is established the connection between what is separately recorded in scripture.
For a statement located in another recension indeed becomes a supplementary part of a sentence through the expectancy of what has been enjoined.

Thus, let the abandonment of the duties of the Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya [castes] be associated with other transitions; however, there would be no fixed rule regarding contemplation (*cintā*) because it is not recited separately. This is incorrect, as the proposed construction is defective. For all those destined for liberation, both [the abandonment and the contemplation] are equally to be accomplished according to their respective modes of worship (*upāsti*).
He is absorbed in thought regarding that [reality], for he knows its greatness; thus he should be established as being in both states.

Whatever auspicious or otherwise [karma] has been established by him in the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) is to be experienced by that very person; therefore, it is incorrect to say that one who hates the Vedic rites would not fall [into hell], such as the Sūhmadi and so forth.
For whatever karma falls away from the wise man through the greatness of knowledge (*vidyā-māhātmya*), that is equivalent to what was to be accomplished by that [karma].
For the intended meaning of the statement is established by its declaration that this is the fruit of hatred toward and devotion to the wise.

In a certain Upaniṣad, the "shaking off" (*karmoddhūti*) of karma for one desiring liberation is heard of as occurring on the path after death; in another [text], it is said to occur in two ways here [in this life]. Let that reflection remain or not. For it is not stated that the fruit is accomplished by karma on the path, nor is there the persistence of a body for the sake of traveling.
For the sake of liberation, knowledge alone should effect it; in the statement regarding the destruction of sin, the meaning is more powerful than the literal reading.

If the karma of the knower were to perish entirely here, merely upon resting within the limit of the gross body, then the scriptural statement "for him it lasts only so long" would lose its significance. Furthermore, it would be untenable [to claim] that after departing and attaining [Brahman], there is no manifestation [of the self]. Thus, [the opponent's position] is incorrect.
There may be a connection with subtle latent impressions (saṃskāra) that follows [the mind] and causes it to remain in a state of mere contraction of the intellect.

If it is argued that the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*) must be the fruit in all *brāhmaṇa*-meditations because it is taught in connection with the study [of the Vedas], and thus its consideration is restricted to this specific context, we say no;
for there is the scriptural statement, "All those who know thus," as well as the subsequent mention, "And those who... [in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*].
On this common path, by following it, his concern is exactly like that [of others].

The Yogi, who bestows liberation upon the seeker by teaching the two paths of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, has sung that no one at all can ever forget this pair of methods. Therefore, through the reflection on the words of those like us who have studied and clarified them, [one attains realization].
The method for contemplating the path is that which has been prescribed through the complete application [of meditation] suitable for attaining the state of a Brahmin.

What has been stated by the authors of the Sūtras regarding the contemplation (*cintana*) of the path beginning with light (*arcis*) and so forth, for the purpose of establishing its being an auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyāṅga*) and the like—if that were the case, then this would belong to the immediately following section (*pāda*).
Let it not be so; for even if it were an auxiliary to knowledge, this [contemplation] is like ritual worship (*bhajana*), since there is no difference in its nature as a form of cognition (*dhī*).
In this context, the formulation of that [sūtra] is placed here because it serves as the basis for explaining the case endings (vibhakti) derived from nouns such as *karman* and others.

If it is asked: "In which [qualification] are non-stoutness (*asthūlatva*) and so forth recited as appropriate for contemplation, and not in another? For if there is no restriction regarding the loss of honor, why should one be restricted to this and not that?"—the answer is no.

Because the removal of defects inferred from their causes is prescribed here in all the *brāhma-vidyās* by the sequence stated in the qualification for bliss (*ānanda-adhikāra*), and thus this rule is universal.

If it is argued that since the comprehension of the essential nature [of Brahman] has already been stated through [qualities] such as truthfulness— which apply to all meditations (vidyās)— this present section concerning additional attributes similar to those would be entirely redundant, we say no;
for in some cases where the essential nature is known through certain [attributes], something else belonging to another [source] must be negated.
Because there is no comprehension of the essential nature through exclusion, even perception is thereby obstructed.

If it were the case that because the things to be excluded are infinite, their exclusion would also be infinite, then the investigation of them would be achievable only by an omniscient being; like crossing the ocean, it could not be taught. Do not say so! For when all particular differences are subsumed under the inclusion of their respective common properties (*sāmānyadharma*), such an investigation is possible; thus, let this "comprehensive summary" (*saṃgraha*) be accepted as unsurpassed.

Because it accords with the natural sense of the Sūtra, the placement of the "possessor of breath" (asubhṛt) first in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and of the "Brāhmaṇa" in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is intended to dispel even slight doubts regarding the course of the topical section (*adhikaraṇa*).

Considering that for those who reflect upon the two statements beginning with "the Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇa*), no other doubt would arise at all, the Bhāṣya has subsequently adopted the prima facie view as referring to the Supreme Self (*paraviṣaya*).

Regarding the statement "That which is directly [the Brahman] in that sun-peak" and "That which is indeed [the Brahman]," although there is a distinction in the responses, it does not differentiate the form [of the object].

Even if it is argued that this difference in the questioners implies a difference in the knowledge [sought], this is not so; for since the inquiry is repeated and the subsequent removal of faults is stated here, no distinction is produced, as both are common to all.

Just as in the *Sadvidyā* section, where the difference in the answers follows the difference in the questions, thereby revealing the supreme deity as the single object qualified by those attributes even though the knowledge is one—
so it is here. Therefore, Uṣasta and Kahola, having combined what was heard from each other, [attained the same realization].
"Let them meditate on the Brahman as the innermost of all"—therein, it is fruitful, together with the practice of sacred conduct (*brahmacarya*).

If it be argued that the Tāṇḍins declare "ether" (ākāśa) to be the place where [Brahman] lies down and the Vājasaneyins teach that by means of it knowledge is divided, and therefore there is a difference in the object of knowledge— this is not so, because this instruction regarding Brahman here is of two kinds;
for the word "ether" used by the Sāma-singers refers to the Supreme (Brahman), preceded by its being the support of all.
By the statement that it is the substratum of the Lord of All, its scope is the cavity; its form, however, is not otherwise.
"The object of meditation for the Chandogas is well-known here as being endowed with eight qualities and favored by the heart;
while for others, it is composed of [qualities] beginning with mastery (*vaśitva*). Let there be a difference in their forms.
"Do not say so; for even that mastery and the rest are here nothing other than the quality of having true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatā*)."
Thus, since this identity is firmly established, the meditation on the "small" (dahara) which follows is likewise easily understood.

If it be argued that "Surely space is superior to qualities and so forth," as was stated previously in the *Dahara-adhikaraṇa*, and therefore there is no room for suspicion of another meaning, and thus this present section does not arise— [we reply]: No, for those who proclaim that the *dahara* is the material cause (*upādāna*), while that which transcends space is the efficient cause (*nimitta*).
Previously cast aside as a consequence, they are here once again rendered rootless.

Even the meditation on the *udgītha* and other auxiliary parts of the ritual may, according to the principle stated regarding the *parṇa*-wood and so forth, be an auxiliary to the rite; however, the mention of its fruit here is merely praise, as that [claim of a fruit] is refuted by the analogy of the *godohana* vessel.
While things such as heaven constitute the fruits in the context of sacrifices, here—in this additional case—it is simply an excellence of potency (*vīryātireka*).
In the case of being made of leaves and so forth, the sentence does not state instrumentality; rather, it declares [them] as objects for meditation.
Regarding the meditation on the *udgītha* as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), another fruit has been mentioned that differs from the fruit produced by the ritual;
having accepted that, the previous inquiry stands as it was, and thus the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is refuted here—do not say so.
For those whose minds are fixed upon the status of this [meditation] as a non-ancillary (*anaṅga*), there arises a doubt regarding the identity of the knowledge (*vidyaikya*) therein.
Having abandoned the states of being with limbs and without limbs, whether separately or not separately, there would be such a consideration regarding what precedes.

On the strength of the statement, "And these desires are true," it is improper to claim that the meditation on Dharma is distinct from the meditation on the attributes of Dharma, and thus the enumeration of the possessors of those attributes (the guṇins) should be performed once according to the principle of *tantra*.
Rather, because each specific qualification differs, the repetition of the contemplation of the possessors of the attributes must be performed for each individual injunction (*vidhi*).
For because of the distinctness [of Indra] from his status as king and so forth, the offering of the oblation to Indra occurs repeatedly.

The claim that "the worship of another [deity] composed of qualities is the cause of enjoyment, and liberation shall follow in due course from the realization of those respective enjoyments"— this is a false statement regarding qualities, as it is merely a figurative designation for something else.
For where in this scripture, up until its conclusion, is any fruit declared to be achievable through the worship of the qualityless?
And one should not formulate anything contrary to the scriptures; this quarter [of the treatise] is renowned for its restriction of qualities.

If it is argued that since each [quality] is meditated upon individually, or even when the entire collection of qualities within the small space (dahara) is contemplated, the repetition of the substratum (guṇin) is necessarily implied by the sense of the context, how then can there be a doubt regarding its non-repetition?
We say no; for once the form of the substratum has been firmly established in the intellect through the qualities, it becomes something other than that [mere collection].
Knowledge alone [is the means], because of the engagement in reflection upon that repetition which is joined with its repetition.

The discussion of the dahara-vidyā has proceeded, and it is clearly known from the Taittirīya that the subsequent section (the ūrdhvānuvāka) is intended for the determination of the subject matter concerning the *prakṛti* (the primordial source). Let it not be so;
for here, by means of those very words uttered in each respective vidyā, the Supreme Person is made recognized.
In that regard, the sentence [of scripture] indeed possesses greater force than the ritual context (prakriyā) when it declares the state of being Nārāyaṇa.
The meaning is that, since all matters are established by these statements, the meditation on the "small" (dahara) is also included here;
for a portion endowed with its own characteristic marks does not require much effort to be reconciled with one [central] goal whose purpose is already attained.
Furthermore, the context would not assist this single [meditation], nor would it be fit to serve as the basis for everything.
Since the intent here is clearly upon reality itself, the attempt to abandon it is futile.

The wise do not respect such unskillful assertions as "the identity of the self," "the identity of the deity," "the equality of the three as established by the Trika system," or "the sovereignty of the three [deities] over others";
for the Upanishads (trayyantair) speak with one voice, and the words of Vyāsa and other principal authorities are in accord with them.
The glorious Nārāyaṇa is our Lord, whose body is the entirety of all things; he is the bestower of liberation and the object of enjoyment for those who are liberated.
It might be argued that the "limb" (aṅga) belongs to the sacrifice already established by the previously mentioned brick-built altar—

just as the mental fire-altars beginning with the *manas-cit* are limbs of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) because their potency is extended there— but this is not correct, for what is presented here is a primary constituent (*aṅgin*) consisting of knowledge.
The extended application (atideśa) is for the purpose of making known the equality of assistance in that [case] by means of direct scriptural statement (śruti) and so forth.

In this context, the sacrifice (*kratu*) consisting of ritual action must be postulated; yet even that appears here as one composed of knowledge (*vidyāmaya*), brought forward by the power of the previously acquired auxiliary elements and by the subordinate members residing within the sentence. For the connection with those drawn from a distance is inferior to the connection with those drawn from what is recited in its own statement.
For injunctionality is indeed resorted to even in the case of what is equal to a restatement when the object has not been previously attained; so it is here as well.

If it is argued that the intellect (*buddhi*) conceives of itself as the "I" during its engagement with the self while wearing the "sheath" (*kañcuka*), and that this occurs due to proximity—just as when one says "Worship me"—we say no, because the connection is otherwise.
For here, the pure Self is the goal to be realized; the notion of a fruit is invariably concomitant with the function of the knower.
When there exists an internal factor in close proximity to the intellect, the accomplishment of the principle of "as was his resolve" (tatkratu-nyāya) is determined by scriptural injunction.

It is appropriate to consider only the agent’s status as an enjoyer when effort is made for the sake of observed enjoyment; even the transition to another body for the sake of heaven and so forth is merely governed by one's own specific qualification.

However, regarding the goal of liberation, because of the teaching on the state of attainment and meditative concentration (*praṇidhi*), the statements concerning the principle of "according to one's resolve" (*tatkratu-nyāya*) [apply].
Since the object is the form of that which is to be meditated upon as endowed with those [qualities], how can there be any suspicion of over-extension (atiprasaṅga) or similar faults?

Since there is a diversity among the various branches of knowledge (*vidyā*) due to the differences in the forms of the objects to be known, even when the object of meditation is stated as it is, that which is to be attained is indeed established as being endowed with all [attributes]. Thus, how can there be a prohibition against reflecting upon the object to be attained?
Therefore, the reflection belongs to the bound soul; the primary meaning of the word "I" (*ahaṃśabda*) is not thereby defiled.
However, from the statement of Prajāpati, its status as something to be meditated upon is established by means of a state free from impurity.
[Objection: This injunction for worship must pertain to specific instances such as the *udgītha*, because it occurs in proximity to its own [specific] chant (*sāman*).
[Reply: It is not so; for here, the presence of all [instances] is established through the gateway of the sacrifice (*kratu*) which comprises all constituent parts (*aṅgin*).
Just as in the case of rice (*vrīhi*), even though the action depends on a specific individual, it applies generally when no restrictive rule is observed.
The scriptural text speaks only of the *udgītha*, and not of a distinction; thus, the "Chāga-logic" has no application here.

The individual Vaiśvānara-selves are indeed distinct because they are described as yielding specific fruits; however, the mention of fruits in the context of the meditation on the whole is merely praise. Or rather, the one whose form is the whole is also to be meditated upon.
Do not say so; for the defect in meditating on the parts has been stated separately, and the mention of their fruits must be taken as praise.
And since it is observed in such cases as the Hṛṣṭākapāla and others, it should therefore be considered to apply to all [such instances].

When there is a firm connection with the whole alone through the function of the purport of the great sentence (*mahāvākya*), then— having restated the individual parts— their status as subordinate (*anyaparya*) is established by the rule of praise (*stuti*) due to the mention of a fruit;
for in the *Bhūma* passage, a fruit is required as a limit for the meditation on Name and the other categories.
Nor has any such transgression been heard of in scripture; therefore, this unequal analogy does not establish the point.

Indeed, the fruit to be known in all branches of knowledge (*vidyā*) is that very same thing, and thus they are designated as "knowledge of Brahman" (*brahmavidyā*); likewise, since meditation and other practices have a single goal, the injunction regarding their performance is such that there is a unity of all *vidyās*.
However, because of the difference in names and forms, when the injunction is conditioned by those [names and forms], a specific distinction (*vaiśiṣṭya*) is established through them.
The fruit of the knowledge of the honey-verse (madhuvidyā) and others is mixed, and likewise it is so in the case of various optional rites (kāmyavidyās).

How could the author of the Sūtras have stated, "Because of the difference in various words and so forth," when there is no difference in the word [denoting Brahman], since these [means] are not distinct like sacrifice, giving, and the rest, because their perfection is established in devotion?
True; this difference of words is merely figurative, intended to strengthen the perception of a difference in form.
And since knowledge is not something that can be enjoined as an instrument, the intention of the Elder [Prabhākara] was to refute that [view].

Alternatively, by stating "because of the difference in words and so forth," the author of the Sūtras has correctly distinguished between ritual performance (*nyāsa*) and meditative worship (*upāsana*), based on a non-figurative difference in words— just as one speaks of "sacrificing" and "offering oblations"—
as well as a difference in name, form, and so on, which is heard in scripture and is equal in other cases; furthermore, the qualification (*adhikāra*) is distinct.
And they declared that there is a systematic arrangement regarding the worship of Madhu and others, based on the attainment of quick results and so forth.

Just like the Jyotiṣṭoma and Agnihotra sacrifices, the various Brahma-vidyās ought to be combined for the sake of attaining superior bliss; yet, no injunction for their worship would apply toward a single goal.

Since they can be performed at different times, there is no mutual contradiction in the stabilization of their latent impressions (*vāsanā*); and thus, for one who has attained the complete Brahman, there is a separate injunction here for meditative absorption (*samādhi*) at the time of death.

Surely, due to the specific differences among form and the other [objects], the worship of the Supreme is not uniform; being differentiated according to the diversity of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), its fruit would logically be considered unequal.
This would not be so, for it will be stated that even in all the sciences (*vidyās*), there is equality of enjoyment as the fruit.
And the attainment of unity by those who follow many paths is well-known both from worldly experience and from the Veda.

Having set aside the relative gradation of fruits in various meditations (*vidyās*), [the author] now, by way of a digression, raises an objection against the previously stated fruit of the *udgītha* meditation and strengthens his position:
"Let it be that no fruit was mentioned in its own scriptural passage; however, the rule regarding the *parṇamayi* [wooden ladle] and so forth does not apply here."
Indeed, knowledge is clearly established here as being the instrument for the fruit, even from the statement regarding its present existence.

The scriptural mention of ritual action here does not convey subservience to that [action], because it merely indicates the locus and the object; furthermore, a statement of counter-injunction is appropriate when there is a loss of knowledge for one who seeks its fruit.
Let there be praise for the *tāra* together with its meditation due to its following [the mantra]; yet by that much alone, it is not an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of the rite.
Having set aside what was to be said previously, this statement is placed here for the sake of introducing the subject to be established later.
The unity of the *vidyā*s, the division of the two *udgītha-vidyā*s, the oneness of the *prāṇa-vidyā*s,

the recurrence [of qualities] such as bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth in all [texts] like the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), the view of the abode of *prāṇa*, the identity of the *śāṇḍilya-vidyā*s, the division of the stability of "day by day" (*aharahaḥ*), and the limit of the location for the "accumulation" (*sambhṛti*).
The classification of male knowledge consists in the fixed rule of study for those beginning with the *śannaḥ* [mantras].
The mutual connection regarding abandonment and so forth, the appropriate time for that, equality with the path of the gods and other features,

the absence of grossness and other qualities everywhere, the transposition of attributes heard by various disciples, the unity of meditation on the *dahara* [small ether], and the injunction regarding the fruits of qualities— these are seen when relying upon the *udgītha*.
The cessation of the qualities within the possessor of qualities for the sake of the qualities is the final realization of the knowledge of the worship of the entirely supreme.

The mental fires (*manaścit*) and so forth are appropriately understood as having the form of knowledge (*vidyā*), situated within the sacrifice that is knowledge; the pure Knower (*kṣetrajña*) is not to be meditated upon [as the fires themselves], for the view of them as the qualities of the sacrifice is applied to the *udgītha* and other elements.
Thus, the worship of Vaiśvānara is performed in its entirety, and the justification for various forms of knowledge (*vidyā*) is established.
Furthermore, for those seeking liberation, conceptualization leads to uncertainty; thus it is said here regarding the meditation on the *udgītha*.
"Surely, having first considered karma, it was stated that the Supreme Brahman is what must be known;
therefore, the statement here that [karma] is a subsidiary part of knowledge is again false, since it has been declared many times that [karma] is to be abandoned.
Do not say so. Karma itself is divided by its various applications through the presence or absence of specific qualities.
And there may be some merit known solely as the "new livelihood" which serves as the cause for the accomplishment of knowledge.

For one who knows the Supreme, renunciation consists in the abandonment of actions performed for the sake of desire; in some cases, it is the abandonment of unworthy actions; in some cases, it is the cessation of the notion of self-sufficiency, and in others, the cessation of the notion of self-interest unconditioned by spiritual means.
Herein, however, non-violence and other such virtues—which prevent harm and are common to all—are included.
It declares that even those things characterized by specific caste, stage of life, and so forth, serve as auxiliary limbs to meditation.

In the statement of the ignorant Mīmāṃsakas— that the Self is the agent of actions and that no Vedic text here [in this world] is superior to that, and therefore the Upaniṣads are useful only through that [agentive] cognition in sacrifices and the like;
and that the Vedic texts concerning the soul and other matters serve as auxiliary members (*aṅga*) to the injunctions for worship consisting of meditation upon those [texts]— [we reply:]...
Having cast aside other sectarian marks, he spoke for the sake of pacifying impurities and increasing the strength of sentient beings.
If the Supreme Brahman, the object of knowledge, is thus firmly established even by these eleven chapters,

why then should the science of Brahman be further disturbed by trivial arguments that are like inscriptions in the sky? Truly, for the sake of the welfare of the multitude of young students who are terrified by the quarrels of those of little learning and intellect, [the author] sets aside the position stated by Jaimini and others and refutes it.

The statement "only while acting" (*kurvann eva*) expresses that for one who knows the Supreme, there is a fixed rule of conduct; however, it does not—through either the intellect or the action—enjoin either subordination (*aṅgatā*) or primacy (*aṅgitā*).
The sentence merely restates that actions are performed preceded by knowledge for another purpose;
for this does not restate the Brāhmaṇa-knowledge, nor is the Udgītha-knowledge a subordinate part of ritual action.

Study is prescribed for the attainment of *svādhyāya* (Vedic recitation), just like the *āghāra* libation; it is not a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the subsequent ritual, whereas the comprehension of the meaning is indeed a subsidiary part of knowledge (*vidyā*). Furthermore, that [comprehension] which is superior [to mere recitation] is distinguished by its own nature and its fruits. In the sacrifices, only the constant knowledge of the Self is invariably required, and no other form of knowledge.
How can the renunciation of desires exist for one who possesses knowledge, if that [knowledge] is also a limb of those [desires]?

Knowledge is not a constituent part of sacrifices and the like, for we do not enjoin it only for those authorized for such rites; nor can it be said that it belongs to those specific rituals, because there are many diverse teachings to the contrary.
Furthermore, the rule regarding the perpetual celibate (*ūrdhvaretas*) is recited by the Jābālas and is likewise restated by others. Therefore—
In this context, however, the rule is that there is grasping through attainment even otherwise by itself; but when passion is present, it is the negation of that [attainment].
Let it not be argued that the mention of *rasatama* and so forth constitutes a praise of the subsidiary parts (*aṅga-stuti*) according to the principle of the *juhv-ādi* hymns;

for this is not so, as these are connected with original injunctions (*apūrva-nirdeśa*) that are devoid of the context of those specific injunctions. Furthermore, various injunctions based on those respective [qualities] are observed here in proximity to this.
Therefore, an injunction, when being postulated, is appropriate only for that which has no other purpose, is taught [by scripture], and possesses a fruit.
Furthermore, because there is no attainment (*prāpti*), neither a restatement (*anuvāda*) nor a figurative praise (*adhiropastuti*) is appropriate;

this is the course [of interpretation] when there is no other way within a single syntactical unit (*vidhyekavākya*). Since there is no attachment [to an alternative], there is no recourse here to that [restatement].
If a displacement (*utkarṣa*) is postulated for a case where no other way exists, then let it be done by force.
Since this statement occurs in the midst of the injunctions for the Vidyās, it must be intended for the purpose of the Vidyās.
Even if [the mantra] is for the purpose of knowledge (*vidyārtha*), it is improper to say that this praise is justified because of the mention of what is non-existent;

for if there were a transgression regarding a perceived object, then the act of "entering" (*viśayana*) would follow—this is merely the talk of a child. Furthermore, on the view that [the mantra] is to be restrained by reasoning, the Veda (*nigama*) would result in being a non-authority (*apramāṇa*) regarding this obligatory (*nitya*) [rite].
But here, since we wish to know the state of being thus, this speech is fruitful only for the purpose of enjoining a vision.
Let the various accounts of the *vidyās* be considered as intended for the *pāriplava* recitation on account of their greatness;
however, they should not be [separate] from the injunctions of the *vidyās*, since a syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) is observed with those [injunctions] read within the same context.
Furthermore, it is stated that in that [context], only the narrative accounts of Manu and others serve the purpose of the *pāriplava*.
Therefore, once that expectation has been satisfied, there is no assumption of a purpose for further subsequent explanations.

Furthermore, because knowledge is a subordinate member (*aṅga*) of sacrifices and the like, it would follow that those who are not entitled to the primary acts (the sacrificer) would nonetheless be entitled to the subordinate member;

thus, knowledge would not belong to those whose vital energy has been sublimated (*ūrdhvaretas*). This is not so, because it is stated that knowledge is a subordinate member fit for all various stages of life (*āśrama*).
Indeed, both in scripture and in tradition, the application of knowledge and the injunction [for its practice] are heard to be equal for all four stages.
Generally, due to the abundance of propriety, the sages have described the state of the stage of liberation (mokṣāśrama) in some places.

To say that knowledge is seen among those of perpetual celibacy (*ūrdhvaretas*) when the dharma of sacrifice and the like has been abandoned due to the injunction to worship another [deity], and therefore it might exist independently even in a householder, is an unconsidered statement.
That knowledge, understood through such scriptural texts as "by sacrifice" (*yajñena*), must be accomplished by him [the householder] through those very means.
The doctrine that [the word *brahma*] has the sense of "desire to know" (*jijñāsā*) is to be set aside according to the principle beginning with "one who wishes to go to a place," and so forth.

[Objection: But surely, in cases such as "he desires to go" (*jigamiṣati*), there is a loss of the sense of desire because there is no actual movement; and since this is stated by the Śruti, it is not so here either, for the absence of movement is the same.
[Reply: Desire arises from a particular state of the intellect (*buddhi-viśeṣa*); when that does not arise, it cannot be produced by ritual actions.
For one who desires to attain the inquiry, that knowledge is not something desired [only now], as it was already so previously.

But surely, in this case, this prescribed action should be applied toward the pursuit of desire; what then? Is it not the case that by generating a particular state of intellect for the sake of desire, [the need for action] would be averted?
Furthermore, you cannot deny the existence of various other injunctions for ritual action intended for the sake of knowledge.
Therefore, by the logic of profound reflection, the use of the prefix *sam-* reiterates the desirability of that which is to be enjoined.

It is incorrect to claim that these qualities— such as tranquility— belong exclusively to those other than householders, on the grounds that because householders are constantly occupied with sacrifices and other duties, their faculties are never at rest and thus they lack such qualities;
for even those established in renunciation and the like engage in various religious practices conditioned by specific motivations.
If one takes all that together, even that is equal here to the abandonment of the fruit and so forth.

Those who have recognized their own transgressions and, through world-renowned means appropriate for themselves, honor their lord with remorse, attain his service once his anger has been gradually pacified. In this way, may the illustrious Śrīdhara— whose benevolence is free from conditions and whose kindness is toward all— be attained by us without obstacle, through our respective offices divided according to what is prescribed by the scriptures as "this" or "that."

There is no restriction regarding food based on the statement of the one authorized for the science of breath (*prāṇavidyā*), because a prohibition that applies in general must be restricted when there is a powerful injunction; thus, it is incorrect [to claim otherwise].
Furthermore, in the event of a threat to life, the mention of permission may occur as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the injunction.
Behold these two [eyes] rejoicing in the state of Brahman, which possesses a greatness greater than that of being established in the vital breaths.
For the Vedic texts declare that the status of the various classes (*varṇa*) and so forth as auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) to the knowledge of Brahman is established through their ritual actions;

therefore, for one who does not abide in Brahman, since those [Vedic injunctions] do not apply, let there be freedom of action (*svairitā*). Not so. For its eternality is also established, in accordance with other states and the appropriate application (*viniyoga*) suited to it.
In this context, the ritual procedure (*tantra*)—as in the case of the optional *agnihotra* and other rites—is to be applied here even to the category of obligatory rites involving another's wife.

If it is argued: "How can there be the knowledge of the Veda for one who has become detached upon obtaining a wife and whose mind is indifferent even toward the stages of life (āśramas), and who has abandoned all dharmas without exception?"—we reply:
No, for even in that state, she [the Vedic knowledge] exists along with its limbs through the general duties of the castes (varṇadharma) conjoined with the discipline of their respective qualities.
This is observed in the case of Bhīṣma and others; however, in the case of a śūdra, there is an absence [of such power] due to the lack of an [appropriate] destination.
Suppose one who has ascended to the three stages beginning with the *naiṣṭhika* falls from them;
even there, let the *brāhmī* knowledge be effective when assisted by its own duties (*svadharma*) as performed during that state.
Do not say so, for although they do not desire such a fall, there are many means of purification (*śodhaka*).
Although that [offering] beginning with praise is worthy of all, he is not fit for it because of such a prohibition.
Sages declare that for minor transgressions and major sins, when such a fall occurs through negligence, the expiation for yogis is yoga itself.
Therefore, even for one who has fallen from yoga, there is still the qualification [to practice]; indeed, the scripture is not to be questioned.
However, the rule that "this is the expiation for as long as one lives" is the intention of the author of the Sūtras and others.

They declare that these persons are unworthy of being associated with the virtuous—even if they have been purified by penances—namely: one who kills a child, one who kills a woman, one who has come for refuge, and the ungrateful;
and the authors of the Sūtras have shown here that this course of action follows the Smṛtis and established custom.
If our scripture were subject to our own command, then the bridge of Dharma would be swept away.

Although they are equal in being parts of Brahman, because of the inequality of their qualities and their union with bodies whose natures are pure or impure, there is both permission and prohibition regarding looking upon, touching, and so forth.
This was previously set forth in aphoristic form; now, however, it is stated here again for the sake of pacifying the agitation caused by various types of taints.
Even though he had correctly realized the Self, he was awakened [to his duty] by means of conduct appropriate to his own body.
For meditation on the *udgītha* and so forth can indeed be performed here by the sacrificer himself, who seeks the fruit;
therefore, if it is argued that this [meditation] has him as its agent, it is not so, because it rests upon a ritual act performed by a hired officiant (*ṛtvij*).
Just as other injunctions regarding qualities and fruits are accomplished by the priest, so too is this one restated.
For feasibility cannot be a limiting condition (upādhi), because it is determined by the force of the injunction according to the relationship between master and servant.

Since it is heard that [the state] is to be reflected upon (*mantavya*), the word "muni" (sage) may be considered a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that; for no injunction (*vidhi*) is seen here, as scholarship (*paṇḍitatva*) has already been attained previously.
Indeed, scholarship follows immediately after hearing and reflection (*śravaṇa-manana*), which consist of the capacity for reasoning and refutation (*ūha-apoha*).
The renown of "mauna" (silence) refers to the excellence of reflection; this is the method of concentration upon the All-pervading One.
If it is argued that "the remaining [conduct] may be maintained through childhood; even for a learned man, such behavior is like the act of a child;
let it be so, for the state of being a child is not easy to maintain, and thus his independence is justified," we say no.
For he is restrained by the scriptural statement, "He does not cease from this until he has been struck down by misconduct."
The intention behind the rule prescribed by the Sage—that one should conceal one's own greatness—would be that it pertains to the regulations for childhood.
For those who worship for the sake of enjoyments, the arising of those [results] may occur instantly through the merits of their own kin;

however, heaven and the like are not possible here in this body, as their attainment occurs only through the purification of the internal mind. Therefore, the rule regarding bathing and atonement applies subsequently, because the possibility of obstacles has not been mentioned beforehand.
In rites such as the Kārīrī, even when performed by those worthy of it and with all their qualities, an obstacle may sometimes occur.

"Let there be an obstacle elsewhere; this most powerful action, characterized by dispassionate renunciation, is called 'withdrawal' (nivṛtti) and should immediately bring about the realization of Brahman.
"Not so; for if the offense against devotion to the Supreme Brahman should be more powerful than that," [it would prevail].
If, upon the pacification of that [defilement], its resulting [state] does not immediately arise, there will be the attainment of the practice of others.
In this [work], the pacification of the four obstacles is appropriately performed at all times to dispel the doubt that ritual acts do not lead to knowledge due to their potential failure,
and to establish the well-known fact that for one free from obstacles, the fruit is immediate; and this serves as a cause for the satisfaction of the virtuous.
At the conclusion of the [first] chapter, the author has placed the two sections concerning the scope of the rules and the qualification of the student.

If it is asked: "Is the occurrence of obstacles here appropriate for those whose actions are directed toward the knowledge of others? Since this [occurrence] has been described as the cause for the worship intended for the sake of enjoyment among those means, why is it mentioned here in vain?"—the answer is no; for the mind falls upon the optional rites with the notion that they are free from obstacles, and therefore, [this description serves] for the sake of abundant dispassion toward them.
There arises the possibility of obstacles to that [practice], and the desire for the goal of knowledge may become fruitful [only through its removal].

Knowledge (*vidyā*) has ritual action as its constituent part, being impelled by the intellect directed toward the most excellent essence; yet, because there is no attainment [of liberation] through it alone, the purpose of the narratives situated in proximity to the injunctions for knowledge is solely to enjoin that [knowledge].
That knowledge, along with its auxiliaries, exists even among those of perpetual celibacy (*ūrdhvaretas*), and among householders as well, it requires sacrifice, charity, and so forth.
Even a householder is fit for rites such as pacification when there is no calamity; for even a learned man achieves success through the purity of food alone.

They say that one who is separated from knowledge for the sake of the stage of learning (*vidyāśrama*) is not truly united with knowledge; yet, such a person is not excluded from the constituent parts of a sacrifice (*kratvaṅga*), nor is the state of a sage (*munitā*)—which consists of the performance of rituals and the accomplishment of meditation—denied to him.
Childhood is the concealment of one's powers and so forth from those who are more powerful; it is not a different kind of knowledge.
In this same way, it was stated in this quarter [of the verse] that the knowledge for the sake of liberation arises from its own generative merits.
Some of evil vision proclaim that the mere knowledge of the meaning of sentences is the means to liberation;

others consider the pair of knowledge and action as the instrument, holding them to be in conjunction. Others have declared the primacy of action, while still others desire a liberation that is unattainable.
All of those [objections] are also refuted here by the statement establishing the procedure for worship as an integral part of the ritual action.

Whatever suffering exists is not to be obstructed by one's own effort because it is fragile and momentary, nor is effort directed toward past objects effective; furthermore, future suffering is not easily avoided when its causes are complete.
Therefore, the injunction to act for the absolute cessation of suffering is only half-acceptable.
Because suffering is eliminated through the removal of its causal complex by means of supreme non-action performed via expiation.
You avoid things such as those hostile to kings and even snakes by means of an umbrella; you wear it before [any other protection].
I desire this here, thinking that evil karma bears fruit when no atonement is performed, and desiring the success of my own words by averting the future calamities that have been imagined.
Beholding this movement of one who is neither a child nor a beast, yet agitated by fear, remain thus in silent composure.

Those who claim that the goal or the means cannot be properly defined because they follow paths other than those prescribed by their own [traditions]— what is the purpose of their engagement in such debate, and why do they continue daily activities such as eating?
To argue that worship is fruitless because the eternality of liberation is established is also incorrect, because that eternality was not previously established.
But the Sāṃkhyas should be questioned here, as they assert that there is eternal liberation even while in the state of possessing the instruments [of action].
If liberation were non-existent, this entire means of attainment along with its accessories would be in vain;
if liberation were established through delusion, then as long as one remains within the nature of the self, there would be nothing but error here.
Thus, for one who asserts that the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is eternally liberated, the chapter on the means of attainment would be fruitless.
For liberation is held by those who know the system to be of the nature of destruction; but for us, it is of the nature of existence.

The self as a continuum undergoes destruction elsewhere through various states such as the skull and so forth; here, however, there is the destruction of the contraction of the intellect and its expansion into that which is not [previously] so, according to scripture. Others, however, maintain that the continuum of a liberated intellect consists in a flow of uniform cognitions (*dhārāvāhana*).
If the causal complex were a collection consisting of the will of Īśvara and so forth, there would likewise be no recurrence [of rebirth].
How could there be a doctrine of difference between Prakṛti and Puruṣa through their respective attributes?

The author of the Sūtras has first described, according to the order of generation (utpatti-krama), the means to liberation along with its auxiliary limbs as "Śrī"; he now reveals the fruit to be accomplished by that means for the wise, categorized by its various stages.
If it is accomplished in his gross body, he declares that by means of a pair of feet; but if it occurs after he has departed, he calculates that by means of another pair of feet.

If it is argued: "Since this knowledge has already been well-stated previously, why does he state it again? If there is something remaining, let it be told; otherwise, what was stated before will not connect with the result here"—we say no.
For while for others who are liberated, the proof is established through the essential concomitance (*avinābhāva*) of the subject at hand, for those whose proof is near at hand...
And here, the connection [of the narrative] serves to manifest the essence of steadfast devotion, which is equal to the state of liberation.

It was stated in the previous section that through pure and superior dharmas practiced in the home, the Vedic knowledge (brāhmī vidyā) shall come to be; however, its supreme nature has not yet been reflected upon exactly as it is.
Whether this occurs once or repeatedly—whether through perception or through memory—was not specified previously.
Furthermore, since it continues throughout one's life and so forth, its non-redundancy here is easily understood.

Knowledge is declared by the scriptures to be the means to liberation, yet its number is not specified; [one might argue] that there would be ease if it were singular, and thus the injunctions here would achieve their purpose through its correctness and permanence, rather than through repetition— this too is baseless.
Because, when there is a particular [case] following from a general statement, it is established that the principle of the "animal" (paśu-nyāya) finds its rest therein.
Furthermore, according to the principle of the *Āgneya* and other [passages], the word "knowledge" (*vidyā*) here denotes precisely the meaning of "meditation" (*dhyāna*);
and in the context of meditation, the term "worship" (*upāsana*) expresses the nature of service by way of supreme devotion.
Moreover, the two terms "knowing" (*vidi*) and "worshipping" (*upāsi*) are heard in scripture as being used interchangeably, signifying a single identical meaning.
In certain cases, where there is devotion toward an effect or a cause, the doctrine of a distinction between types of devotion is used figuratively.

The Supreme Self is attainable by that person who, among those striving in yoga, is the object of His own choice; and He is grasped because of being beloved, for even devotion arises from His qualities as taught in the scriptures.
That devotion is an intellect whose nature is love, and when it reaches its highest excellence, there occurs the non-sublation of memory [of Him]. Thus it is established.
And this is called the constant mindfulness (dhruvānusmṛti) because of its continuous flow, like a stream of oil.
Regarding passion and so forth, one must practice hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditation (*nididhyāsana*) as a single integrated process;

therein, the word "to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*) expresses its excellence through the state of extreme clarity. As for those who maintain that the vision arising from the word has the [Supreme Self] as its object, they do so because of the mention of "knowing" (*vedana*).
The elaboration of contradictions and so forth should be investigated here with subtlety by those who are skillful.

In the case of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), the application of the term "vision" (*dṛṣṭi*) would be merely figurative due to its clarity; likewise, for you as well, the word "vision" applies to the intellect (*buddhi*) when it is directed toward the eye.
Furthermore, the terms "smeller" (*ghrātṛ*) and "taster" (*spraṣṭṛ*) could not be used in their primary sense for that which is devoid of instruments.
Therefore, our own grasper, which possesses many logical merits, must indeed be abandoned for yours.

The arrangement of door and doorway cannot be established in any way if rest belongs to the particular; for if it were of the nature of the universal, it would not be easily grasped by the particulars, nor could it be conceived as identical with the agent.
Since the object is one, memory—though figurative—is appropriate when expressed through the term "perception" for the sake of establishing clarity.
That the term "seeing" is applied metaphorically to mindfulness is a different matter; for us, it is not [unreal] because of its result.

One who is incapable of performing the *kṛcchra* and other penances, yet possesses firm austerity and is worthy of self-restraint, should perform the recollection of Keśava for all purposes; thus it is appropriate that there be such an alternative according to one's fitness.
Because it is common to all, this [recollection] benefits one in all defects and in all occasional rites (*naimittika*).
The Sage also considers liberation here to have its root in that very same form of meditation.

But surely, it is said that those who have taken refuge in Mukunda, even if they are devoid of meditative yoga (dhyāna-yoga), transcend death and go to the supreme abode like those who practice self-restraint (yamin). True, they too [attain this]; however, this is because of the weightiness of the word "even" (api) [implying] a restriction of scope, as well as its lightness [in comparison].
The treatise on meditation, which has attained its purpose, was composed by yogis who possess the power of vows and are masters of yoga.

Dharma is worthy of praise and the like because it pacifies impurities and assists in the increase of the essence of being; likewise, surrender (prapatti) removes obstacles during times when there is no other recourse. Indeed, when one who is capable and compassionate has been chosen as a refuge, everything that is to be accomplished becomes easily achieved.
And it is heard in a certain mantra: "Desiring liberation, I take refuge [in You]."
The omnipresent Lord is declared to be absolutely distinct from the individual soul by means of defining characteristics and other proofs;
therefore, in this meditation for the sake of liberation where darkness has been dispelled, there is no room for arguments such as "I am Brahman.
For one who knows reality and is free from passion, the practice of meditating "I am He" is not appropriate here.
Therefore, even the expression "I" applies here in its primary sense to one's own inner self.
In the meditation on Vasu, Indra, and others, the contemplation of one's own self as conjoined with the *prakṛti* was previously described;

however, here, the pure, eternal, and all-pervading Self is likewise joined with itself. Nevertheless, when there is a distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), such a contemplation may occur through the use of words in different grammatical cases (*vyadhikaraṇa*).
The mention of "I-grasping" (ahaṃgraha) is for the sake of establishing the firmness of the realization of the true nature [of Brahman], which is dependent upon the Veda.
In the meditation on unity (*aikyopāsti*), how could there be the thought "I am you" or "you are I" regarding that which is without distinction?
The expression of difference and non-difference—such as the relationship between a hand, a jewel, and the space within it—is not primary.
Furthermore, for those who say "you are equal to me" or "I am equal to you," even a figurative usage (*upacāra*) is not appropriate.
Therefore, this cognition "I" with respect to the innermost Self of all is established by reason and its natural form.
Non-duality cannot be easily asserted when duality has been abandoned, because it is its very opposite;
yet duality contains non-duality within it, for these two here are indeed non-different from their own essential nature.
And such a state of both duality and non-duality would be established precisely through the non-abandonment of the rule of those two.
Everything would be established in its proper place for those who follow valid cognition, but not at all for others.
Surely, in non-duality, difference must be something established by delusion, like a flower in the sky, which is to be negated?
Not so; for if it were non-different from Reality, its establishment as being established by delusion would certainly not be possible.
And if its difference from that [Reality] is false, know that the answer has already been given.
If it is truth, then the admission of divisions within truth is merely a vain running away from afar.

If it is argued that even when viewing the Name and so forth as Brahman, the cognition "I am That" would arise as before due to the commonality of being meditation on Brahman—this is not so; for the inner self is not a mere symbolic representation (*pratīka*). It is in no way possible to view anything other than Brahman [as Brahman], because Brahman is the supreme of all.
When [the object] is perceived as something else, its apprehension here must necessarily be through its own specific characteristics.

Even if the self is not actually Brahman, let the perception of it as Brahman be fruitful in some way; yet this does not undermine the established nature of reality, just as the notion of being Garuda [does not negate one's actual identity].
One who quickly abandons even this much delusion—the conceit "I am this"—would attain liberation.
The state of the great serpent Nahuṣa, who had been cast down from his position by the pride of having usurped Indra's sovereignty.

Because the deities are subservient to that [purpose], and because the ritual act is enjoined as the instrument for producing the fruit, let there be the perception of the higher [deity] in the lower self, such as the Sun and so forth. It is not so; for even though the ritual act is enjoined as primary, it is merely a means for propitiating Him.
Since it is the deity herself, being pleased by that [action], who bestows the fruit, she is therefore the primary factor in effect.

In this context, the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*) is untenable because it involves seeing one thing as another; furthermore, if one holds the view that truthfulness (*yāthārthya*) is inherent in all cognition, then "seeing one thing as another" is logically impossible.

Therefore, in the first case (the theory of non-apprehension), there would be no dispute, for it is not disputed that error is a state of non-cognition; whereas in the second case (the theory of misapprehension), it is a doctrine of delusion.
Because it is by means of an injunction that one establishes a pair of cognitions whose intellects are afflicted by the non-apprehension of such a distinction.

If one denies the object to be seen, the resulting perception—being merely a wandering [mental] construction—would be the delusion of non-duality; therefore, in this context, the perception of suchness is prescribed as the supreme remedy. Some maintain that there is no fault in such a perception, according to the principle of the "seer of the eye" (*tākṣryadṛṣṭa*) and so forth.
Elsewhere, is not the other-view twofold—both in terms of individuality and in terms of genus—unapprehended?

For those whose minds are attentive, how can there be a perception of the *brāhmaṇa* as being only one primary thing? Some say it is by way of oneness; for no fault is to be suspected in a powerful injunction.
Others say that here, the conceptualization of difference arises from one's own whim, like the delusion of seeing two moons.
And just as in the Vedas, the ignorant wander about, perceiving Brahman in many diverse ways.

In the Vedic scriptures, yoga is not seen as belonging to one who is merely sitting; rather, they declare that "meditation is always [to be practiced]," and the rule regarding the grass mat, deerskin, and so forth, is an injunction of restriction intended for cases where sitting might be optional.

Therefore, this [yoga] would be possible for one whose senses are unshakable whether standing, walking, or lying down. But how could there be an uninterrupted continuity of cognition in one who is subject to effort and sleep, which are states not previously established [as conducive]?

For the sake of attaining one-pointedness of mind, they observe the discipline of place, time, posture, and so forth; yet, mindful that at other times it is also possible when there are intervals, they constantly reflect upon this.
With their minds fixed on the Supreme through the abundance of direct mental impressions, they maintain awareness of dependence and similar states.
For at the proper time, all the actions of the yogin indeed become acceptable through the practice of detached application.

That which has been declared here in the first [pāda] as being subordinate to ritual action and meditation, and that which was stated by the authoritative teachers to be the supreme dharma—namely, the vision of Brahman through yoga—is established as primary; therefore, the other [elements] should be understood as being subservient to it. And thus...
Generally, when a yoga has commenced, the application of time is determined by the degree of proficiency and lightness [of the practitioner].
It may be asked: "The ancillaries of knowledge (*vidyāṅga*) were mentioned previously; why then is there this further consideration of the ancillaries beginning with *āsana*?

Is it not sufficient to explain them by dividing the portion concerning perceptible objects? True, but the state of continuous flow known as meditation (*dhyāna*), which must be cultivated day after day, cannot be achieved without first establishing the ancillaries such as *yama*.
This is what must be elucidated: that [the goal] would be achieved through one-pointedness of mind, even in the absence of all other exertion.

If, within this very life, devotion takes the form of supreme meditation, then one’s ritual action would find its rest therein; however, it is improper to claim that thereafter the contemplation of Brahman is fruitless.
For in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, virtuous conduct throughout one's entire life is prescribed for the purpose of attaining the world of Brahman.
For that [practice] is indeed for the increase of meditative absorption (dhyāna), and it is also prescribed in some cases as lasting until death.
"It is taught by the lords of sages that karma which has not been experienced cannot be avoided even in a multitude of kalpas;
furthermore, the scriptural statement regarding the destruction of the attachment to sin and the mention of the glory of supreme knowledge [would otherwise be contradicted].
Let it not be so; for the statement "that which has not been experienced," etc., speaks to the firmness of karma in producing its fruit.
In this context, however, devotion to another [deity] is enjoined by way of expiation for the sake of pacifying the effects of one's actions.
Its nature as an expiation (niṣkṛti) is established for the purpose of uprooting the previously mentioned evil;

here, the principle of heaven and so forth does not apply. For when obstacles are removed, the transformation of the intellect occurs spontaneously. It should be maintained that the non-staining by sin is the endurance of what arises from negligence, in order to follow the command [of scripture].
If it were not so, there would be no possibility of liberation for one who has not ceased [from activity], because of the scriptural declarations and because of the engagement of yogis.
Non-attachment is the non-arising of the power of action; its cessation upon arising is destruction.
That power belongs to the Ordainer and consists of the bestowal of appropriate fruits in the form of punishment and grace.
As for the question, "How can there be atonement when [the fault] has not arisen?"—this is not to be questioned at all.
"Indeed, it is his very heart that must grasp this speech which is free from attachment, thinking, 'Let no unrighteousness befall him.'"
But one who knows the Supreme and is always vigilant does not, with deliberate intent, produce further evil;
rather, he quickly dispels what has arisen through appropriate remedial measures or consumes it.
This was seen in the case of Vṛtra and others, while the attainment of the King of Cedi and others resulted from the power of destiny.
The sage considers that liberation belongs here and now, or at some other time, to one who is established in Brahman through disciplined yoga.

For merit (dharma) cannot undergo either attachment or destruction through the favor of another’s enjoyment, as that would entail the consequence of it being a sin; moreover, the scripture declares that [the devotee] is liberated from all evil.
If it is argued that its merit is destroyed by enjoyments, that is not so, because even his desire-born (kāmya) acts are not considered sin.
Therefore, because its characteristics are not established, it is heard in scripture that it is not well-performed, and that this [action] possesses the nature of sin.
If merit is conducive to knowledge, it bears fruit here because it bestows that knowledge; however,
even that which is not useful for it should be avoided as a hindrance, like a sin— for instance,
when a servant of a sovereign is confined in prison by a pair of shackles.
At the time of softening, the gold and the black iron must be broken together.
