If one who is dispassionate does not desire that which is performed for the sake of a specific fruit, yet should perform it through the force of attachment, then that fruit arises from that; nor does one who is ignorant of Dharma bestow any fruit previously unearned.
Therefore, [the performance of rites] is sublated by the goals of knowledge (vidyā); if you ask what else could be more so, it is because [such acts] involve further obstacles.
There may be some attachment born of delusion toward other objects, yet there is no attachment whatsoever toward kinsmen, even when one feels remorse.

If it is argued that "the sin whose effects have already begun perishes for one who knows the Supreme," and that a distinction is made from the *niradhi* [state], and furthermore that "all evils" are said to perish—this is not so, because it is contradicted by perception and other means of knowledge;
for the *Sadvidyā* (Knowledge of Being) declares, "For him there is delay only as long as... and those who know the scriptures do not remember [any such destruction of karma].
Even terms such as "liberation while living" (jīvanmukti) are merely figurative; by them, the dull-witted are deluded.

There are methods for pacifying the onset of diseases and other afflictions, such as giving gifts and performing worship; moreover, the Lord himself has taught that even his own incarnation was subject to rebirth.
Therefore, it appears that the doctrine of the necessity of results regarding actions already begun is difficult to maintain—do not say so.
Indeed, for those who have not performed expiation, the necessity of the fruit [of their actions] is the desired view of the author of the Sūtras and others.
If there is contact with merits, then it must be admitted that he becomes bound by them;
if, however, there were no contact with them, then the culmination of merit would be fruitless for the knower of the Supreme hereafter.
Therefore, the claim that even dharma must be abandoned here according to the sequence of adharma is incorrect.
The dharma of the Agnihotra and other rites does not lead to bondage; rather, it nourishes the sprout of knowledge.

If it is argued that the statement "requiring all" (sarvāpekṣā) refers to the subordinate status of ritual actions in the enjoyment of the fruits of others' works, and that the subsequent mention of the Agnihotra and so forth also implies this, making the former statement redundant— this is not so;
for since knowledge is independent [of rituals], the suspicion that it might lack auxiliary support has already been refuted.
But here, the phrase "again" implies the consequence of an absence of cohesion; thus, a disparity in their respective principles is established.

From the phrase "pointed out from this body" (*nirdiṣṭāsmāccharīrāt*), it follows that the word "as long as" (*yāvat*) and so forth refers to *prārabdha* karma—that is, karma whose effects have already begun—and thus [liberation] for the knower lasts only until the end of that body.
This is not so; because of the diversity of *prārabdha* karma, the word "as long as" cannot function to establish that specific limit, as it would otherwise be redundant.
Furthermore, for one whose final body possesses firm and emerging meditative absorption, liberation follows from the recollection of previous births.
But surely, the word "asmāt" (from this) here would be redundant; it would not apply to the body, for its purpose is established by the fact that it aims to illustrate the likeness to a prison.
Indeed, the Lord himself sang, "This world is full of suffering," in order to manifest that it must be abandoned.
And by qualifying this [earth] as "the abode of beings," Manu reveals its nature as something to be abandoned.

All living beings are equal by their very nature; here, diverse karma is indeed beginningless and uniform, so defects such as inequality do not arise in the Lord. Otherwise, there would be a violation of the scriptures. Therefore, an objection regarding delay in liberation and the like is of little substance.
In the manifold stream of karma, all tantras maintain that the distinction between the time of the action and the time of the fruit is dependent upon the specific nature of the act.

The knowledge of Brahman is to be repeated; and the contemplation of the Sun and other deities upon the symbols (pratīka) that are limbs of ritual action may or may not be repeated. Furthermore, such meditation (praṇidhi) should be performed daily along with its prescribed seat.
Regarding sin and merit, there is destruction and so forth; however, their state as objects of experience persists as long as the effects of past actions (ārabdhakārya) remain.
It has been stated here that "the state of being an effect" refers to its own appropriate manifestation, and liberation occurs when that which has begun has ceased.

In the second chapter, the true nature of the living being (*jīva*) was skillfully expounded through its eternality, omniscience, and other attributes; then, the exhaustion of the great traveler through the forest of the world was described during the states of waking and so forth. Furthermore, that which is the supreme object of meditation for the seeker from the beginning of his spiritual practice until its conclusion has been stated.
He describes the commencement of the departure for one who abandons the body here at the conclusion of the *prārabdha* (the karma that has already begun to bear fruit).
Although such agitation of the subtle body and its collection of organs occurs in one who has reached the stage of detachment (*vairāgyapāda*), nevertheless,
this connection is provided here to make known that death may occur even for a knower of Brahman at any time.
Furthermore, a general statement is appropriate here in order to describe the specific details regarding his departure from the body (*utkrānti*).
Speaking even of death as being among the fruits of knowledge, he says that which is dear to him should be contemplated.

If it is argued that the meditative contemplation (*cintana*) of this [meditation on the vital breath] does not have its fruit here— whether one adopts the order beginning with speech (*vāk*) or some other order, or the order explicitly stated by the Śruti— itself, we say no;
for the scriptural teaching of this attainment (*sampatti*) would not be appropriate as something purposeless if it were not constrained by such a specific sequence.
Therefore, it must be established as appropriate that such reflection is beneficial in some way or another.

In order to pacify the agitation caused by the various disputes and arguments that disturb the community of the Vedas, [the scriptures] have declared that for the knower, both the commencement of the work already begun and the equally effective departure at death are the same; or else, they have stated that the individual soul is eternally liberated, or that liberation occurs while still living.
He will explain in detail, starting from the piercing and entry into the channels, for the sake of attaining the state of Brahman.

Having perceived here that his own life-limit is beset by many undesirable things, the yogin should do what he ought to do; however, that which one does for one's sons and others is not to be done here—this is why it was not mentioned.
Furthermore, that which was prescribed in the Gītā and other texts for the time of death is also a method of prior yoga.
In this context, the understanding should be cultivated as before: that whatever is attained will necessarily correspond to its own nature.
"The group consisting of action, knowledge, and the senses does not undergo dissolution in the mind, because it does not originate from that [the mind];
since its activity is dependent upon it, the word 'attainment' (sampatti) here refers to its cessation.
This is not tenable, because if both were to dissolve, the resolution of the objection would be identical.
The mere connection with prosperity is for the sake of establishing the primacy of the word "speech" (vāk) as the object of the instrument.

It has been stated that the mind (*manas*) is a modification (*vikāra*) of food; however, since the vital breath (*prāṇa*) consists of water according to the passage concerning the attainment of the vital breath, it might be argued that the dissolution of the mind into the vital breath occurs because of the possibility of a relationship between material cause and its modification.
Do not say so; for the scriptural statement regarding their consisting of those [elements] intends their nourishment by them.
Therefore, they declare that here, as before, there is merely a conjunction, namely "mind" and "vital breath."

The Prāṇa, having eleven organs, subsequently enters into the Tejas, because it is heard in scripture thus; if it is argued that this contradicts scripture by assuming the attainment of other elements in the interim, we say no, because the conjunction with the Self is also stated.
When the Prāṇa meets the soul which has attained its own state, it does so along with the subtle elements extracted from its own body.
And the attainment of splendor shall be like the reaching of the ocean by the Yamunā after it has fallen into the Gaṅgā.

If it is argued that it is more reasonable for [the soul] to reside in fire alone—as in the passage "He who has resorted to fire as his body" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.8.1)—because there is no contradiction with such texts, and that the "umbrella-bearer logic" (where the term for the bearer applies to the umbrella) does not apply here; [we reply: this is not so, because elsewhere other elements are mentioned [as the soul's abode]. Furthermore, for the sake of the world's manifestation, the Lord previously made this [soul] threefold from what was formerly the elements.
And he [the author of the Sūtras] has already stated previously that the designation of "that" (Brahman) and "this" (the world) arises from abundance.
Right here one finds the heart; one becomes immortal here through the scripture.

For one who is devoted to the heart, departure [from the body] is not appropriate. Those who possess false secret doctrines desire a path and so forth for him; this [instruction regarding the heart] is not for the sake of attaining something else, as it is superior to that which possesses qualities, since there would be a loss of authority [if it were].
Therefore, by means of the statements beginning with "immortality" (amṛtatva) here, such a state of his is described.
When the karma of one who knows the Supreme has entirely dissolved at the time of death for the sake of experiencing [the fruits of past deeds],

then the subtle body’s following [the soul] for the purpose of its journey would be fruitless, since the soul is determined to be atomic in size. As for the claim of meeting [the soul] on the path, let it be so, provided it occurs with a body appropriate for that purpose— such is the response to the objection.
It must be stated that the cessation of all ignorance depends upon reaching the supreme state, and so forth.
At the beginning of the eon, this subtle body (liṅga), arising from the subtle elements and other constituents, is destroyed at the end of the eon;
it follows each individual sentient being, residing within the gross body whether that body be fixed or unfixed.
Described by the Sāṃkhyas as being like a curved object inside a bellows, it is thus celebrated.
The subtle portion of the previous form is considered here to be the seed of the subsequent body.
It is indeed said that bondage dissolves through the knowledge of reality; however, the claim that liberation occurs for one still alive without first departing [from the body] is worthless.
For it would be a contradiction of one's own words, like saying "my mother is barren," in the doctrine of liberation while living.
If he is liberated here in this life due to the awakening to reality, then this knower of reality, being embodied, would be subject to suffering.
If that suffering is false at that time, tell me when you accept its truth.

If it is argued that because embodied beings depart from this body while recollecting whichever state they intend, and thus go to that very state, therefore an equality of departure (utkrānti) is not possible— this is not so, because there is equality in respect to those [subtle elements] alone.
Indeed, inequality occurs in the case of the final cognition and so forth, according to the principle of the distinction between types of knowledge (vidyā) and other factors.
In a discourse based on some commonality of properties, there is no establishment of total identity that possesses necessity.

However, at the time when the departure of the soul (jīvotkrānti) is described, that refutation [of the elements] is applicable to the wise one; but since the departure of the elements occurs later, its application [to the wise one] might somehow be consistent.
Therefore, although this connection with the heart (hārdayoga) is common [to all], it is established here subsequently.
Even though this [process] is equal, the channels are unequal due to their different openings and the resulting difference in what is attained.

When an embodied being strives to attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and has already acquired a subtle body, what further need is there for the supreme attainment when one has already resorted to the Deity who is the very essence of bliss? Therefore, let the established tradition remain as it is: "Your own splendor is in the Supreme. This has been long established.
Let it not be so; for while the fruit arises from following pride, the supreme transition leads to the pacification of weariness.

"May there be attainment in the deity; let there be dissolution, for she is the source of all and capable of being perceived again"—this [argument] is subject to the fault of syntactical discordance (*vācyavairūpya*) due to its connection with what is improper. Furthermore, separation from the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) is not possible here, and the construction of creation is too cumbersome.
The journey of the transmigrating being along the path beginning with smoke has also been described as occurring through embracing that [Supreme Reality].
In the extremely subtle network of channels, it is not easy to distinguish the channel of liberation;

therefore, for a person being liberated, the movement through the channel at the crown of the head is not restricted. Let it not be so that the scriptural statement declaring immortality for one who goes upward by that [channel] is impossible.
Through the entry into one's own *nāḍīs* by means of the great splendor of the heart’s serenity, which is delighted by knowledge.

The one known as Hārda, being self-dependent, remains alone within the heart-lotus together with his own unimpaired perfection; having concealed his own body, he dwells as the householder of the seven worlds.
Within the wheel of channels (nāḍīcakra), he resides in the Suṣumnā, which sustains everything and extends from the navel to the crown of the head.
Having pierced [the heart] and cast out the seeker of liberation like an arrow shot through the central cavity, the Leader [leads him forth].

If it is argued that the upward movement of the yogi, which was described in the statement "by these very [rays]" as having recourse to the rays of the sun, is restricted to daytime and not possible at night due to a lack of logic—
that is not so; for even during nights, there are rays subtler than shadows, as is known from scriptural evidence.
If the heat of the rainy season and so forth does not occur at night, this should be understood according to the logic of the snowy day.

The death of all beings at night is considered inauspicious; therefore, it is argued that a yogi should die during the day, lest he should pass away at night—this would constitute a final, inferior death.

However, it has been stated that the *prārabdha-karma* (the karma whose effects have already begun) is exhausted only when its fixed time arrives. Thus, there is no delay whether it occurs by day or by night; for through knowledge (*vidyā*), he attains the Supreme.

Where liberation is reckoned for one individual by astrologers according to fixed planetary positions, that would be the final body; however, there is no exclusion of other [possibilities] beyond that.
For even here at the time of death, there is no such distinction between day and night, nor between different locations, and so forth.
And one should contemplate in this way: "They prepare a bed for him here and there," and so forth.

Even if a master of yoga should cast off his body during the sun’s southern course (dakṣiṇāyana), he attains union with the moon here; yet, through the practice of that [path] and the remembrance of it, he returns again.
Do not say so; for the principle previously stated is not contradicted here, and thus his union is indeed with the moon.
For the sake of rest, according to the law of the sun, she awaits the terrible time for the benefit of the world.

Furthermore, this [attainment] of the daughter of Jahnu (Ganga) is restricted by the karma already set in motion (*prārabdha-karma*), by which her own will was such; moreover, he became a Vasu and was not directly liberated.
Therefore, a yogi may attain liberation even during the night, whether on earth, among the ancestors, or among the gods.
Praise and censure would pertain to objects other than those two; however, the two paths were indeed spoken by Gītā.
Whatever else is not dexterous [in the body] is merged into the mind; that too, joined with it, is merged into the vital air (prāṇa);
that, together with them, is merged into the presiding deity (adhyakṣa); and he, possessing all those, is merged into the subtle group of elements.
Departure (utkrānti) occurs as a conjunction with these, and that conjunction with the Supreme is merely a state of close union.
Then, by means of the rays [of the sun], one should emerge through the Brahma-nāḍī; thus there is liberation during both day and night.
Having emerged through the aperture of Brahma and grasping the rays of the sun connected to the channels,
the yogi proceeds by that path to which offerings are sent by the hosts of gods coming forth to meet him;
this state of Maunkeya is established here by the Sage through five distinct methods of yoga.
May this path to liberation, ringing with the bell of freedom, lead us to the city on the far shore of the ocean of delusion.

The Upaniṣads teach different destinies in the various recensional branches (śākhā); therefore, by the logic that there is a disparity in knowledge, the destiny must also be disparate, and there is no fixed rule regarding the path beginning with light (arcir-ādi).
This is not so, because here, in all cases, the identity of that very same thing is established through recognition (pratyabhijñāna) by means of those respective [terms].
In this regard, everything such as deficiency, excess, and so forth, is established as non-contradictory.

The departure of Caidya and others— those born in Ayodhyā whether stationary or moving, such as Puṇḍarīka and his kin, Bhīṣma and the rest— who abide in the worlds of the *vyūha* manifestations arising from the sequence of worship; of the creators (*dhātṛ*) and their sons when their office has ended, and of others who desire to attain the state of Brahmā— that departure should be contemplated by those of sharp and broad intellects according to their respective fitness.

Marut has also attained the world of the gods together with Vatsara in the midst of the Ādityas; yet, due to a difference in conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), there is no identity between them here, but rather an option (*vikalpa*) because their status is equal.
Do not say so; for this one who is well-known as "he blows" (*pavate*) is the abode of the Marut deities.
Because it is said to be the sustainer of that, this non-conceptual unity with it is therefore appropriate.
Varuṇa and Indra, mentioned in the Kauṣītaki Āgama, are also protectors of creatures;

they must be placed somewhere. Otherwise, even if the scripture were not oppressive, that [other] scripture would be rendered fruitless. Therefore, it is incorrect to say that they should remain there after the recitation of the world of Vāyu.
Because of the connection, "after lightning, Varuṇa" (RV 1.24.7) occurs; since these two [words] are recited as subsequent, they are subsequent to that.

As for the fact that this non-human [chariot] possesses the capacity to lead one to the Supreme as heard in scripture, that remains uncontradicted even if it functions through an intermediary; moreover, that [capacity] is abundant when it is accompanied by the appropriate means.
Furthermore, that which is called the "mental" [chariot] is said to be the cause for attaining the world of Brahmā after the lightning.
Therefore, that leader is none other than he; know that the carrying across is accomplished by means of the lightning alone.
These [signs] may be places of enjoyment, or they may be the indicators of the paths beginning with Fire;
this [usage] exists merely by way of common parlance, so the term "time" (kāla) is not impossible [in this context].
Since its leadership and masculinity are clear, in some cases it performs the function of carrying [the breath], and likewise other functions are performed by others.
"When there is doubt, the determination [of meaning] comes from the remainder of the sentence"—thus they have declared that the words "fire" and so forth refer to the presiding deities.

Having heard this, the son of Dharma fell [toward it], and that flood of darkness—the host of those devoted to the three aims—would rush toward it; yet the wheel of the water-drawing machine at the river of the ancestors would be whirled about.
This path, beginning with the *arciḥ*, has been assigned by the Vedas to those who do not return.
In this regard, it is said that words such as "day," "fortnight," and "month" denote an exceeding carrier [of time], unlike other [such] words.

Previously, the attainment of the moon was described for those of meritorious deeds on the path beginning with smoke; that [attainment] is one thing. But the *sāyujya* (union) mentioned in the section on the science of *nyāsa* is of a different kind. Elsewhere, a different [attainment] is stated for those who travel by way of the rays of light, resulting in reaching the eighth lunar station. Thus, a well-established order has been set forth by those whose hearts are fixed in contemplation; and in this same manner, other subtle matters are explained.
Some living beings consider these [beings] to be certain of those beginning with Agni, the lord of the earthly world;
however, if there were identity of name here, the postulation of other intervening presiding deities would be a heavy burden.
Others, moreover, perceive the non-human being as the leader of the supreme Brahman who has reached his own station.
Because they are eternal, they declared all these to be likewise the eternal servants of Vaikuṇṭha.
Bādarāyaṇa spoke of these as the leaders who occupy the station of Brahmā;
for such [beings], there would indeed be the fitness for that state of transition, yet for those who have attained the Lord, nothing further remains to be known here.
Because of proximity, he is called "of the nature of Brahman" (brāhma), and liberation is said to be together with him, the dweller in the lotus.
The claim that this is "logical" is not correct, because it does not avoid contradicting the higher stations, the modes of movement, and other details set forth in various scriptural passages.

Jaimini has determined that this path beginning with light (arcir-ādi) leads to the supreme abode because of its connection with the act of going and because of the primary sense of the scriptural statement regarding Brahman; this is logical.
However, something must be said here: it leads those who know the higher [Brahman] and are established in the Brāhmaṇas associated with themselves.
Even those who are established in their own self as that very body, and those who are fully established through the various openings [of the senses], [attain the goal].
Those who meditate on individual souls— whether as conjoined with primordial nature (prakṛti) or in their pure state, according to their preference— or even those who,
having perceived the mass of insentient matter through themselves or through another,
meditate upon it: all of them, because their minds are fixed upon a mere symbol (pratīka), are not qualified for the path beginning with light (arcis).
Furthermore, this faultless transition resulting from meditation on the Brahman has already been stated as an indicative mark in the Sūtras.
The manner of restoration, the specific culmination of the application of karma and so forth,
the section on the divisions of knowledge, the pacification of obstacles to liberation through the power of supreme devotion,
the determination of the final state, and the attainment of rest in the various paths— all these are distinguished [in this work].
Whether liberation is attained directly or gradually—all this is not to be rejected by others who lack any other recourse.
Having attained this path of the gods upon the final fall of the body, he transcends the multitude of principles that end in darkness and crosses the celestial river there;
having obtained a divine body and the like, free from birth and abode, he goes to that station of Viṣṇu.
Blessed by the harmony of his heart, he enjoys great esteem until the moment of ascending his funeral pyre.

In the *Saṃghāta* hell there is no permanence whatsoever, nor is there the absence of the elements such as earth; likewise, for the Blessed One of perfect and boundless power, nothing is unachievable by means of the *paryaṅka* posture and so forth.
[This refutes] the arguments of the logicians that upward movement would be futile for the sake of attaining pervasiveness, and so on.
May she, who is independent and whose purpose is wondrous, pacify the chatter of those intoxicated by the most trivial things.
Where existence and non-existence are both present without qualification, there a contradiction arises;
yet, even when the pervasion is obstructed, the establishment of one's own object occurs through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) due to its own superior intrinsic power.
This is seen and desired by all, for if it were not so, there would indeed be no means of valid cognition other than direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The contradiction regarding direct perception, or the mutual [contradiction] such as sleeping on a banyan leaf, and other such wonders, should be inferred in this manner.

There is oneness for one studying the excellent path in the assembly of the Brāhma-vidyā; in that wind, there is also the scriptural mention of the world of the gods, as well as the connection with Varuṇa and others above the lightning.
The leaders, ending with the non-human [beings], lead those who know it to the supreme state; such is this path.
In the third quarter of the fourth chapter, the course [of the soul] has been thus described through the topical sections (adhikaraṇas).
It has been stated by the [first] quarters that there is the abandonment of both those of gross form and those of subtle form who possess a mass of sins;
by the final [quarter], it declares the unconditioned great bliss of one whose collection of adjuncts (*upādhi*) has been shaken off.

Here, the manifestation of the Self is to be contemplated through three *adhikaraṇas* (sections) and three meters; thus there are two *peṭikās* (chapters). Both of these arise from itself and are not dependent on an external adjunct, O Lord.

If the manifestation of this nature of the inner self— which is unceasingly self-luminous as "I"— were established [by that means], there would be no fruit whatsoever, as it would be no different from deep sleep.
Therefore, the liberated one assumes another body, like that of a deity, based on the term "form" (rūpa).
Let it not be so; for here, by the word "by itself," the result would be the negation (hrasva) [of the suffix], since the meaning is established as being expressive of the form.

Those who have declared that "this abiding in the nature of one's own eternal Self is the attainment" [of liberation] do not understand that this alone would not be the fruit of knowledge, for it is eternally established and not something to be accomplished.
However, even an already established reality becomes a "fruit" through its penetration by what is to be accomplished; that [penetration], moreover, is the destruction of ignorance and the like.
Or rather, the aphorism beginning with "He is called liberated" (mukta) does not contradict the fact that there is experience for one who has attained perfection.

At that time, the soul shines forth with a greater degree of bliss than its own form which was previously appearing as eternal; even when there is merely the manifestation of the perfected state (*siddha*), the term "attainment" (*abhiniṣpatti*) is employed.
This attainment is said to be adventitious, consisting in the absolute abandonment of the contraction of the intellect.
At that time, the word "own" (svena) expresses that which is characterized by a nature free from obstacles.

Generally, whatever is seen in this embodied self— who is a treasure-house of faultless virtues— or in those two manifestations of his power during meditative absorption, becomes like a mere speck compared to the experience of liberation;
for that entire [experience] becomes as sweet as the ocean of nectar when it is mixed with a flood of sugar-candies.
Therefore, one who says that there is no fruit in the self-luminosity of the Self is as pitiable as a tortoise in a well.
Just as the Mallikā jasmine produces a pure blossom at its proper time, free from any coloring adjuncts, so too does the Lord’s compassion produce a fruit equal to that of a Sūri,
wherein all obstructions have been stilled. Therefore, even when such an expansion of wisdom is adventitious, it remains free from obstruction.
The sequence of one’s own giving has been described here for the inward-turned seeker who has attained perfection.
Some, disregarding the distinction of liberation as being directed toward this side [of existence], maintain that there is only the experience of one's own self;
in that case, it must be considered whether the cessation of the experience of Brahman occurs through an external condition or by itself.
Since defects exist in both cases, it is therefore appropriate to use the term "liberation" here only figuratively.
Even regarding the various distinctions such as sālokya and the rest, this path should be discerned by those who are attentive.

"The individual soul and the Lord are eternally distinct; for the Scripture here says 'together' regarding the enjoyment of the liberated one, and Smṛti speaks of equality endowed with supremacy. Therefore, let it be that he shines forth as separate from Him.
"Do not say so; for in liberation, the Reality indeed manifests, and thus the aspect of perceiving the difference between these two is accepted [only until then]."
But once the identity of the body with the self is established, the perception of it as being restricted to its own nature is not possible here.
If, as stated in the mantra, co-existence exists in the state of the enjoyer, then the Brahman would not be the Pradhāna;

therefore, let it be so in its state as the object of enjoyment, since that is appropriate according to the explanation of the Brāhmaṇa. In either case, because of the nature of Brahman, the other [the world] would have to be distinct from it here; and this [objection] is merely a hollow argument.
Once difference is established, the abandonment of its own inherent persistence is what must be demonstrated here by the Sūtra.

That supremacy which is heard in scripture regarding equality is not [meant] here in every respect; this has also been studied [by us], for just as there might be a statement regarding a stone and gold being equal in their capacity to support a weight, so too is that statement used here.
Thus, while that state of having a body remains, it is established by the abundance of various uncontradicted scriptural authorities.
The statement beginning with "By the Brāhmaṇa alone," etc., proclaims equality, for it is likewise studied as being of such a nature.

"What would be the fruit of [the Self] being knowledge? Let such similarity to Brahman exist through qualities; let that [similarity] exist here through attributes that are not its true nature; rather, let there be the manifestation of the form of pure consciousness alone.
Thus, the student's two proposed positions are rejected due to contradiction with both types of scriptural authority.
Then, having shaken off the twofold manifestation, he brought about its non-occurrence through the illumination of the perfected reality.
The two terms *mukti* and *kaivalya* are recited consecutively in the lists of synonyms;

and since *kaivalya* is defined as the abandonment of association with anything else (*anyayoga-tyajana*), how can there be a connection between this [term] and the subject (the self) and its attributes?
Do not say so, for here there is indeed nothing other than the very nature of Brahman that exists as something established in itself.
A substance cannot be devoid of qualities; this pair of substrata is free from any flaw.

If it is argued that even for the Creator (Dhātṛ) and others, a multitude of instruments must be required, and that the same should apply to the liberated one whose will is true, that is false, because such a position cannot withstand logical scrutiny. It is accepted that there is a dependence on substances and so forth; however, in that case, dependence on merit and its opposite is untenable.
There would be no frustration of one's desires, because there is no ulterior motive and because the will of the gods is uniform.

Just as the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of this entire universe proceed from the Will of the Universal Creator through a succession of diverse volitions, so too do the actions of those eternally liberated ones proceed here; by virtue of their uninterrupted function, these actions are distinct at every moment, yet they flow in such a continuous stream.
The directness of that cognition, however, persists incessantly and unbreakably, like the cognition of Brahman.

The state of having true resolve belongs to the meritorious, beginning with the lords of subjects, as it is observed in the case of human undertakings and desires, whereas it is otherwise seen in the creation of various other living beings.
Therefore, the success or failure of these successions of desires depends upon the merit and demerit of those beings.
However, the desire to act mentioned in the case of one who is liberated has its object unimpeded; thus, the presence of gradation is not a fault.

In the Sūtra, even one who is liberated is described as having no other lord; therefore, who could be his superior? Since it is stated by the Śruti itself that he is "self-ruling" (svarāṭ), there is a contradiction for those [opponents] previously established [their position]. Do not say so; here, the status of being a subordinate, which was prohibited against others than the Lord, is what is being rejected.
He who is recited as the "Self-Lord of the universe" and its "Lord"—that lordship of His is indeed unassailable.

The author of the Sūtras, rejecting the conflicting views of the sages— some of whom declare the liberated one to be bodiless, while others describe his various births, or his learning and activities such as singing and playing music—
he asserts his own position: that both [conditions] are possible for one who is independent.
And all that may arise even without action would be equal to that [result] of one who has attained the Supreme Brahman.

Since merit and the like do not exist in liberation, the state of being devoid of a body conditioned by them is not a defect; and when one who is fit for suffering abandons the body, the presence of an auspicious body on the side of sentient beings is also not contradicted.
This being so, what kind of state of liberation would have been indicated here by the Sage?
It is not so, because the intention here is not to establish an absence of restraint regarding the voluntary assumption of a body.

If there were various bodies simultaneously attained by a person who has reached equality with Brahman, then their nature would necessarily involve pervasion; thus, the prior [doctrine of] atomicity would be abandoned.
This is not so, for the establishment of pervasion occurs through the statement regarding the entry into the universe, which has that [atomicity] as its cause.
It is not possible to refute the destiny ordained for Saubhari and others by means of their equality with Brahmā.
If there were simultaneity of many bodies, how could this liberated one be minute (aṇu) as their sustainer?
If it is argued that he sustains them through the medium of consciousness, then, being possessed of all-pervading awareness, he would sustain everything at all times.
Not so; for the power of the liberated one, though omnipotent, is restricted in its scope by his own will.
Previously, through the power of such yoga, even the bondage of karma had to be considered while assuming many bodies.
The sages have designated the power known as the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) as being enveloped by its own actions;
thus, although the intellect (*buddhi*) of the person is partless, it is accepted as having manifold transformations.
Let that [Self] be so; for according to such statements as "like the tip of a hair," it may be atomic (*aṇu*) in liberation, yet it may also be infinite.
It would not be so in the case of the Jaina and other systems, because there is no loss of the uniformity of the transformation once it has been fully realized.
Indeed, as each individual soul departs, withering occurs in the branches of the tree;

therefore, when the veil has been removed, primary infinity would belong to this [Self] without any further gate. Let it not be so; for in the case of the branches, "destruction" refers to the cessation of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) which determines the locus of experience.
By the logic of the field and so forth, this [agent] would be devoid of intentionality; thus, the abandonment [of action] is established.
"Being one, yet not one; distinct from another, yet not distinct; liberated by its own nature;
the enjoyer of all that it desires by itself"—thus do they wander in the arguments of the Pṛthukakṣība.
Let them examine [this] for their own words are contradicted and they violate hundreds of Śrutis, due to the figurative interpretation (anyaparya) of those various statements.
May those whose minds are arrogant due to their reliance on Jainism abandon quarrels and take refuge in the true path.

It is traditionally taught that one obtains everything through mere volition (*saṃkalpa*), and it has been aphorized that there is no fixed rule regarding the assumption of bodies according to one's own will; therefore, [your objection] is merely "grinding what is already ground.

That is not so, for the intention of the author of the Sūtras in stating such lack of fixed rule—concerning the process of voluntarily assuming multiple bodies—is a restriction on the course of scriptural passages that would otherwise be mutually contradictory.

Although it was previously stated that the liberated one is of the nature of the Supreme and non-different from It—thus [establishing] the aspect of activity—even so, the "supreme equality" heard here is unshakeable;
for even the arising of everything proceeds from That by mere volition. Thus [the opponent] offers this counter-argument.
At the end of his office, he cuts short his own activity while establishing equality of enjoyment for the other two who possess activity.
The wise have calculated *sāyujya* (union) as equality in enjoyment (*bhoga-sāmya*), because it is not contradicted by the power of words and other criteria;
however, that [equality] is not possible unless there is equality in activity (*vyāpāra-sāmya*), for that would entail the loss of the relish in one's own actions.
Therefore, even the world-engagement beginning with creation is equal for the liberated soul to that of Brahmā.
Let it not be so; for how could that characteristic belong to both that [entity] and another?

In certain passages concerning the account of creation, liberated souls (muktas) are nowhere mentioned as being the cause of the world; let there be freedom of action for them as they have studied [the scriptures], but from that it does not follow that they possess the capacity to originate the universe.
Because their cognitions regarding the Lord—who is the object of enjoyment in every form—are equal, there is equality in their enjoyment.
In the Ānandavallī, equality was indeed reckoned by the Lord as being in bliss alone.

Desiring to speak of the blisses accompanied by joy, she intends to describe them as being a hundredfold greater than the human bliss— even that of a desireless Vedic scholar— and extending in succession up to that of Brahmā (Viriñci).
How could this lower, painful state, though desired, be more extensive than those respective enjoyments in the case of one who is liberated?
That would indeed be true; for this is merely a partial description of one who resembles a person dear to Mukunda.

The Śruti declares here the infinity of bliss in such passages as "from whence words turn back"; and this has been stated by the eminent teacher Yamunācārya: "Its cessation occurs merely from exhaustion. Indeed, there can be no measure of this bliss, even if one were to recite hundreds of injunctions; its worshipper is like the sky [in its vastness].
And it has been said: "What difference is there between a mountain and the lord of the oceans when both have sunk into the water?"
The universe is not the body of the liberated one, for it is observed that there is no non-separate establishment (*apṛthaksiddhi*) between them;

nor is it its material cause (*upādāna*), because in that case it would be improper to speak of Him as "all-powerful" (*sarvaśakti*). He does not desire to create what is impossible; His will is unimpeded regarding everything other than that.
Even when activities differ, an absence of unevenness in their essence is seen somewhere in the world.

The favor of a sovereign, stabilized by the specific nature of various services rendered, bestows upon his servant equality with himself, with the sole exception of the insignia of lordship that the master himself does not desire.
In this same way, that which cannot be obtained by others is attained by those who have approached the compassionate Lord as their refuge.
The state [of the yogin] is one in which the suspicion of regression has been shaken off, which possesses the flavor of the unconditioned, and which is characterized by stability.

Regarding this, some say that the final Sūtra constitutes a separate topical section (adhikaraṇa) because it attains its own direct meaning; they argue that the word "this" (imam) must refer to something to be excluded from repetition, and thus a doubt arises [regarding what that is].
However, such a view is not seen in the Bhāṣya and other works, and it is more straightforward to regard this Sūtra as a supplement to the preceding one.
Furthermore, there may be the suspicion of partiality regarding the creation of the entire world, due to the consequence of repetition.

The Lord, having gradually released the individual soul (jīva) engaged in the staff-dance that accompanies the aesthetic delight of the play of creation and so forth, enjoys [him] as one blessed by union;

for it is declared in the sacred tradition that He does not cause him to return here again due to the absolute cessation of karma— thus, there is the subsiding of any doubt arising from statements regarding the inexhaustible fruits rooted in karma.

The essential points of the fourth quarter of the final chapter are as follows: Liberation (*apavarga*) is the manifestation of one's own nature, which is the perception of one's own true form as determined by the absence of limiting adjuncts (*nirupadhi*).

It is the vision of that which is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) together with its own modes (*svaprakāra*), which are adorned with the crown of the *tadvacchati* [the state of being conjoined with Him].

Furthermore, there is the attainment of perfection through mere volition (*saṅkalpa*), followed by freedom from the constraints of necessity (*niyama*). Upon attaining equality with Brahman (*brāhmasāmyaprāpti*), there is the relinquishing of those portions of characteristics that pertain to that [limited] state. This is the essence of the fourth quarter of the final chapter.
Having become the agent, one should bring forth meditation and its power from this hut-like prison of the body;
then, having emerged through the path of the *brahman-āḍī*, one should attain the goal which is self-luminous and accessible by the excellent path.
Furthermore, by the Supreme Brahman, who creates his own desired objects at will, there is the experience of the highest enjoyment alone.
How could one established in the Māyāvāda doctrine possibly reconcile the essence of the final chapter with the doctrine of equality?
Because it analyzes the distinctions between honor and dishonor and so forth, it belongs to the first part, the section on karma;
because it recites immediately after [the section on karma] such passages as "or various deities," it belongs to the middle part, the section on deities;
and because this section explains the nature of differentiation and so forth while refuting the Saugatas and others, it belongs to this [final] part.
In the three sections of Mīmāṃsā, there is nowhere even the slightest scent of falsehood.
This voyage across the ocean of the three Vedas has been described by the teachers who act as its helmsmen;
it clearly leads one to the further shore of the knowledge of the true meaning of reality. However, regarding liberation, another path must be observed.
In matters requiring action, the authors of the Kalpasūtras have occasionally stated various distinctions arising from doubts concerning what ought to be done.
Even if this were the case in some instances regarding reality, that too would not be false, for the cognition of the portion relevant to oneself remains valid.
When the weight of the sequence of reasoning that is exclusively devoted to the conclusions of the Vedas is maintained, the mass of mountains becomes like cotton;
the chatter of others, which is like a heap of darkness, is eclipsed by the light of the sun of the realization of Brahman established therein;
and all other methods become mere servants in the sole sovereignty of the means to liberation.
Other human goals are rivals to but a single drop of spray from the unique ocean of the nectar of liberated bliss.
Having first distinguished between the higher and the lower through unerring scriptures regarding the categories of reality,
one who feels intense fear for cyclic existence and possesses intense, perfected passion for the supreme attainment,
having mastered a particular branch of knowledge along with its auxiliaries, remains with internal obstacles stilled.
Having attained [this state], he enjoys the bliss of Brahman, free from all limiting conditions and beyond return; such is the meaning of the Vedic revelation.

May this series of essential points from the chapters, sections, and topics of the Brahmasūtra— which is like a ladder for climbing the chariot-path of the three ages, which uproots every kind of malicious and wicked mind, and which is skilled at pacifying the exhaustion of the virtuous through the realization of truth— grant you perfect contentment.

In this section, which consists of one hundred and fifty-six chapters and clearly delineates the divisions of the topics, may some follow what we have said; for what is the use of others who are fortunate only in their criticisms?
Seeing this entire universe as subservient to those whose minds are bound and enslaved by the machinery of the three qualities (guṇas), [one should not concern oneself with them].
Since our Lord has become our witness, we do not here engage in idle jesting.

The entire universe, with its distinctions of substance and so forth, has been clearly expounded in the *Tattvamuktākalāpa*; here, however, the form of the *Śārīraka* [Brahmasūtra] is presented in a firm and systematic arrangement from beginning to end.
Therefore, like nectar vomited forth from the ocean by those who have bound their faith unweariedly, these two works should be held by learned masters, passing them from hand to hand.

Thus, having set out upon the path proclaimed in the *Śārīraka*, with tears welling in their eyes, they were led by the pure-hearted sages who had crossed to the further shore of the ocean of *māyā* and were sent forth toward them;
[they were guided] by many ornaments for the heart, which were fashioned from the essence of the *Upaniṣad-sūtras*.
Having adorned her like divine apsarases, they honor her for the sake of her becoming a goddess worthy of worship.

Ranganatha himself rejoiced, having made me resound with these verses— which possess the fragrance of jasmine from the braided hair of wisdom, which shine with the pure light of the efforts of wise men in service, and which are graced by the assembly of the Vedas— blowing them like the conch Pāñcajanya through the greatness of the Praṇava.

From the vast ocean of the Upaniṣads, which is the nectar of immortality, the lord of sages named the Teacher of the Unerring Vedas— the son of Parāśara— churned it with the churning-sticks of his aphorisms and extracted its essence.
That very essence, thus extracted by the Lord of Ascetics, who has ascended the mountain of the syllable Om, now rests within my heart.
May that horse-faced one (Hayagrīva), together with my gurus who are like swan-like clouds for the sake of debate, [protect me].
